sources.title: Alex Hormozi's millionaire blueprint: own equity, focus on one thing, build offers, compound patiently
sources.originalTitle: If I Wanted to Become a Millionaire In 2024, This is What I'd Do [FULL BLUEPRINT]
sources.summary: A three-level blueprint to a million-dollar net worth. Own equity instead of earning income, go all in on one avatar/product/channel, craft a high-value offer, remove yourself so the business has enterprise value, and compound with patience and reputation.

principles.text: Own your way to wealth instead of earning it; equity plus time beats income eroded by taxes and expenses.
principles.quote: there's two ways that you can become a millionaire you can earn your way there or you can own your way there and the faster way is to own your way there

principles.text: Don't diversify early; put your time and attention on one opportunity until it overflows.
principles.quote: the wealthiest people in the world go all in on one income stream and they keep adding it up over and over and over again until it overflows

principles.text: Market is the strongest variable, then offer, then persuasion. Pick a hungry crowd with pain, purchasing power, easy targeting and growth.
principles.quote: the market is always going to be the strongest variable in how much money you make

principles.text: To reach $1M+, pick one avatar, one product and one channel and get better at it instead of adding complexity.
principles.quote: One Avatar one product one channel this is the simplest formula to getting $2 million plus

principles.text: Make goals about activities, not outcomes. Do 100 primary actions over 100 days.
principles.quote: if you do 100 primary actions over 100 days you'll usually get the first result that you ultimately want

principles.text: Remove the founder from the business so it has enterprise value; boring, long-term compounding is what makes you rich.
principles.quote: boring is what makes you rich

sources.title: Alex Hormozi on Diary of a CEO: Offers, leverage and skill stacking from $1,000 to $100M
sources.originalTitle: The Man That Makes Millionaires: How To Turn $1,000 Into $100 Million!: Alex Hormozi | E235
sources.summary: Hormozi recounts losing everything in 2016, then rebuilding by licensing his gym turnaround system. He explains how he thinks about offers, value, leverage, skill stacking and choosing where to apply a skill, plus the mindset (pain, input/output math) that keeps him going.

principles.text: Make an offer so good people feel stupid saying no; if not enough say yes, improve the offer.
principles.quote: I just have to make things that are so good that people will feel stupid saying no and if we can't get enough people to say yes we need to make the offer better

principles.text: Value = dream outcome x likelihood of achievement, divided by time delay and effort/sacrifice.
principles.quote: we boiled down value into four variables

principles.text: Repackage what you have for a narrow niche that values it most to raise prices.
principles.quote: we redid the entire business model around finding only that Niche

principles.text: Leverage is output over input; stack labor, media, capital and technology to get more for each step.
principles.quote: leverage as the difference between what you put in and what you get out

principles.text: Sell the same skill to customers who value it most; bigger clients pay far more for identical work.
principles.quote: find the people who value what you have the most

principles.text: Stack complementary skills; each new skill makes the others more valuable.
principles.quote: every skill you add to your skill tool belt makes the rest of your skills more valuable

sources.title: 13 Years of Brutal Business Truths: Priorities, Talent, Brand and Getting Better
sources.originalTitle: 13 Years Of Brutally Honest Business Advice in 90 Mins
sources.summary: Alex Hormozi compresses 13 years of business lessons into eleven truths. Core themes: sell premium before selling to the masses, solve the real constraint, hire A-level talent, get better rather than bigger, protect deep-work time, and build brand through consistent delivery.

principles.text: Sell premium to rich people first; the middle and mass market require huge infrastructure and efficiency.
principles.quote: Sell to rich people until you have the money to sell all the poor people. The middle is where you get killed.

principles.text: Most founders lack priorities, not information. Define current state, desired state and obstacle before working.
principles.quote: if you can't clearly state current state, desired state, obstacle, you're running around like a chicken with your head cut off.

principles.text: Hiring A-level talent at higher pay is one of the biggest arbitrages in business; output multiple dwarfs cost.
principles.quote: I still think to this day one of the biggest arbitrage that exist in business is paying A talent A wages to get 10X the output.

principles.text: Better leads to growth, bigger leads to bloat. Growth is a lagging indicator of getting better.
principles.quote: Fundamentally, growth is a lagging indicator. The things you do to create growth are the leading indicators.

principles.text: Protect the first hours of your day for the highest-leverage work and let non-existential fires burn.
principles.quote: I work uninterrupted for the first four to six hours of my day on the things that I think have the highest leverage in the business.

principles.text: Break your money-making system into its smallest input actions and ask why you can't 10x them to find the constraint.
principles.quote: you can quickly understand where the constraint of the business is by simply asking why can't we 10x this?

sources.title: Alex Hormozi on the Entrepreneur Life Cycle: Focus, Hiring, Skill Acquisition and Courage
sources.originalTitle: The Man That Makes Millionaires: Turn $0 to $10k With This Step By Step Formula! Alex Hormozi
sources.summary: Hormozi walks through the six-stage entrepreneur cycle, why splitting attention kills most founders, how to hire and train (barrels vs. ammunition, 3Ds, specific feedback), and how to learn skills through volume plus feedback loops. He also covers choosing ideas (pain, profession, passion), standing out by being yourself, and defusing fear by playing it out in specifics.

principles.text: Fear lives in the vague. Play the worst case out in specifics and it shrinks.
principles.quote: I think fear exists in the vague not in the specific

principles.text: Pick one business and stick with it. Splitting attention across ventures is the biggest career mistake.
principles.quote: the biggest entrepreneurial mistakes I've made in my career have all come from splitting my attention every one of them

principles.text: Commitment means eliminating alternatives. Give yourself no way out to get through the valley of despair.
principles.quote: I Define commitment as the elimination of Alternatives

principles.text: Business ideas come from pain, profession or passion. You only need one, and personal pain makes the most compelling story.
principles.quote: business idea is typically come from one of three PS so it comes from a pain that you're currently experiencing a past profession

principles.text: Standing out means leaning into being yourself. You can't beat someone at being them, but you can beat them at being you.
principles.quote: you're not going to beat me at being me but you'll beat me at being you

principles.text: Learn skills through high volume plus feedback loops: do 100 reps, study the top 10%, then repeat with those lessons.
principles.quote: you do a hundred of those and then you say what are the top 10% of these okay what did these top 10% have different than the other 90

sources.title: 13 Years of Marketing Advice: Hormozi's 13 Rules for Scaling Ads, Offers and LTV to CAC
sources.originalTitle: 13 Years of Marketing Advice in 85 Mins
sources.summary: Alex Hormozi condenses 13 years and nine companies into 13 marketing rules. Core themes: start cheap or free to create flow, scale with more then better then new, obsess over hooks, build around LTV to CAC, and narrow to a specific avatar. He also covers the four ways to advertise and the value equation.

principles.text: Start free or cheap to get flow, then raise price 20% per batch until conversion times price drops.
principles.quote: after that every five I just go up by 20%. ... And you just keep going up by 20% until the conversion rate times the price goes down.

principles.text: Create flow, monetize flow, then add friction. Run volume through the system to see where it breaks.
principles.quote: create flow, monetize flow, then add friction. And so, it's like you have to run water through the machine.

principles.text: Scale with more, then better, then new. Spend most effort on more and better of what works.
principles.quote: the vast majority of entrepreneurs want to spend 80% of their time on doing new stuff when really they should spend 90% of their time doing more and better of what is already working for them.

principles.text: Put most effort into the hook and first 5 seconds, since the front end offers 100-300% gains while the back end offers far less.
principles.quote: I can absolutely get CTRs from 1% to 4% by just optimizing the hell out of the front end. And that's a 4x increase.

principles.text: LTV to CAC (on gross profit) is the key metric; aim for at least 3:1 and collect CAC back within 30 days.
principles.quote: the rule of thumb is that you want to have at least three to one on LTV to CAC. But again, LTV is not lifetime revenue, it's lifetime gross profit

principles.text: Squeeze winning ads: re-shoot with new backgrounds, props, pacing, filters or re-ordering to multiply a winner.
principles.quote: if you if you take one thing from this video from advertising, squeeze the living hell out of the winners.

sources.title: How to sell better than 99%: Hormozi's 4-hour sales masterclass on closing, objections and scaling teams
sources.originalTitle: How to Sell Better than 99% Of People (4 HOUR ULTIMATE GUIDE)
sources.summary: Compilation of Hormozi's best sales talks: closing as logical decision help, the three-bucket objection map (circumstances, others, self), the CLOSER framework, tone and conviction, and how to scale and compensate a sales team. Includes real case numbers on show rate, close rate and in-house vs outsourced sales.

principles.text: Every objection is a distortion that falls into three buckets: circumstances (time, money, fit), other people, or self. Peel them layer by layer.
principles.quote: the objections that people offer you where they cast their power to are distortions of reality

principles.text: Handle obstacles before price is mentioned; after price they become much harder objections. Kill zombies up front.
principles.quote: it's much easier to address things before you ask for money than after if you do it after it's called an objection

principles.text: Close by resolving the concern and asking again. Sales volume is proportional to how many times you ask.
principles.quote: if you do not ask for the sale you will not get it that is a promise once you ask if you ask again you'll increase the likelihood that they buy

principles.text: Sell the destination, not the process. Keep the pitch under three minutes and tell short stories instead of features.
principles.quote: sell the vacation not the plane fright

principles.text: Best closers listen about twice as much as they talk and answer questions with questions.
principles.quote: the best best salespeople listen twice as much as they talk

principles.text: Conviction fixes tone. Belief in the product transfers more than script skill, so fix the product and reread testimonials.
principles.quote: conviction will correct your tone if you believe in what you sell you will say it the right way

sources.title: Alex Hormozi's Ultimate Sales Blueprint: multipliers, training, scripting and closing
sources.originalTitle: The Ultimate Sales Training for 2026 [Full Course]
sources.summary: A full sales course drawn from 4,000+ closes. Most revenue gains come from what happens around the sale: selling seven days, sub-minute lead response, 15-minute slots, lead allocation and show-up rates. Inside the call he teaches proof-promise-plan, the pain cycle, AAA overcomes, and never answering a question you can't predict.

principles.text: Sell seven days a week; weekends add about 29% more selling days and lift show-up rates.
principles.quote: and so if you want to immediately increase your sales by 29% sell on weekends

principles.text: Respond to leads within one minute; speed of response is the single biggest lever on close rate.
principles.quote: if you can contact a lead within 60 seconds of them showing interest or opting in or giving you their contact information you have a 391 per increase in the likelihood that you can close the Prospect

principles.text: Route the best leads to the best closers instead of round-robin; it cuts net waste.
principles.quote: the best leads should go to the best closers and the worst leads should go to the worst closers

principles.text: Never answer a detail question blind; ask a question back to find what they actually want.
principles.quote: you as a Salesman should never answer questions you don't already know the answers to

principles.text: Pain drives motivation; spend your time on the prospect's pain, not on the product.
principles.quote: the pain is the pitch

principles.text: Never discount to close; change terms or components instead, or re-anchor higher.
principles.quote: never change price to close a deal now you can change terms so if you want to change how much they pay today then you have a payment plan

sources.title: How Hormozi would fix a $480K couples-coaching business: offer, ratio, events, ads
sources.originalTitle: If I Wanted To Scale A Service Business In 2026, Here's What I'd Do
sources.summary: Hormozi live-consults a supply-constrained coaching business burning cash on a 5-day challenge funnel. He fixes capacity by changing the delivery ratio, collapses two offers into one simple high-ticket offer, pulls cash forward with layaway, and turns daily organic content and in-person events into the ad and renewal engine.

principles.text: Before building a new product, ask what problem you are solving and whether it can be solved without a new business.
principles.quote: the number one question I ask when they just vomit a whole bunch of information on me is I just say like, what problem are we solving?

principles.text: Fix supply constraints by choosing one lever: price, delivery ratio, productizing, or hiring. Each builds a different business.
principles.quote: When you are supply constrained, you can either raise the price so fewer people buy and the people who buy you get paid more for or you change the ratio of delivery

principles.text: Keep the offer to a few high-value components. Extra bonuses create unused value and cancellations.
principles.quote: each thing we add on its own should be worth the price of the whole thing.

principles.text: Pull cash forward with layaway: flexible payment plans, but delivery starts only after an upfront amount is paid.
principles.quote: you can do layaway, right? Which is you can pay on whatever plan you want, but you won't get delivery until you pay X amount.

principles.text: Build an ad machine: let normal business operations and customer experiences generate the marketing so growth self-sustains.
principles.quote: I want to have the normal function of the business create the marketing for the business.

principles.text: Test creative cheaply through organic posts first; video is high variance, so run many and keep the winners.
principles.quote: Video has higher volatility than images do. But your best ads will be video and your worst ads will be video.

sources.title: How to grow any business: Hormozi's four business shapes and the hairy problem each must solve
sources.originalTitle: How To Grow ANY Business FASTER (Masterclass)
sources.summary: Hormozi argues every business is one of four shapes (e-commerce, service, education/info, software), each with a built-in growth curve and a core "hairy problem." What founders mistake for a broken business is usually a feature of the model, and solving that problem is where the enterprise value and competitive edge come from.

principles.text: Your biggest pain is usually a feature of your business model, not a bug. Find the hairy problem and focus effort there.
principles.quote: most people think that there is something inherently wrong with their business when it is in reality a feature of this business, not a bug.

principles.text: Value the hairy problem by the enterprise value it unlocks, then fund it accordingly instead of doubting the business.
principles.quote: once you can appropriately appreciate the value of the hairy problem that you're trying to solve, you can then put the right resources towards solving it

principles.text: E-commerce is cash and supply constrained; spend about 70% on brand and top of funnel so you aren't a commoditized smash-and-grab.
principles.quote: The most successful companies that persist over a long period of time in e-commerce tend to have a 7030 split in terms of how they spend their money. 70 going towards top offunnel and brand awareness

principles.text: In service businesses talent is the bottleneck, so recruiting, onboarding and training are core. You're really in the teaching business.
principles.quote: if you're in a service business, you're actually in a teaching business. You have to teach your talent how to do what they do.

principles.text: Education revenue is unsticky, so split pricing: high price for the one-time value, lower recurring price for consumable pieces.
principles.quote: the appropriate billing structure is very high high price price to value for the onetime thing that is inherently valuable but has no recurring and then make sure the recurring elements of the business are also appropriately priced which might be significantly lower

principles.text: Software wins on revenue retention and friction removal: build for retention, add a viral loop, and strip friction from the outcome.
principles.quote: you cannot actually make something good. What you do is you find a good outcome that everybody wants. That's the easy part. And that you remove all friction between where someone is and them getting that outcome.

sources.title: How Hormozi would take a roofing startup from $32K to $250K/month in 90 days
sources.originalTitle: How I Would Build a $10M Service Business (If I Had to Start Over)
sources.summary: Hormozi coaches a two-month-old roofing contractor by finding the highest-return motion (high-volume repairs), then layering a menu close, VSSLs, a maintenance membership and speed upcharges on a door-knocking engine. The business went from under $32K to about $250K in 90 days.

principles.text: Focus scarce time and money on the highest-return activity you can already do reliably.
principles.quote: I want to focus all efforts on the highest return stuff that you can do right now.

principles.text: Look for work other people cast aside, then systemize it so it earns strong gross profit at high volume.
principles.quote: I love when there it's like when when there's something that's been cast aside by other people, right? Like no one wants to do this particular thing, but then you orient a business in such a way that you can actually make really good gross profits on it.

principles.text: Use the menu close: unsell what they don't need, prescribe what they do, offer A or B, then card on file.
principles.quote: Step one is that Amanda's going to unsell what they don't need. >> Mhm. >> So, she gains trust.

principles.text: Sell speed: let customers pay to move to the front of the line. Same work, more margin.
principles.quote: If you're ever not sure how to add margin to a business, especially if you're supply constraint, meaning you have more people who want your stuff than you have the ability to do, add speed incentives for people to just move to the front of the line.

principles.text: Tack a maintenance membership onto the end of a service to turn one-time customers into recurring ones and raise LTV.
principles.quote: if you can tack that on the end, it takes the business from being one-time business to recurring business, which is obviously significantly more valuable and dramatically increases LTV.

principles.text: Make commissions concrete per action so reps know exactly how many doors equal how much money.
principles.quote: Want to go make 10 bucks? Knock that door. Want to make another 10 bucks? Knock that door.

sources.title: Lead magnets: how to get 3-5x more customers from the same traffic with a mini offer
sources.originalTitle: Watch This To Generate 1000s of Leads (In Any Niche)
sources.summary: Alex explains why asking cold traffic to "book a call" wastes most visitors, and how a free or low-cost mini offer that solves a narrow problem converts far more leads without extra ad spend. He covers three lead magnet types, four delivery formats, naming and testing, and a CTA formula.

principles.text: Offer a mini offer that solves a narrow problem and exposes the next problem your core offer solves.
principles.quote: you offer something kind of like a mini offer that's a complete solution to a narrow problem. And so, it's typically lower cost or free just to see who's interested and raises their hand

principles.text: A lead magnet lifts conversion on the same traffic, so it drops straight to the bottom line.
principles.quote: you're actually not going to get more traffic. You're just going to convert a higher percentage of it. And this is why it's such an easy strategy for businesses to do.

principles.text: Test the packaging and headline of a lead magnet more than its contents.
principles.quote: you can change how many people want your lead magnet by 2, three, 10x simply changing the headline of your lead magnet itself rather than changing any of the contents.

principles.text: Sell at the point of greatest deprivation: give the first need away, then sell the next one.
principles.quote: you want to sell at the point of greatest deprivation. When someone hasn't drank water in a while, that's when you want to sell them the water.

principles.text: Qualify who gets the free lead magnet so you avoid freebie seekers and tire kickers.
principles.quote: You don't have to give the lead mags to everybody. You can only give to people who are qualified. Crazy. You just add a drop down that makes somebody qualified

principles.text: Ask often, but earn the right to ask by delivering value between asks, with a clear CTA and a reason to act now.
principles.quote: you want to maximize your ability to ask times the amount of times you ask. And so maximizing your ability to ask means that you're continually providing value between your asks.

sources.title: Email marketing: Hormozi's tactics for turning email into a high-ROI channel
sources.originalTitle: Learn Email Marketing in 39 Minutes!
sources.summary: Hormozi explains why he regrets waiting years to email and breaks down the format, segmentation, deliverability, cadence and CTA tactics behind his Money Minute newsletter. The core idea: treat email as content where every step rewards the reader, keep it plain and valuable, and make unsubscribing easy to protect deliverability.

principles.text: Email is a follow-up channel on contacts you already paid to acquire, so the only real costs are software and writing.
principles.quote: you spent the cost to acquire the lead now you're just reminding them that you exist and so basically the only real cost is just whatever software you use

principles.text: Make unsubscribing easy; keeping uninterested people captive makes them go dormant and hurts deliverability for everyone else.
principles.quote: you want to make unsubscribing easy don't keep people captive and let me explain by that is I don't want to keep sending emails to an uninterested segment of my list

principles.text: Segment your list by opt-in qualifiers; who receives the email matters far more than how good the email is.
principles.quote: it's way less about how good the email is and so much more about who's getting it and so segmenting the list is basically like if you have any qualifiers on your optin

principles.text: Reward every action in the email (open, read, click); behavior repeats because of what happens after it.
principles.quote: I want to reward every action that someone's takes and so if someone first reads the email then if they've been rewarded in the past from asum minute they'll click and they'll open it

principles.text: Keep emails plain-text with few links and little money language so they look like normal email and avoid the promo tab.
principles.quote: we want our emails to approximate that as closely as possible because the equal opposite of that is that it looks like the Vegas Strip inside of the email

principles.text: Write a batch of emails upfront to break the barrier to starting; use quality threshold rather than a rigid cadence.
principles.quote: I actually sat down and wrote 24 emails and it took me like half a day and then I thought well shoot I could have been doing this off a half day's work

sources.title: How Hormozi would scale a $309K personal styling business toward $1M+ with funnel, affiliate and ad fixes
sources.originalTitle: Building a $1,000,000 Business for a Stranger in 56 Mins
sources.summary: Hormozi audits a luxury personal styling business with strong retention and LTV:CAC but a leaky funnel and low lead volume. He prescribes a prioritized plan: fix conversion with a lead magnet and BANT qualification, add attribution and raise ad spend, then 10x a proven affiliate channel through manual outreach.

principles.text: Know what percentage of customers come from each source, then double down on the channel that delivers the most for the least effort.
principles.quote: I like to understand what percentage of customers are coming from every source so that I can see like is sometimes there's one where it's like oh 90% of my customers come from this

principles.text: A great lead magnet is pre-digested: do more front-end work so the prospect does less and gets value immediately.
principles.quote: we want to have an exceptional lead magnet which typically means we have to work more on the front end so that our Prospect has to work less and so it's kind of like pre- digesting the food

principles.text: Between a more valuable but slow lead magnet and a less valuable but immediate one, customers prefer the immediate one.
principles.quote: if you have the choice between two lead magnets one thing that's more valuable but takes longer and the other is less valuable but immediate this is the one that customers will rather have

principles.text: Give away your valuable lead magnet only to qualified leads, and qualify with BANT: budget, authority, need, timing.
principles.quote: when you give a very valuable lead magnet away you don't have to give it away to everyone and so we want to make our lead magnet super valuable but only give them to qualified customers

principles.text: Add good friction that repels bad leads while keeping good ones; avoid bad friction that drives everyone away.
principles.quote: good friction is something that increases the overall quality of the lead and gets out people who uh suck bad friction gets everyone out

principles.text: If you have a machine that turns $1 into $16 in 30 days, put in as much as you can; don't cap ad spend out of fear.
principles.quote: if you have a machine in front of you where you put a dollar in and and it spits out $16 back in 30 days why would you have any kind of limit on that budget

sources.title: Alex Hormozi on branding: deliberate pairings that raise prices, conversion and loyalty
sources.originalTitle: $100M CEO Explains How to Build A Brand in 2024
sources.summary: Hormozi defines branding in actionable terms: a deliberate pairing of your product with outcomes your ideal customer likes. Good branding drives premium pricing, better ad response and loyalty. He explains how to build it by curating pairings, recovering from bad ones, and measuring influence, direction and reach.

principles.text: Branding is a deliberate pairing of your business with outcomes your ideal customer wants; good branding means pairing with good outcomes.
principles.quote: branding is a deliberate pairing of things through an outcome

principles.text: Advertising is letting people know; branding is the pairing that results. You can have good advertising and bad branding.
principles.quote: advertising is letting people know about your stuff branding is the pairing that occurs as a result so it was good advertising but bad branding

principles.text: A strong brand gives pricing power, better ad response, and loyalty that protects against competitors.
principles.quote: good branding drives that premium pricing good branding also improves advertising

principles.text: Pair deliberately and stay focused; random, distant pairings weaken a brand. Add the good and pull out the bad.
principles.quote: distant and random pairings hurt a brand because they're so hard to make the associations with

principles.text: Recover from a bad pairing by overwhelming it with more of what your audience likes, not by trying to erase it.
principles.quote: what we try to do is just overwhelm it with way more of the stuff that the majority of our people actually like

principles.text: Premium brands must deliver on the product; brand carries a good-enough product, but a weak one loses repeat purchases.
principles.quote: it's not going to keep the business you'll get the first purchase you just won't get the ones after that

sources.title: Alex Hormozi's six steps to building a brand that commands 10x pricing
sources.originalTitle: 10x Your Profit. 10x Your Pricing. 10x Your Business. [Here's how]
sources.summary: Hormozi defines branding as pairing something unknown (you) with something people already like, then walks through six steps: what branding is, why it matters (LTV:CAC), pick the who, find what they like, advertise the pairing, and keep your promises. A strong brand lowers CAC, raises prices, and drives repeat purchase.

principles.text: Branding is just repeated pairing of what people don't know (you) with something they already know and like.
principles.quote: branding is this big fancy word but all it means is the association between two things

principles.text: Brand matters because it improves the core arbitrage: lower CAC, higher LTV, higher prices, and exclusive repeat buying.
principles.quote: if brand can allow you to convert a higher percentage of your audience get those people to buy more times from you get them to not buy from anyone else and get them to do that at a higher price

principles.text: Pick a who that is growing, can afford it, is easy to target, and is in pain.
principles.quote: these are the four basic things growing they can afford it I'm easy to find and they're in pain

principles.text: Advertising is making known; branding is what you make known. Pair yourself with what your who likes and their problems.
principles.quote: advertising is the process of making known branding is what you make known it's the content of the advertising

principles.text: What others say about you outweighs what you say, and what they experience outweighs both. Keep promises to create a virtuous cycle.
principles.quote: what other people say to them matters way more than what you tell them

principles.text: Every new association trades some audience for a better-fit one; keep one core pillar and prune what doesn't fit.
principles.quote: whenever you make an association you trade a certain percentage of your audience for ideally a greater percentage of the type of people you want

sources.title: SPCL framework: how Alex Hormozi builds influence with content (status, power, credibility, likeness)
sources.originalTitle: My Actual Social Media Strategy For 2026
sources.summary: Hormozi explains his SPCL framework (status, power, credibility, likeness) for building influence, defined as the likelihood of compliance with requests. He argues for live, long-form, high-volume content aimed at the right avatar rather than chasing views, and for setting realistic view expectations based on niche market size.

principles.text: Aim for influence (likelihood someone complies with your request), not maximum views.
principles.quote: it's how to build influence rather than how to get as many views as possible or anything like that.

principles.text: Stack all four SPCL elements; each works alone, but together they maximize influence.
principles.quote: they all can work independently, but the idea is that you want all four to be stacked together. And this is what gives you the most influence

principles.text: Power comes from say-do correspondence: people follow your directions, good things happen, so they comply with later asks.
principles.quote: if I say something and then you do it and then a good thing occurs, a reinforcing event happens afterwards. You are more likely to comply with a following request.

principles.text: Be yourself; acting like a different person or archetype has no ROI on likeness.
principles.quote: There's zero ROI in trying to be or act in a way that is different than who you are.

principles.text: Long-form and live content give far more reinforcement cycles per prospect than shorts; shorts mainly feed longs.
principles.quote: I see the purpose of shorts as many times a way to get someone to watch a long

principles.text: Content is the targeting; make content for your avatar and judge it by niche-appropriate response, not views.
principles.quote: If you want to attract the right avatar, make content for that avatar.

sources.title: How to get customers fast: free giveaways, LTV, fewer need-to-believes, affiliates and truth
sources.originalTitle: How To Get Customers So Fast It Feels ILLEGAL
sources.summary: Hormozi lays out levers for getting customers quickly: give away what others charge for, keep marketing small and high-skill, ask what it would take to be number one, invest in pre-production, minimize need-to-believes, split test, raise LTV to outspend rivals, build over-generous affiliate deals, and let truth carry your ads.

principles.text: Find what others charge for, give it away free, make it better, then measure leads and conversion.
principles.quote: look at what other people are charging for step two look at the Hard costs of what it would cost for you to deliver it step three give that thing away for free step four see how many leads you get step five see how many you convert

principles.text: Keep marketing teams small and high-skill; the best advertisers don't need many people.
principles.quote: the best advertisers don't need many people and if you have no one who's in your quote marketing department that means you

principles.text: Ask what would have to be true to be number one, then put resources behind it instead of incremental gains.
principles.quote: what would it take to be number one and another way of asking this question is what what else would have to be true for us to be number one in our market

principles.text: Invest in pre-production: concept and prep have far more leverage than fixing things in post.
principles.quote: post has very low leverage and very high cost whereas pre has incredibly High leverage and very low cost but it just takes more mental work

principles.text: Minimize what a customer must believe to buy; ideally none or one belief.
principles.quote: I want to reposition or repackage the product and offer in such a way that there's either no beliefs they have to believe or only one

principles.text: The ability to spend more is LTV; ad costs only rise, so LTV must rise too.
principles.quote: advertising only becomes more expensive over time the cost to get a customer literally only goes up

sources.title: Alex Hormozi on Jay Shetty: first dollar, core four, closer, and money models
sources.originalTitle: Alex Hormozi: How To Make So Much Money You Question The Meaning Of It
sources.summary: Hormozi explains how to go from zero to first income: work for free for qualified people, use the Core Four to promote, the CLOSER framework to sell, and volume (rule of 100) to improve. He also covers money models, mindset around fear, criticism and focus, and why active income beats speculation.

principles.text: Skip speculation; increase money per unit of time by building income-generating skills (promote, convert, deliver).
principles.quote: I think of just money per unit of time. And that kind of takes out this binary or what I would consider a false binary of active and passive

principles.text: Get first clients with a 10 by 10 free offer: ten people, ten hours, one-on-one, to learn, earn testimonials, and discover the offer.
principles.quote: Just 10 by 10. So give 10 people 10 hours. And so you can say, "Hey, I'm going to do 10 hours of work for free." That is a really compelling offer.

principles.text: Raise price 20% every five customers until people stop saying yes.
principles.quote: you just keep bumping the price by 20% every five people until eventually people start stop saying yes.

principles.text: Volatility comes from insufficient volume; do 100 reachouts, 100 minutes of content or $100 of ads daily, then double down on the top 10%.
principles.quote: volatility is a symptom of insufficient volume.

principles.text: Persuade by stating facts and telling the truth, including damaging admissions; it cuts imposter anxiety and builds trust.
principles.quote: you'll be significantly more persuasive and have less anxiety by just stating the facts and tell the truth.

principles.text: A money model collects enough cash from one customer in 30 days to acquire and serve two more; a superior one gives padding to be bad elsewhere.
principles.quote: you collect enough cash from one customer in the first 30 days to get and service two more customers.

sources.title: Alex Hormozi on starting small, paying down ignorance debt, and building a $150M portfolio
sources.originalTitle: Alex Hormozi: How He Built A $150 Million Empire And His Best Business Advice
sources.summary: Hormozi walks through how to go from zero to six figures: pick one channel, one product, one avatar, start a service business from what you already know, and treat early income as education. He covers his gym story, front-loaded offers, why investing in skills beats the S&P 500, and his content vendor-to-in-house playbook.

principles.text: Start with a service business built on what you already know; the early goal is to learn, not earn.
principles.quote: you're trading that time for money in order to learn not to earn you need to earn in order to pay your pay your rent eat Etc but the the major thing you're doing is you're paying down ignorance debt

principles.text: You don't need a novel idea: copy what others do and do it a little better by fixing what people hate.
principles.quote: the best way to start a business is just look at what everyone else is doing and just try and do it better

principles.text: Don't plan 100 steps ahead; take a step and the next one becomes clear. Expect a graveyard of failures.
principles.quote: once you start taking steps The Next Step becomes illuminated you trying to think 100 steps into the future when you have no context is is irrelevant because chaos is going to break your plan anyways

principles.text: Favors people ask of you signal what you can charge for; mine past jobs, parents' industries and interests for offers.
principles.quote: what people ask you to do as a favor is an indication of the things you can charge for later

principles.text: Six figures needs one channel, one product, one avatar; seven figures is doing that consistently.
principles.quote: getting to six figures is literally just like sell something to someone like that's that's all you have to do to get six records like one channel one product one Avatar like that's it

principles.text: Invest in your earning capacity before markets; income problems aren't investing problems.
principles.quote: you will get a significantly higher return investing in your own ability to make money than you will in any any market

sources.title: How Hormozi trains and runs high-volume sales teams: scripts, adherence, curiosity and show rates
sources.originalTitle: The World's Greatest Sales Interview with Alex Hormozi and Daniel G “Off the stage Episode 10”
sources.summary: Hormozi explains how he built sales systems after thousands of in-person gym sales: compress the script, drill it until reps breathe it, ask questions instead of making statements, and fix show-up rates through availability and speed. He also covers team incentives, culture, and why fewer, better things make communities stick.

principles.text: Keep the sales system simple and delete what isn't essential so everyone executes the few things that matter every day.
principles.quote: simple scales fancy fails that's one of our little internal isms

principles.text: The first goal for a sales team is script adherence; if reps follow the script and don't close, the script is the owner's problem.
principles.quote: my first objective with a sales team is adherence because then I have a controllable

principles.text: Ask questions instead of making statements, since every statement gives the prospect something to disagree with.
principles.quote: every time you make a statement you give something give the other person something to disagree with

principles.text: Aim for a decision, not a sale; caring more about the prospect than they do wins, even if that means pushing away a bad fit.
principles.quote: the end point of a sale for me is a decision not a sale

principles.text: Raise show rates by maximizing appointment availability, using short time increments, and pulling bookings to same or next day.
principles.quote: the number one uh lever on throughput in an organization is availability

principles.text: Do the opposite of what the prospect expects when they object: agree and stay relaxed rather than fighting.
principles.quote: whenever somebody gives you an objection do the opposite of what what they think you're about to respond to

sources.title: Alex Hormozi on the Iced Coffee Hour: gym launch to Acquisition.com, leverage, constraints and mindset
sources.originalTitle: Meet The $100,000,000 Man Who Sold Everything | Alex Hormozi
sources.summary: Alex tells how he quit consulting, built six gyms with a cash-positive offer, then sold his gym playbook to other owners and moved into Acquisition.com. He advises the hosts to monetize the audience they already have, work on the real constraint, and pick simple high-margin businesses.

principles.text: Design the offer so customer acquisition pays for itself on the front end, then use the back end for profit.
principles.quote: if you follow the cash flow, it's like I put $10 out and then I got 500 and then I got 250 and then I got a,000.

principles.text: Sell a defined result with a guarantee instead of a membership, and charge when customers are most excited.
principles.quote: charge people when they're the most excited upfront. Uh, so like charge them $500 for define program rather than a membership because no one really wants a membership. They just want like a result.

principles.text: Selling the know-how many times costs the same as making it once, which is leverage.
principles.quote: the cost of making the thing once versus selling it 100 times was the same. And that was when I basically understood the the value of having leverage.

principles.text: Find the constraint and work only on it until it is debottlenecked.
principles.quote: only focusing on what is the thing that is is stopping us from getting to the next level and then ruthlessly working on that thing until it is debottlenecked

principles.text: Monetize the audience you already have instead of chasing more reach.
principles.quote: you don't need more eyeballs. You need more monetization of the eyeballs you have.

principles.text: Look for businesses selling something unique, expensive, sticky and cheap to produce, run by a strong manager.
principles.quote: unique, expensive, sticky air. So I want something that only I can sell.

sources.title: Alex Hormozi on leverage, offer ladders, AI workflows and boring-business wins (TBPN)
sources.originalTitle: Alex Hormozi's Playbook for Building Billion-Dollar Businesses
sources.summary: Wide-ranging TBPN interview. Hormozi covers choosing high-leverage paths, price ladders where each tier adds another double of revenue, using AI to restructure workflows instead of starting new ventures, and why content must tie back to money made.

principles.text: Output equals volume of activity times the leverage of that activity, so pick the right boat first.
principles.quote: What you accomplish is a direct output of the volume of activity that you do multiplied by the leverage of the activity itself. And so you have to pick the right boat.

principles.text: Customers are fractal: build price tiers, each adding another double of revenue, and make offers available.
principles.quote: typically like at each level you have another double. So it's like if you're at, let's say, a $100 a month price point, there's going to be another double of revenue at a $500 a month price point.

principles.text: Use AI by moving from org-chart thinking to workflow thinking, so output rises and margins improve.
principles.quote: take it from an org chart based thinking to workflow based thinking

principles.text: Anything unique in AI starts with your own data layer, which most small businesses lack.
principles.quote: if you want to have anything that's unique it starts with data if you want to build any kind of AI right that's actually useful

principles.text: Pick a goal and the likeliest path, then stick with it for years with a feedback loop for improvement.
principles.quote: once you pick that path, know that if you stick with that path for 20 years, the likelihood that you fail is basically zero. As long as you have some feedback loop for improvement.

principles.text: Content or personal-brand work that doesn't turn into money made is ineffective work.
principles.quote: If what you do does not translate into the money that you make and money that you make is the goal then you are doing work that is not effective.

sources.title: Alex Hormozi on opportunity, niching, skills and brand: lessons from Gym Launch's near-collapse
sources.originalTitle: Alex Hormozi: Choose Customers Who Value What You Sell
sources.summary: Hormozi tells how Gym Launch nearly collapsed, then recovered by selling his gym-launch playbook to gym owners, which showed him how elastic his pricing was. He also covers how to judge an opportunity, how to narrow a market, hiring on character, why skills compound, and what a brand is.

principles.text: Judge an opportunity on three variables: market size, value-to-cost gap, and competitive dynamics. Look for all three.
principles.quote: i see it as three variables so you have uh the total number of potential units to sell

principles.text: Narrow to your best customers. Find what the top 20% have in common and sell only to that group, with no extra operational drag.
principles.quote: what if we only sold that amount of people and we sold now the same hundred but they were all of that 20 percent right well we would 5x our revenue

principles.text: Test price elasticity by raising the price. Each higher quote kept closing, which exposed how underpriced the offer was.
principles.quote: next guy how much eight grand next time how much 10 grand next and then i did 60 000 in sales that day

principles.text: Hire on character before skill. His three values are unimpeachable character, sincere candor and competitive greatness, in that order.
principles.quote: unimpeachable character sincere candor and competitive greatness and so those are the only three things and we look for them pretty much in that order

principles.text: Skills are the asset that keeps appreciating and stacking, whatever the economy or currency does.
principles.quote: skills are the only thing that will always appreciate in time

principles.text: A brand is reputation, meaning what people say about you when you're not there. You build it from the inside out.
principles.quote: i see brand as reputation and i see reputation as what people say about you when you're not there so that is your brand

sources.title: Alex Hormozi on Diary of a CEO: Retention, Pricing, Hiring and Reality as the Moat
sources.summary: Hormozi explains why $1M businesses stall before $10M (no stickiness), why undercharging causes founder overwhelm, and why AI belongs inside a business rather than being the business. He also covers starting with an unscalable premium offer, treating hiring as marketing, and building real-world credibility as a moat.

principles.text: Build retention first: if customers stay, revenue stacks and growth compounds instead of resetting each year.
principles.quote: if every time you get a customer they never left, then the business will do nothing but grow.

principles.text: Use AI inside your business on the real constraint; advertise the customer's outcome, not the AI.
principles.quote: They should use AI in their business. They're trying to advertise as AI businesses when you should just advertise the thing that your customer cares about, which is the solution to their problem, the outcome.

principles.text: Price on what the customer will pay, not what you feel you deserve; don't sell out of your own wallet.
principles.quote: I think what we feel we deserve matters the least in that. I think it's all about what the customer is willing to pay.

principles.text: Start with an absurdly valuable, premium, unscalable offer; add zeros to the price, then scale down later.
principles.quote: start with the most absurdly valuable thing you possibly can. So whatever price you want to charge, add 1 or 2 zeros to it.

principles.text: In an AI content world, real track record and reputation are the moat.
principles.quote: when reality is the moat, it means that your brand is the moat. It means your reputation is the moat, which can only happen in reality.

principles.text: Treat hiring like marketing: run the same lead gen, nurture, sales and onboarding process for employees as for customers.
principles.quote: almost all problems in business can be solved by more people finding out about your stuff, either to work for you or to buy from you.

sources.title: Theory of constraints: stop starting new businesses, remove the one thing blocking growth
sources.originalTitle: the-only-2-real-things-restraining-business-growth-ep-325
sources.summary: Alex uses three founder conversations to argue that plateaued businesses are stuck on a skill gap, not market saturation. The fix is to name the single constraint, phrase it as a "how do I" question, and put all effort there instead of launching another business.

principles.text: The only excusable reason to plateau is exhausting your total addressable market; otherwise you just don't know how.
principles.quote: the only reason a business should plateau that is reasonable, that is not your fault, is that you have reached the total addressable market.

principles.text: A system grows until it hits a constraint; remove it and growth continues until the next constraint.
principles.quote: a system will grow until it is constrained, right? It has a constraint, and then once you remove the constraint, it'll continue to grow. until it reaches another constraint.

principles.text: Prioritize problems: usually only one or two things truly constrain growth, and only one is the real constraint at a time.
principles.quote: one of the things that we have done well is prioritizing what problems to solve.

principles.text: Ask a specific question like 'what's stopping us from $5M a month?' rather than 'why am I not growing?'
principles.quote: what's stopping us from being at $5 million a month? What's stopping us? And until we can clearly answer that question, there's nothing else we need to do.

principles.text: Reframe skill deficiencies as 'how do I...' questions so they become solvable problems.
principles.quote: let's phrase the deficiency as a question, which is how do I learn how to recruit, manage, and train a sales team.

principles.text: A new business won't fix a stall because you carry your own ceiling into it; businesses grow to the entrepreneur's level of incompetence.
principles.quote: the businesses will grow to the level of incompetence of the entrepreneur. So if you're a $4 million entrepreneur, the next business will be a $4 million business.

sources.title: Alex Hormozi on focus, elite talent, brand and skills: the shifts behind $40M to $100M+
sources.originalTitle: alex-hormozi-how-to-invest-in-yourself-to-become-a-self-made-millionaire
sources.summary: Alex explains three shifts behind Acquisition.com's growth: ruthless single-objective focus, paying for elite talent, and betting on brand with delayed payoff. He also argues for investing in your own skills over stocks, treating volatility as a volume problem, and turning vague traits into concrete behaviors.

principles.text: Focus from the top down: pick one objective, finish it, then move to the next. Sequencing beats parallel work.
principles.quote: you actually get 5 things done faster when you do them in order than trying to do all 5 at once.

principles.text: Pay for elite talent. The best people return 100x, so a high salary is still the cheaper option.
principles.quote: it's worth paying someone 1,000,000 of dollars a year if they can make you tens of 1,000,000 or 100 of 1,000,000 of dollars a year.

principles.text: Brand pays off on a delay, so start planting now and keep investing even when results lag.
principles.quote: you wanna dig the well before you're thirsty.

principles.text: Early on, invest in your own skills rather than the stock market. Active income beats passive returns at small scale.
principles.quote: don't invest in the S and P 500. It's invest in the S and Me 500.

principles.text: Inconsistent results usually mean too little volume. Raise the number of attempts before you judge the method.
principles.quote: most volatility comes from lack of volume

principles.text: Ask what it would take to reach a goal, then decide whether the price is worth paying.
principles.quote: what would it take? And the reason I love that question is because it assumes success.

sources.title: Stop trying to get rich, get better: build product back to front to compound LTV and referrals
sources.originalTitle: stop-trying-to-get-rich-get-better-alex-hormozi-video-transcript-bcb8adbc7a19
sources.summary: Hormozi argues most small businesses are stuck in the "selling business", pouring leads into a leaky bucket. Instead, spend the early phase perfecting the product, so referrals, repeat purchase and brand cut CAC and raise LTV as you scale. He also covers finding activation points from retained customers and why the first phase is to learn, not earn.

principles.text: Getting rich is an output; getting better is the input. Focus on the input that creates wealth.
principles.quote: Getting rich is an outcome; getting better is an input.

principles.text: Lead shortage is usually a product problem: you can't afford leads because the product doesn't retain or generate referrals.
principles.quote: The problem is not that you don’t have enough leads; the problem is you can’t afford them because your product sucks.

principles.text: Win the LTV game: whoever makes customers most valuable can outspend on acquisition.
principles.quote: I rephrase that as, ‘He who can make his customers the most valuable wins,’

principles.text: Ad costs rise and efficiency falls at scale, so you need a compounding vehicle like referrals to hold LTV:CAC.
principles.quote: You need an equally strong compounding vehicle that works in your favor to maintain your LTV-to-CAC ratio.

principles.text: In the first phase, learn rather than earn: nail the model so customers stay and growth never stops.
principles.quote: The point in the first phase is to learn, not to earn.

principles.text: Find activation points by studying customers who don't cancel, then drive onboarding toward that experience.
principles.quote: Everything is about looking at the people at the end, looking at the thing that preceded them getting to that point, and then putting all of your focus on getting people to have that experience.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A three-level blueprint to a million-dollar net worth. Own equity instead of earning income, go all in on one avatar/product/channel, craft a high-value offer, remove yourself so the business has enterprise value, and compound with patience and reputation.

chunks.heading: Net worth math: earning vs owning your way to $1M
chunks.text:
- Alex defines a millionaire as net worth above $1M excluding the primary residence (assets minus liabilities). He separates liquid net worth (cash and tradeable assets) from total net worth.
- His credentials: millionaire in his early 20s, first cash million in the bank at 27, over $100M net worth by 31. He says he has helped over 100 others reach $1M+ net worths.
- **Earn path:** to net $1M after tax you need roughly $2M of gross income. At $200,000/year for a decade, saving 100%, you reach $1M liquid. Time works against you because taxes and living expenses come out every year.
- **Own path:** a business making $250,000/year in profit, truly automated with a team running it without you, could sell at about a 4x multiple, which is $1M. The income is almost the same, but the net worth arrives as soon as the profit does. He notes this is a small profit for business-sale purposes.
- He says entrepreneurs are investing too: "you're just heavily indexed on one stock which is your own."

chunks.heading: Don't diversify early: focus all your time and attention on one thing
chunks.text:
- Diversification is "a hedge against ignorance" (Buffett). Alex reframes it as focus: when you're early, your scarcest resource is time and attention, not money.
- His analogy is seven cups filling at once. Spreading attention across crypto, day trading, forex, flipping, Airbnb and ATMs means no cup reaches the overflow threshold, where profit starts spilling over.
- Wealthy people do have multiple income streams, but they got there by going all in on one stream until it overflowed, then diversified to maintain wealth.
- "It's not which one will work, it's which one will you work on." Any of them could work with enough effort.
- He thinks it is arrogant to believe 10% of your attention across 10 things will beat someone putting everything into one.
- **Five stages of the entrepreneur cycle:** uninformed optimism, informed pessimism, valley of despair, informed optimism, achievement.
  - Most people quit in the valley and jump to a new opportunity, restarting at uninformed optimism. "There's poo on both sides you just didn't know about it until you got there."
  - His goal is to compress the time to informed optimism.
  - After achievement, reset the target (for example, 10x bigger) and repeat. Having been through it once, you know the dip will come and you keep going.
- Compounding also depends on not diversifying: splitting your effort interrupts the compounding.

chunks.heading: Build for the long game: product first, then marketing
chunks.text:
- The tower analogy: stacking blocks end to end is fastest for 10 seconds but collapses at 10 days. Building on a stable base wins over a longer horizon.
- Typical mistake: build a product, advertise it, get sales, then do more marketing and sales. If the product is poor, customers tell their friends it stinks, and ads get more expensive as the reputation sours.
- Correct sequence: make the thing, tell people, then keep fixing the product until customers become happy and refer others. Don't crank up marketing until that happens.
- If a business is stuck (for example, a $1M business that can't reach $10M), it was often built without a foundation. Sometimes the fastest route to $10M is to start over and build it right.
- Hiring: seek talent, not "a body in the seat." He may interview 20 people for one role rather than three.

chunks.heading: Finding a hungry crowd: market, offer, persuasion
chunks.text:
- **Hot dog stand story:** a genie offers a wish. Cheaper, tastier or faster hot dogs are all the wrong wish. The right one is the best corner in front of a starving crowd.
- **Order of leverage:** market first, then offer, then persuasion.
  - Market: toilet paper during Covid sold out regardless of quality. Selling to newspapers, which are shrinking about 25% per year, is a headwind.
  - Offer: a free-to-start, risk-free, pay-on-results offer outsells a "pay me and maybe you get results" offer by 10x to 100x.
  - Persuasion matters most when all the offers look the same.
- **Four criteria for a market. You need all four:**
  1. Pain: people who must have the solution, not just want it.
  2. Purchasing power: a friend's business helping unemployed people fix their resumes had huge pain but couldn't grow because they were broke.
  3. Easy to target: nurses are easy to find, while "psychedelic Aztecs in Croatia" are not.
  4. Growing market: a friend with a rev-share offer to newspapers had a great offer and strong persuasion, and beat competitors every year, yet couldn't grow because the whole market was shrinking.

chunks.heading: One avatar, one product, one channel (to $1M and beyond)
chunks.text:
- Alex's simplest formula to $2M+: one avatar, one product, one channel.
- **Avatar:** one very specific person you help.
- **Product:** below $1M, adding more products adds complexity with too few customers to justify it. Ask how to sell three times as much of the same product to the same person.
- **Channel:** you can reach $1M+ on any single channel.
  - Outreach: reach out at volume, whether cold calls, cold emails or DMs.
  - Content: post more and better.
  - Paid ads: spend more, profitably. If you can't scale past $1M/year profitably with paid ads, "you have a business problem or you have a pricing problem."
- Adding a second channel, such as cold email when you already make $500,000/year on YouTube, complicates things too early.
- Channel diversification reduces risk for an acquirer, but at this size it doesn't matter yet. Get better at the one thing.

chunks.heading: The value equation: how to build the offer
chunks.text:
- From his book *$100M Offers*, which answers "what should I sell." Value has four variables.
  - **Dream outcome (up):** how much the prospect values the result. A millionaire outcome is worth more to most men than being handsome.
  - **Perceived likelihood of achievement (up):** a $50 ebook and a year of one-on-one personal training target the same weight-loss outcome, but the training feels far more likely to work.
  - **Time delay (down):** micro is the daily time required, such as 3 gym sessions a week plus meal prep. Macro is how long until the result, such as 18 months to lose 50 lbs.
  - **Effort and sacrifice (down):** effort is what you must start doing. Sacrifice is what you must stop doing, such as margaritas on Mondays and sleeping in.
- The perfect hypothetical offer is a button that gives you abs instantly with no effort.
- **Hidden costs:** often the most expensive part of an offer isn't the money but what the buyer must do. Marketing agency example:
  - Version A: 60-day ramp-up, two one-hour calls a week, fly to the studio, no traction for 60 days.
  - Version B: "I'll draw stuff on my own and start posting immediately, and your phone's going to ring today."
  - Same core service, but he calls B about 10x more valuable.
- The offer affects every department: marketing, the sales script, the sales process and delivery.
- At acquisition.com (which invests in and buys businesses, and doesn't sell coaching), Alex says portfolio companies average 1.8x revenue and 3.0x profit over the first 12 months. Over 24 months they average 2.8x revenue and 4.7x profit.

chunks.heading: Marketing and sales: the eight advertising methods and the founder's role
chunks.text:
- **Sequence:** make the thing ($100M Offers), get leads ($100M Leads), then convert. After that, go back and improve the product, then promote more, in a virtuous cycle.
- **Core four (you do):** warm outreach (one to one, friends), content (one to many, people who know you), paid ads (one to many, strangers), cold outreach (one to one, strangers). If nobody is buying, "you're not doing enough of these core four."
- **Other four (others do it):** customer referrals, employees, agencies, affiliates (influencers).
- Pick one method at first. Learn a core four method before using lead getters.
- **Why the founder should do both marketing and sales early:**
  - It's cheaper.
  - You need to understand the skills tactically so you can teach and hold others to a standard ("no it is, let me show you how").
- **Sales process:** early on, throw things at the wall and see what sticks. When someone buys, backtrack through the steps and replicate them. Do the same inside the sales call: ask question one, then two, then three. Write a script, because later hires won't be as convicted as the founder, and the process keeps conversion up.

chunks.heading: Paying yourself, setting goals, and the scientific method
chunks.text:
- **Paying yourself:** it depends on risk tolerance. Alex regrets taking nothing out while rolling every gym's profit into the next, then losing everything when he sold the gyms and was left with nothing.
  - Taking cash out forces cash flow to appear and forces you to cut personal spending. A full bank account makes for better, less stressful decisions.
  - He suggests a bank account that goes up every month as a personal goal.
  - **Capital-intensive businesses rule of thumb:** 33% to the owner, 30% to growth (such as new locations), and the remainder to cash reserves for the business and for you.
  - **Watermark method:** work out what growth costs per month (for example, two more hires or locations). Always leave that amount in the account and distribute everything above it.
- **Goals should be inputs, not outputs:** a friend kept easing off after hitting $10k, $20k and $30k months. Alex told him to make the activities the goal, so every day he either did the activities or didn't.
- **Rule of 100:** do 100 primary actions per day for 100 days and you'll usually get the first result. He says "count in hundreds."
  - Warm outreach: 100 friends a day.
  - Cold outreach: 100 people a day.
  - Content: 100 minutes a day.
  - Paid ads: $100 a day.
  - Do the 100 even if you didn't sell today, because it sets up tomorrow's sales.
- **Scientific method for portfolio goals (four boxes):**
  1. What problem are we solving? (Tie goals to a real constraint. "Redo the logo" must answer what constraint it relieves.)
  2. Hypothesis: "if X then Y," for example if we redesign the website, conversion rises.
  3. How we measure X and Y, for example a split test every Monday over the quarter, and whether conversion beats the current 10%.
  4. Did we do it, and did it work?
- If we did it and it didn't work, the constraint or hypothesis was wrong. If we didn't do it, fix why we aren't doing it.
- He likes solving problems by deciding they aren't problems.

chunks.heading: Staying rich: asymmetric bets, enterprise value, people, and reputation
chunks.text:
- **Only get rich once:** from a mentor's Goldman Sachs mentor, "you should only have to get rich once." After a win, play with house money and never bet the empire. Alex's line: "fortunes are created through taking huge risk with small amounts of money, but fortunes are preserved by taking small risks with lots of money."
- Outsized returns come from betting against conventional wisdom. Given a 10% chance at a 100x payoff, take it every time. He cites Bezos: business has a long-tail return distribution unlike baseball's cap of four runs.
- **Quad marketing calendar:** market in four directions at all times: prospects into customers, customers into repeat customers, candidates into employees, and employees into engaged and developing staff.
  - Most founders only advertise to prospects. Then they have no one to deliver, and feel like a "genius with 1,000 hands."
- **Enterprise value (EV):** the same $2M/year profit is worth far more if the business runs without the owner.
  - Genius with 1,000 hands: $5M revenue and $2M income gives about $1M a year after tax, with no enterprise value.
  - Systematized: with the same revenue and profit but the genius removed and the people and processes doing the work, the asset might be worth $10M.
  - Earning $10M of net worth through income would take about $20M of income.
  - At acquisition.com the pattern is to take a $2-5M business, systematize it, and apply a multiple. His example is $10M of profit at 7x, taking someone from a $1-3M net worth to $70M.
  - Small AI-enabled teams can reach $1M/year in profit. To reach $10M, $20M, $50M, $100M and beyond, people are still required.
- **Reputation and brand:**
  - Life experiences are flowers in a bouquet. Associating similar strengths builds a coherent reputation, and one negative experience (his example: a drunk-driving accident) distorts how the rest is seen.
  - A brand is "an association between something you know and something you don't know." His example: the acquisition.com hat people ask to buy at airports. Luxury brands work the same way via celebrity association (Louis Vuitton with Kim Kardashian), and brands drop celebrities when negative associations form.
  - **Goodwill (customer surplus):** value received above what was paid. Alex says it compounds multiplicatively, and faster than revenue. He says you can build a $100M brand in 3 years, which can outpace building $100M in revenue.
  - Brand examples he cites: The Rock's Teremana ($6B), Kardashian's beauty line, Conor McGregor's Proper 12 ($1B+), George Clooney's tequila ($1B).
  - Early on, invest in goodwill and monetize later.
  - Buffett: any number multiplied by zero is zero. Never risk your reputation for short-term money. His example is that starting an OnlyFans would make money but would be a "broken flower."

chunks.heading: Compounding, patience, and defining enough
chunks.text:
- **Compounding:** $100 at 10% becomes 110, 121, 133 and so on. Buffett has made more in the last decade than in the rest of his career.
  - Equity is a great compounding vehicle because you can reallocate capital inside it. For example, 10 locations growing 10% a month: infrastructure built over time allows faster pace later.
  - Panda Express: about 2,000 locations took 45 years, then it added 600 in a single year, more than any prior year.
- "Boring is what makes you rich." Going from $100M to $110M adds $10M, while going from 0 to $10M in year one is unlikely.
- Munger: the money is made in the waiting. The hard part of a plan is sticking with it, not deciding on it (for example, 3 gym days a week for a year).
- **Patience means figuring out what to do in the meantime.** In the marshmallow test, successful kids distracted themselves (moved away, sang, put the marshmallow in a pocket). Building skills gives you more ways to wait.
- **Define enough:** he bought a Bentley, then returned it at a loss six months later, realising he didn't care.
  - His rough monthly costs of a 1% lifestyle:

| Item | Monthly cost |
|---|---|
| Private flying | $50,000 |
| $500 dinners nightly | $15,000 |
| Lamborghini lease | $5,000 |
| Nutritionist, therapy, performance coach | about $10,000 |
| Housing | $50,000 |
| Total | about $150,000 |

  - That total is just under $2M/year after tax, or close to $4M pre-tax. He says you can live very comfortably on about $50,000 a month after tax.
- Put a number on food, travel, clothing, experiences and health to see how little you need to satisfy personal needs.
- Two levels of wealth: personal needs covered, and then unlimited, where money is used to play the game.
- Wealth is not about not working. It is about "getting addicted to freedom," which means having the option to work. Without a challenge you atrophy, like lifting weights well below your max.
- **Infinite games:** the goal is to stay married, stay in business and stay healthy at 50, not to win once. "You win as long as you never quit" (Churchill).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi recounts losing everything in 2016, then rebuilding by licensing his gym turnaround system. He explains how he thinks about offers, value, leverage, skill stacking and choosing where to apply a skill, plus the mindset (pain, input/output math) that keeps him going.

chunks.heading: How Alex turned a $1,000 bank balance into $26M in 12 months (Gym Launch origin)
chunks.text:
- In December 2016 Alex had six gyms and a turnaround business. After a partner took his gym money and a payment processor froze his launch revenue, he had to wire $222,000 in sales commissions. That left him about $1,000, and he screenshotted the balance.
- His turnaround model: fly a sales team into a gym, fill it with memberships, keep the money, and let the gym deliver the service. He had no way to process the cash and about 60-80 contracts a day were piling up.
- Fix for processing: he found a high-risk processor (8% fee, 10% held back, $50,000 monthly limit) and added more processors of $50,000 each over the following weeks.
- By the end of February he had about $330,000 profit. Then about $150,000 in refunds hit because some gym owners told customers to demand refunds.
- Pivot: eight gym launches were booked for the next month. Alex called those gym owners and offered to sell them the system instead of flying out. He quoted $6,000 on the first call, then $8,000, $10,000 and $12,000 on the next calls. He sold about $60,000 of licensing in one day.
- The license was his internal sales-training and nutrition-orientation material, plus white-label landing pages and ads already proven to convert. He used videos of himself and taught gym owners how to run the ads.
- He then called the roughly 30 gyms he had already turned around and made about $300,000 that month, nearly all profit. That covered the refunds.
- Gym owners averaged $30,000 in extra cash collected in their first month. They did it cheaply because they skipped the fly-in salesperson's commission, rental car and hotel and ran the offer in their own gym.
- Result of the first full 12 months (January to January): $26 million top line and $17 million EBITDA. He says he went from broke to $3 million in the bank in about six months.
- His lesson: the knowledge, sales skill and marketing were the same all along. Rearranging the offer's variables took him from a few million in revenue with almost no profit to millions in revenue and profit.

chunks.heading: Making offers people "feel stupid saying no" to, and the four value variables
chunks.text:
- At a 2013 Facebook ads workshop, a gym marketer told Alex the secret to sales: "make people an offer they'd feel stupid saying no to." It became a core concept in every business he runs.
- He defines an offer as "the terms of exchange."
- He says people who say "provide more value" rarely define it, so he broke value into four variables:
  1. **Dream outcome.** A bigger or higher-status outcome is worth more. Men would pay more to make more money than to lose weight, because money brings relative status.
  2. **Perceived likelihood of achievement.** A surgeon with 10,000 five-star reviews beats a new graduate, even if the veteran is faster. The opposite of this is risk.
  3. **Time delay.** The gap between buying and getting the result. Liposuction pays 20 times more than a personal training pack because the result is immediate. Personal training takes an hour and a half of arm-wrestling to close.
  4. **Effort and sacrifice.** Effort is what the buyer must start doing (waking early, eating foods they hate). Sacrifice is what they must give up (sleeping in, "Margarita Mondays").
- The first two are the top of a fraction and the last two are the bottom. Each has an "evil twin": risk, delay, effort and sacrifice. Raise the top, shrink the bottom.
- The ideal offer is a guaranteed dream outcome that arrives immediately and effortlessly. Entrepreneurs innovate toward that ideal without ever fully reaching it.
- Scarcity (units) and urgency (time) add value by enhancing those four variables. Example: one Gatorade bottle left on Earth, or JK Rowling announcing no more digital Harry Potter copies from tomorrow.
- If not enough people say yes, "we need to make the offer better." He calls the offer the highest-leverage thing in a business because it affects pricing, profit, marketing, sales and delivery. It is also one of the hardest things to change for the same reason. It is the topic of his first book; leads (who to sell to) is the second.

chunks.heading: Niching down to raise prices: the PR company example
chunks.text:
- Alex invested in a generic PR company serving small business owners. It had high churn but a strong sales engine.
- About 85% of customers were small businesses. In three or four months, 15% bought the most expensive package and stayed "forever." Those customers were people who wanted to fundraise, not dry cleaners or plumbers.
- He proposed serving only that niche. The company rebuilt its model around that segment and cold-called and cold-emailed only that narrow window.
- Result: it raised prices 10x and got higher email response rates than before, because the messaging spoke to one avatar and delivered more value to them.
- His general method: list everything the business is good at, then ask whether it can be rearranged for a specific customer so that what it does is far more valuable to them.

chunks.heading: Selling to bigger customers: "same work, more zeros"
chunks.text:
- Alex says the biggest debt people pay is ignorance, and the most expensive thing is information they don't know.
- Example: a conversion rate optimization (CRO) freelancer lifts a $1M/year store by 20%, which is $200,000 of value. At 10% of that they earn $20,000. The same 20% lift on a $100M/year business is $20M, so 10% pays $2M. That is 100x pay for the same work.
- His viral tweet: "solve rich people problems." He phrases it another way: find the people who value what you have the most.
- He tells the father/son car story. A beat-up car is worth $1,000 at a dealership, about $500 as scrap metal and $100,000 to an antique dealer. The lesson is that it isn't who you are, it's the people who value you most.
- He says selling a $10,000 package, then $100,000, then multi-million is the same skill. Bigger deals are often easier, because the customer wires the money without haggling over a $50 item.
- His first pricing in 2014 was gold, silver and bronze packages at $200, $500 and $1,000.
- He thinks a skill is worth most when applied where it is in highest demand. Another guest's equity-for-marketing story illustrates the same idea; Alex agrees with it.

chunks.heading: Leverage: the stairs of his income and the four types
chunks.text:
