- Alex defines leverage as the difference between what you put in and what you get out. He says people who aren't making as much as they want usually have low-leverage inputs.
- His income steps, in order:
  - Employee to self-employed: four figures to five figures a month.
  - Hiring staff (he hadn't realized he could): six figures a month.
  - Licensing, which is digital with near-zero cost of goods: seven figures a month.
  - Capital: eight figures a month.
  - He guesses nine figures a month would come from technology or more media.
- The four types are labor, media, capital and technology (he credits Naval). Labor is the lowest leverage, media is made once and licensed endlessly, capital needs no time sacrificed, and technology is built once and used by millions.
- He says stack as many types as you can, and as much of each as possible. Joe Rogan and a smaller podcaster both use media, but with very different amounts.
- Capital has degrees too: friends and family, then institutional money, then public markets.
- His summary: "the people who move faster in life don't actually move faster, they get more for every step."

chunks.heading: Skill stacking and finding the constraint
chunks.text:
- Each added skill makes the others more valuable. His example is a math person who learns bookkeeping, becomes a CPA, learns tax law and insurance, then capital and debt markets, then M&A, then sales. That person becomes a CFO and then a rainmaker. He also uses Jay-Z (rhythm, rapping, promotion, label, recruiting artists).
- Skills don't have to be related. The longer you play, the more unique your mix becomes.
- He dislikes entrepreneurs who learn a new thing and dismiss the earlier skill that made it possible.
- He says he isn't the best at any single part of business. He is "decent enough" at each that none is the constraint (copywriting, hiring). So find the system's constraint and bring that skill to "good enough."
- Advice for a skilled creative (his example is a media employee): either go into business with two or three co-founders with complementary skills, or choose between artist and entrepreneur. With a wallet maker, raise prices until you become a luxury brand ("the Versace of wallets") or mechanize production.
- His definition of growth: get more customers, or make each worth more. For "get more customers" he says there are eight ways, and you pick the one you're best at.

chunks.heading: Learning sales and building skill through inputs and outputs
chunks.text:
- Alex recommends two years of high-volume transactional sales: door-to-door, cold calling or a gym front desk doing 20 consults a day. You need many repetitions and quick feedback.
- He says most people who survive the first three months of sales will be fine. For new reps: shadow the best person and do twice their volume, because you're not as good, and compress the time in calendar days.
- Sales teaches handling rejection and interpersonal skills. He argues marketing is "sales one to many," and many of the best marketers started in sales.
- He defines influence (sales, leadership, management, marketing) as getting people to comply with a request. His list of what makes an entrepreneur: the power to influence, drive (toward a mission or away from a fear), impulse control, and the ability to boil success into inputs and outputs.
- He builds belief from "unreasonable that it doesn't work" statements. Example: do more sales volume than anyone, shadow the best for five years, and collect 5,000 no's, and it's unreasonable that you won't become a very good salesman.
- GMAT example: after an average first score, he read a study showing score rising in a straight line with problems practiced. He bought 16 prep books and did four hours of problems every night for three months, and scored in the 99th percentile.
- Content example: if posting once a day on one platform gets some views, post on every platform, then multiple times a day on each. He treats it as a system.
- He says to aim to be directionally correct rather than get it right the first time, and to use anger or sadness as fuel because negative motivation is underrated. He says pain motivates faster and stronger than pleasure.

chunks.heading: Portfolio, free content and how he works now
chunks.text:
- Alex's stated mission at Acquisition.com is to make business accessible to everyone. Courses are free and his books cost 99 cents. The idea is to give value first, using lessons from portfolio companies, so companies come to them already having received value.
- His audience survey: 25% have a business and 75% want to start one. Content aims to be wide (first-time founders) and deep (large-company divisions).
- Timeline: Gym Launch (licensing) grew, Prestige Labs (supplements) started two years later, and a gym lead software company about a year after that. In 2021 he sold all three. The supplement and licensing businesses went to American Pacific Group for $46.2 million for two-thirds of the company. The software company went to a strategic buyer in an all-stock deal.
- Acquisition.com began investing in 2020 and he sold partly because early investments went well. He takes mostly minority stakes of 25-49% as "growth partners," writes a check and adds value. He is in talks to take a majority in one company whose founder wants to move on.
- He says he works constantly, with only exercise four times a week as a hobby, and rests when output per unit of time drops sharply. He screens hires with a values question: if your shift ends at 5 and a 30-minute question arrives at 4:59, what do you do? He says to be transparent about expectations, since honest fit helps both sides.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex Hormozi compresses 13 years of business lessons into eleven truths. Core themes: sell premium before selling to the masses, solve the real constraint, hire A-level talent, get better rather than bigger, protect deep-work time, and build brand through consistent delivery.

chunks.heading: Sell to rich people first, then go down market
chunks.text:
- Alex's rule: "Sell to rich people until you have the money to sell all the poor people. The middle is where you get killed."
- Tesla started with the $250,000 Roadster, then a $100,000 car, then the X, then the Model 3. Each step down was harder because low prices need infrastructure built for huge volume.
- Walmart and Amazon were built for volume from day one and win on efficiency (coach flights, fold-out chairs, paper cups).
- A premium niche needs no mass infrastructure. Five clients paying $5,000 a month can fund a good business and a couple of competent hires.
- Relative value is the lever. A $100 payment is 10% of a $1,000 net worth, so that customer expects a lot. A rich person barely notices $100. Rich people pay more in absolute terms for lower relative value, and that margin lets you over-deliver.
- Alex lives on both extremes:
  - Acquisition.com is the premium brand: one or two deals a year, owners already worth about $50 million who want to get to $250 million.
  - School is the mass brand at about $99 a month. It took 5 years and tens of millions in development and still loses money, to give beginners a full business toolkit.
  - He built Acquisition.com first so he could afford to fund School.
- Hack for selling to the rich: copy what someone else sells to rich people, do it in half the time, and charge twice the price. Rich people pay for time above all else.
- Using the value equation, richer buyers want more certainty (perceived guarantee through reputation), less delay, and less effort. White-glove, concierge service works because $5,000 vs $10,000 a month is a small difference to them.
- Sell the wealthy on time saved, not money saved.

chunks.heading: You lack priorities, not information
chunks.text:
- Strategy is prioritization: unlimited options, limited time, money and people. How you allocate them is your strategy.
- Story: an entrepreneur at about $10M a year had 56 companies. One company was about half the revenue. Alex asked how easy it would be to 5x that one alone. He ended the other 55 partnerships and did it within a year.
- First question Alex asks anyone who is stuck: "What's the goal?" Then: what's the current state, desired state and obstacle? Without those, you're "running around like a chicken with your head cut off."
- A media company with 40 million subscribers wanted to optimize SOPs. Alex pointed out they had no product to sell and wanted to monetize. A mediocre product would make far more than moving media from 97 to 98.5 out of 100.
- A workshop attendee asked about Alex's Closer Framework but already had a 40% close rate. Sales wasn't his constraint. Leads, back-end conversion, or team capacity probably was.
- Founders solve the problems they like and know. Double down on strengths as an individual, but the business must be balanced like a physique. It is only as strong as its weakest link, and the weak link is usually what the founder dislikes (people, hiring, management).
- Businesses often grow only to the constraint of the founder's specialized skill. Either learn the next thing or hire someone who has it.

chunks.heading: How to hire and evaluate people when you don't know the role
chunks.text:
- Pattern recognition saves time. Hiring the wrong sales director repeatedly can cost a year or more of growth. "You tried hiring John. And John sucked." That doesn't mean no sales director can work.
- Interview many people and act like an ignoramus to learn the role. Don't jump at the first candidate.
- School's founder Sam interviewed 600 developers before finding his co-founder. Method: ask each person for the best people they know, and keep climbing the ladder, purely to gather information.
- Alex's litmus tests:
  1. Quantity and quality of metrics the candidate uses to describe the role. A customer success hire who can only say "make sure people are happy" can't drive an outcome. A strong one names activation within 48 hours, time to value, CSAT, churn as a lagging indicator, sale-to-onboarding time, early drop-off at 24/48/72 hours, and reviews by day 30.
  2. "How does what you do make the business money?" A CFO should cover cutting costs (an extra 3 to 5% to the bottom line) and supplying data for decisions. A sales director should say they raise lead-to-sale conversion for the team, not "I'll drive sales."
  3. If they can't tie their job to revenue or profit, they won't do it.
- The vaguer your direction can be, the more skilled the person must be. "Hey John, fix churn" works only with a skilled John, so smart hires are more efficient. Still learn the details so you can judge their work.

chunks.heading: Raise the talent bar and pay for A players
chunks.text:
- Advice from a mentor: "Your best talent you haven't even hired yet."
- Thought experiment: with 10 of your best teammate, you would make far more money. So why isn't your attention on getting more of them?
- When Alex met private equity buyers while selling Gym Launch, he saw the gap in average talent on their side. Those people earned $1M to $5M, or $300K to $500K in their 20s. He reset what he would pay.
- Stupid rules (be on time, no Netflix on customer calls) signal low standards. He has implemented such rules himself.
- Amazon's rule: every hire should raise the average bar of the team. Left alone, sixes hire fives and fives hire fours. Alex asks "Do they raise the bar?" in interviews.
- In the early days he hired people whose jobs he could do better, so the business was capped at him. He now prefers someone with 10 years' experience who learned on someone else's money.
- Don't give big titles (COO) to a friend or relative with no experience. The Peter Principle: a good salesperson promoted to sales manager becomes a bad manager. Many gains sit behind hard conversations.
- Framing for demoting someone: bring in an experienced person, pay for the first person to learn from them, and refocus them on what they do well.
- Acquisition.com spends the most resources on recruiting. They message people on LinkedIn, e.g. "you ran ads at a $200M DTC business; take ours from $20M to $200M, or who do you know?"
- Pay arbitrage: five B players at $100,000 each can equal one A-plus player at $170,000 in knowledge work.
- Alex's own examples:
  - First $50,000 employee managed gym one so he could open gym two, which made $250,000 profit a year (5x).
  - First $300,000 salesperson brought $5 million in sales that year (about 14x).
  - First $1 million employee (35 years' experience, 40+ sell-side deals) saved $3 million a year in her first 90 days and used her network of bankers and private equity firms to sell companies (about 50x).
  - Returns increased as he paid more.
- Attract top talent with a meaningful mission. Every Elon Musk company is framed as saving the world.

chunks.heading: Get better, not bigger, and fix the obvious problem
chunks.text:
- From Chick-fil-A founder S. Truett Cathy: pursue better, not bigger, and customers will demand you grow. Chick-fil-A grew one location at a time with little debt. Boston Market grew fast on Wall Street money, diluted talent, and went bankrupt about 10 years later. Missionaries beat mercenaries.
- "The business is growing or I am."
- Elon's and Chamath's rule: enter a market only if you can be an order of magnitude better. Elon skipped chocolate because he saw no 10x version.
- Growth is a lagging indicator; the things that make you better are the leading indicators. Making growth the goal turns an outcome into an input.
- Tactic: each quarter pick one confident improvement per function, and stack them rather than swap them.
  - Sales example: contact leads in 5 minutes instead of 30.
  - Marketing example: only run ads with tested hooks, and make 5x more of them.
  - Keep building checklists (ads, follow-up, sales-to-success handoff, activation). "100 golden BBs, not one silver bullet."
- If you keep asking for cheaper leads, you may be mispriced or just not good enough to earn more per customer.
- The big obvious thing is usually the problem. Ask owners: have you tried your own food, done your own workouts, been your own customer? "The magic you're looking for is the work in the work you're avoiding." (Chris Williamson quote.)
- Test from Peloton: make it so good that the next person a customer talks to hears about it first.
- Advertise only enough to pay bills while the product improves. Add gasoline once word of mouth drives growth. Alex bought into School.com after watching it since 2018 and seeing it grow with zero marketing.
- His windfalls came in distinct windows when he "backed the truck up":
  - Gyms: 30:1 return on ads because Facebook was underpriced.
  - Gym Launch: spent $100,000 and made $10 million, helped by word of mouth in a small niche because the licensees' gyms got results.

chunks.heading: Protect your focus and block time for what matters
chunks.text:
- Few things kill a business within hours. Gym story: a 5:30 a.m. call about a broken water pipe. Alex's answer: get a bucket and call a plumber. Eleanor Roosevelt: "That could have waited till morning."
- "Priorities literally mean prior." You must let some fires burn. The only real short-term killer he names is losing payment processing.
- He works the first 4 to 6 hours of the day uninterrupted on the one thing that, if true, would make other problems go away. Early on he woke at 4 and worked until 10.
- Meetings only in the afternoon, and he sometimes pushes them far out. He tells people he isn't taking meetings until his book launches, then until the company sells, so the no isn't personal.
- Executive assistants book "from the back forwards": if the day ends at 5, the first meeting is 4 to 5. The more his wife and partner Leila takes off his calendar, the more money they make. Her productivity is a stacked day: delegating, interviewing, reviewing projects.
- High-level entrepreneurship means always hiring ahead. At the top, every business is the same: marketing, sales, product, finance, legal, tech people.

chunks.heading: Build brand as your long-term investment
chunks.text:
- Brand is "an association people make between something they know and something they don't." Rub something they like onto your business.
- Three channels: what you say or show (controllable), what others say (referrals, reviews), and what customers experience (strongest). Product and brand are linked. Referrers risk their own relational capital, so treat referred customers well.
- Rule of marketing: "state the facts and tell the truth." Don't promise what you can't deliver.
- Brand strength shows up as price premium. Example: 1 million units at $3 above market is $3 million. A $300,000 fighter endorsement yielding $3 million extra is 10:1. Metrics apply as in direct response, just over a longer time horizon.
- Direct response is like a paycheck (stop paying, stop earning). Brand is like a 401k that compounds.
- Delivering on promises creates a moat (Apple buyers keep buying Apple). Reviews approximate experience.
- Lead magnets, challenges and nurture sequences approximate brand by compressing trust into hours. Big brands build the same trust across millions of people. It took Alex about a decade to learn this.

chunks.heading: Know your inputs and outputs, and avoid hacks
chunks.text:
- Ask "Why can't we 10x this?" to find the constraint. Example: a team spending $5,000 a day on ads and five salespeople. Why not $50,000? Bad ads mean ad process problems, call volume means hiring problems, delivery limits mean back-end systems problems.
- Break the constraint into the smallest inputs.
  - Ad process: weekly, rewatch your top 20 ads, collect ads you liked across platforms, remake the best ones, reformat them (old footage new edit, or same message new take), and make about 30 net-new remixes. Half a day prepping and half a day filming each week. Ask to see the saved hooks and remixes.
  - Hiring math: about 100 LinkedIn reach-outs yields one hire. If you lose a third of a rep a month, 3 reach-outs a day only replaces churn. To double the team in a quarter, about 500 reach-outs and about 50 interviews, so 10 to 15 interviews a week. Employee churn works like customer churn.
- Most people stop at what they're comfortable with (a 5-person sales team, $1,000 a day in ads). Alex has gone from zero to 40 salespeople in a company. A billionaire fund founder ran 200 interviews in 7 days.
- Stop chasing hacks and platform algorithm tricks. Ignore algorithm advice unless the platform's goal changes. Make something so good people share it.
- One exceptional thing beats 100 mediocre ones. Quantity teaches you how much work quality takes. A video 20% better might get 5x the views for about twice the work.
- People want value per second, not seconds of value. "You make the money in the edit... in the distillation, not in the creation."
- Coats of paint: edit in separate passes, each looking for one thing (punctuation, data, typos; for video, lighting, transitions, sound). Review at different times and moods.
- Document the process that produces quality as checkboxes (wireframe with hook, story, steps, conclusion; record; check transitions). This makes training and replacing yourself easier.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi walks through the six-stage entrepreneur cycle, why splitting attention kills most founders, how to hire and train (barrels vs. ammunition, 3Ds, specific feedback), and how to learn skills through volume plus feedback loops. He also covers choosing ideas (pain, profession, passion), standing out by being yourself, and defusing fear by playing it out in specifics.

chunks.heading: Fear, shame and the decision to start: "play it out" and guaranteed bad vs. a chance at good
chunks.text:
- Alex says people from zero to one think they need a tactic, but what they need is "the courage to be willing to be wrong" and to take shame by failing in front of people whose opinions they care about.
- His own path: white-collar consultant at 22 with a GMAT above Harvard's mid score and a clear path (top business school, consulting or banking, private equity). He left the state and drove halfway across the country before telling his father, then took a minimum-wage personal trainer job cleaning gym floors to learn the gym business.
- He says the decision to leave was the hardest of his career, and that in about 90% of universes he is "just a consultant somewhere."
- Fear is a label problem. He argues you are only a coward if you let fear change your behavior in a way that moves you away from what you want.
- Quit math: 3-6 months of personal savings, plus a side business that has matched your job income for 3-6 months. He notes this is almost never the real reason people don't quit.
- His decision frame: "guaranteed bad, chance at good." He asks people to look at "the don't," the alternate path, which is a guaranteed outcome they don't want.
- Fear "exists in the vague, not in the specific." Play the worst case out step by step:
  - You get a story you can tell, and possibly a better job later.
  - The real loss is some savings.
  - Worst case you stay on a couch or at your parents' place.
  - The leftover cost is self-inflicted shame, which becomes funny later.
- Delay discounting works both ways: people say they'll quit tomorrow for 20 years, and they "massively discount what a whole lifetime of misery would be."

chunks.heading: Picking an idea: the three Ps, first principles and leverage
chunks.text:
- Alex says business ideas come from one of three Ps, and you need only one:
  - Pain: a problem you've lived.
  - Profession: a skill from a past job, which is proven because the economy already pays for it.
  - Passion: something you'd spend time on anyway, such as model cars or Dungeons & Dragons.
- Pain gives deep prospect knowledge. His example is nasal products: he has tried every product since 8th grade, so he knows what's wrong with each. That story is more compelling to investors and customers than a feature list.
- Missionaries make more money than mercenaries, because they feel the problem. "What everyone wants to see is obsession."
- Anyone can break a business into fractional jobs (sales, marketing, customer success, support, design, web) and learn one to trade for money.
- The foundation is time. Everyone trades time for dollars, so the goal is the highest return on that time.
- He built Acquisition.com on two theses, shown in the logo as a fulcrum for leverage:
  - Supply and demand are the two foundations of business.
  - Leverage gets the most output from each input.
- Three levels of leverage:
  - Attract attention: one piece of content a million people see beats one-on-one outreach.
  - Convert attention: a checkout page or video sales letter beats a phone salesperson.
  - Deliver: software and media can be made once and sold a thousand times.
- With nothing, your assets are your brain, hands and time, so skill acquisition is the first move.
- On goal size: the bigger the goal, the narrower the path. $10M or $100M is possible in almost any business over a long enough timeline. Trillion-dollar goals need tech and AI. He says about $25M covers essentially any consumption.

chunks.heading: Standing out in 2025: courage to be yourself
chunks.text:
- Using a new personal trainer as the example, Alex says not to try to out-science the PhD who is already jacked.
- Your fingerprint, life and experiences are unique: "you're not going to beat me at being me but you'll beat me at being you."
- His own brand mix is business, marketing and sales, plus fitness, philosophy, his wife Leila, and dry or dark humor. The proportions differ for each person.
- Most products and services are commoditized. Personality creates a brand premium, like Prime against equivalent drinks: "if I have two things that are basically equal and I just like this guy better," people vote with their dollars.
- Sequence for a trainer: long term is building content, short term is outreach to people you know with a compelling offer.
- Branding is a mosaic. Each piece of content is a tile, and the proportions of colors become the brand. Don't plan "one post about family, one about finances"; be yourself and the proportions shake out.
- Leila's advice: "never dilute yourself." There are more people who need the message than who hate it, and impact brings equal and opposing force.
- Being disliked is a fixed cost, so be disliked for being you. He cites the Nike ad he posted on LinkedIn: about 80% neutral or negative, 20% "that is me."
- He is fine changing his views as he learns. His first podcast, from July 2017, started 90 days after he lost everything, and episode 8 is called "stop branding."

chunks.heading: Hiring, people and the swamp
chunks.text:
- Alex believes an organization's potential is tied to the combined intellectual horsepower inside it. The richest founders own small stakes: Jensen Huang about 4% of NVIDIA, Bezos 7-9% of Amazon, Musk about 20% of Tesla.
- He cites Keith Rabois's barrels and ammunition model: most people are ammunition, and the rate limiter is the number of barrels (people who can fire independently). He also cites the idea that the square root of headcount generates 50% of the work.
- Building a business is like a video game. Each new company you start, you move faster through the early levels, but each function has bosses (first sales hire, sales manager, marketing director). The goal is pattern recognition across every function.
- Standards rise with scale. A director of sales at $1-10M differs from one at $10-100M.
- If you don't know the job, do it yourself, then train with the 3 Ds: "document, demonstrate, duplicate." You document the steps, demonstrate them in front of the hire, then they do it in front of you. If you can't follow your own checklist, fix the checklist.
- A players hire A players, and a bad leader's rot can cost "three-quarters" of what's beneath them. Remove them fast; the pain of the fix "feels wrong but is right."
- Mental test: picture 5 versions of your best employee. If that would 10x the company, nothing else you're doing is likely worth more.
- Hiring mix (the "barbell"): young hungry people in learning mode, and late-career people who are there to share what they know. The middle, who want a tit-for-tat, are the biggest pain.
- Hire for the smallest skill deficiency. For low-skill roles, hire on attitude and train aptitude. For high-skill roles, hire the skill and teach the behavior.
- To lure someone exceptional, ask "what would it take?" He lists four elements of equity: control, risk, profits and sale value. Most hires want profits and upside, not risk or control.
- The swamp is roughly $1-3M in revenue. At $1M with 20% margin, an A player costs about 100% of profit. The choice is to sacrifice profit or work six more hours a day. "We have to be willing to make impossible choices."
- Example: a restoration company paid his aunt $60,000 a year only to call leads at once. It converted 55% of leads and brought in millions in revenue. He cites research that calling within 60 seconds can 4-5x lead conversion.
- To free up your time, log what you do in 15-minute increments for a week. Then hire for the roles taking 40% or 15% of your time. If you can't find a unicorn, hire three people for the pieces.

chunks.heading: Interviewing, feedback and culture
chunks.text:
- To test candidates, present the actual problems of the role and ask how they would fix them. A good answer covers:
  - The quality and quantity of metrics they track.
  - The behaviors that move those metrics.
  - How those metrics and behaviors drive revenue.
- Beginners think in binary ("ads don't work"). Experts break a failure into parts (hook, click-through rate, traffic quality, offer clarity, page congruence). He keeps asking "what does that mean?" until the candidate reaches concrete actions.
- If they can't explain it simply, they don't understand it, or they are obscuring it. Ask support reps how their job makes the company money.
- Culture is "the rules that govern reinforcement": what you reward and punish. Not correcting a late arrival sets the rule that lateness is fine. He cites Drucker: culture beats strategy.
- Reinforce immediately, as with training a dog. In script training he interrupts about 30 times in the first 30 minutes, covering a third of the script, with a repeat-until-right cycle.
- "Kind, not nice": not giving feedback is unkind.
- Criticism is a gap between actual and desired. An insult is the judgment attached to it. Use stop / start / keep, with a condition and a behavior.
- Example: a high-performing director people called a "dick" changed in a week with three or four specific behaviors (don't interrupt, don't give unsolicited advice).
- Replace "lazy" with data: slow Slack replies, incomplete projects, a messy background. Then set rules such as a 10-minute reply window during work hours.
- The ability to train people from B to A+ is large "Alpha," because you keep the gap between their pay and their output.

chunks.heading: Staying focused: the entrepreneur life cycle and the 10-year slug
chunks.text:
- The six stages (a loop he calls "the entrepreneur life cycle"):
  - Uninformed optimism.
  - Informed pessimism.
  - Crisis of meaning, or valley of despair.
  - Then either restart at stage one, living "the same six months for 20 straight years," or continue to informed optimism.
  - Success.
- The "woman in the red dress" is the Matrix metaphor for a shiny new business that is actually an agent trying to pull you off the path.
- His former CFO (four companies from $0 to $100M, over 40 M&A deals, one for $5B) told him "the grass is always greener... you just don't know that it's fertilized with [expletive]."
- 2024 was the first year he had no FOMO. He measures focus by the quantity and quality of things you say no to, and defines commitment as "the elimination of alternatives."
- Doing three things is "an exercise in arrogance and ego." Splitting attention caused his biggest mistakes. Bolting an e-commerce business onto his licensing company slowed revenue growth. At one point he ran Gym Launch, six gyms, and chiropractor and dental agencies. He distinguishes being an owner from being a CEO.
- Compare year 3 of your current thing against year 0 of a new one, not year 0 against year 0.
- Timeline: about 5 years to find which way is north, another 5 to build something that creates generational wealth. Most multibillion companies reach big numbers between years 6 and 10.
- After quitting a job you will work more and earn less for a long time. The first-dollar rush reinforces quitting, which he calls the lesson to "immediately unlearn."
- Entrepreneurs mostly fizzle rather than quit. He notes the "currency" of hardship changes at each level. Quoting Elon Musk, running a business is "staring out to the abyss and chewing glass."
- Your hypothesis is likely wrong from the start. Experts diagnose the constraint. His example is Facebook's fix of "10 friends in 14 days."
- Entrepreneurship is a game to be successful, not to be right. That can mean stepping aside as CEO.

chunks.heading: Growth mechanics: volume, testing, allocation and learning
chunks.text:
- Do more first. His mentor's gym flyer test size was 5,000, and then 5,000 a day. Alex put out 300 and called it failed. Low volume reads as volatility.
- Alex's team publishes 450 pieces of content a week. Most people post one or two and wonder why they lag.
- The Core Four to advertise: post content, run ads, cold outreach, and warm outreach.
- The 70/20/10 allocation (Google): 70% to core, 20% to adjacent, 10% to moonshots. Don't pull the stars off the core to build the new thing.
- Three strategic buckets:
  - Get more customers.
  - Increase lifetime gross profit per customer.
  - Decrease risk.
- Strategy is prioritization of unlimited opportunities against limited resources.
- Two question types: ones a spreadsheet can answer (LTV, CAC), and ones testing can answer.
- He tested book titles the same way ("$100M Leads" kept winning) and tested the cover and subheadline too. People want "the hole in the wall, not the drill."
- Market-expansion hack: spend $1,000 running your best promotion in five candidate markets, compare lead cost, and open in the cheapest one.
- The Four Rs of customer success: retain, review, refer, resell.
- Fast skill learning:
  - Do 100 reps.
  - Study the top 10%.
  - Add what they share to the next 100.
  - Repeat, as in Chris Rock's comedy sets.
- Consulting-style rapid learning: interview five experts, ask each for five more, categorize the notes, distill the truths, and infer next steps. Expert interviews cut through information overload.
- "Models, not mentors": you don't need one, but learn from people ahead of you. He drove across the country to seven-figure Sam's gym. A meetup of gym owners saved him years on equipment, square footage and rent. His rent limit was no more than $1.50 a foot.
- The value of a skill is the delta: $1M a year minus $50,000 means not knowing it costs $950,000 a year.
- Procedural knowledge (doing) beats declarative knowledge (knowing about). Be a practitioner, not a parrot. If you can't explain why you believe something, "it's not your belief, it's someone else's." Aphorisms can't be re-derived into the full reasoning.
- YouTube opening formula: proof, promise, plan, then picture and pain. He says this nuance separates a 10,000-view video from a million-view video.
- On copycats: if a thumbnail or format is all that makes you special, "we're [expletive] anyway." The 99% below the surface is culture and the next step competitors can't see. Copying means you are second.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex Hormozi condenses 13 years and nine companies into 13 marketing rules. Core themes: start cheap or free to create flow, scale with more then better then new, obsess over hooks, build around LTV to CAC, and narrow to a specific avatar. He also covers the four ways to advertise and the value equation.

chunks.heading: Start with free or low prices, then raise 20% per batch
chunks.text:
- Alex's rule: start low or free, because "it's very difficult to come down." Early on, the goal is to get flow through the system.
- His examples:
  - **Online personal training (13+ years ago):** clients donated $500 or $1,000 to a charity of their choice in exchange for 12 weeks of training. He got his first ~13 customers through posts and DMs. Afterward he asked if they would pay him directly, and many did and referred others.
  - **Gym Launch turnarounds:** for 2+ years he flew to gyms and set up pricing and marketing for free. He paid for flights, hotel, food and the ad spend, and only made money if the gym made sales. That tested the system in 30+ markets and led to licensing it to 5,000+ locations. He sold the company to APG for $46 million.
  - **Software company (Allen):** he began with free customers to get case studies and testimonials. Alex says this applies to big owners launching a new product or division, not only beginners.
- Four returns from free customers:
  1. They convert to paying after the period if you do a good job.
  2. They refer others.
  3. They give testimonials and reviews.
  4. They give feedback. Ask "tell me how I can make this better."
- Make the testimonial and referral contingent on doing a good job.
- The real test is whether they stay and pay at full price afterward.
- Give a reason for the discount, such as being new at this or trying something new, so you get grace.
- Tactic: after the first batch of 10-20 case studies, raise the price 20% for every 5 customers. For example, $1,000, then $1,200, then $1,500. Keep going until conversion rate times price falls. That is the sweet spot.
- His saying: "create flow, monetize flow, then add friction." Run water through the machine to see where it breaks, "rather than just trying to get rich on Excel."

chunks.heading: More, better, new: the scaling order
chunks.text:
- **More comes first.** A content mentor showed Alex he was posting once a week while the mentor posted 3x-10x more on each platform. The advice was just "do more."
  - A billionaire friend posted once a day. Alex's team was posting 50+ times a day across about 5 million subscribers.
  - A portfolio CEO made about 15 new ads a month. Alex made 35 a week when going from that size to 5x.
  - Alex's saying: "volume negates luck." People ahead of you are often doing 100x the volume, not 2x.
- **Competition and saturation.** A $2M/yr chiropractor ad agency spending $40K a month thought it had saturated Facebook. Alex pointed out that all chiropractor agencies together probably spend about $4M a month. That spend is the opportunity.
  - Paid ads are "an auction for attention." If your LTV is higher, you can outbid everyone and still profit.
- **Switch to better when the return on effort of better exceeds one more unit of more.** Going from 1 to 2 salespeople is a big jump. Going from 10 to 11 is only +10%, so a 20-25% throughput gain from tweaking scripts, headline tests or CTAs wins.
  - After better, go back to a 10x more.
- **Find the constraint.** Ask "What would stop me from 10x-ing the business right now?" If nothing, do it. If something would break, fix that first, then scale. Businesses grow until their constraint.
- **New comes last.** The cost of change is certain and the return is not. Entrepreneurs want to spend 80% of their time on new, but should spend about 90% on more and better of what works.
  - Do new things only when nothing works, or when you have hit a real ceiling. For example, a local gym spending about $10K a month that has saturated its radius should move to YouTube, Google search, display, direct mail or radio.
- **Give a new channel time.** Payback can take 3, 6 or 12 months. Don't judge on one month of spend. Track progress along the path: clicks, then opt-ins, then the right people, then calls or events, then sales.
- A second channel doubles lead flow and also makes the business more stable and more valuable.

chunks.heading: Optimize ads front to back: hooks, headlines and call outs
chunks.text:
- Alex cites David Ogilvy: after the headline, you've spent 80 cents of your ad dollar. In 13 years, the importance of the first 5 seconds, the headline and the packaging has only increased.
- Evidence:
  - Thumbnail changes alone can raise average view duration by 2-3 minutes.
  - Dean Graziosi spent $250K on a Larry King infomercial with no results. Larry King was flown back to re-record the first 30 seconds of the hour-long interview. The re-run did $100M in sales.
  - A huge creator stopped a copycat video 5 seconds in because the thumbnail and first 5 seconds weren't confirmed. The copy had 30M views against the original's 10M.
  - At an 8-figure portfolio company, changing only the landing page headline lifted booking rate 62%. The opt-in rate stayed the same.
- Effort split: if he has an hour, he spends about 55 minutes on the first 5 seconds. Per session he writes about 50 hooks, 3-5 "meat" sections and 1-3 CTAs.
- Why the front: a back-end fix like show rate going from 50% to 75% is a 50% jump. Hook work can take CTR from 1% to 4%, a 4x.
- Writing rules:
  - Assume the viewer doesn't know you, is in a rush, and has a third-grade education. "Clear beats clever, deletion beats explanation."
  - Shorten it, then run it through a third-grade reading-level calculator and keep editing. This doesn't attract dumber people. It makes the copy accessible to everyone. 30% of people can barely read, and some of them are rich.
- **Call outs.** A call out is whatever gets your audience's attention. Specific ones ("moms in Nevada," "homeowners in Clark County") make the reader say "this is for me." Very specific call outs often bring in more qualified leads than broad ones.
  - Find call outs by looking at competitors' long-running ads, which signal what works. Write down the words your customers use. Start with a problem or a question they'll say yes to.

chunks.heading: Alex's weekly ad creation process and the kaleidoscope method
chunks.text:
- **Collect data constantly.** He keeps no premium (ad-free) accounts so he sees and hears ads. He screenshots or records interesting ones into one swipe folder. If you are your avatar, "the ads count double."
- **Record the same day.** He does one session a week, first thing in the morning. He "crams for the test" by reviewing the swipe file and his best ads from the last 1-3 years, watching the first 10-30 seconds of each.
- **80/20 hooks.** Of 50 hooks, 40 are proven and recycled and 10 are new experiments. Most people flip this. The experiments become the next control if the old hooks fade.
- Meat angles: education, a belief to break, lists, steps, stories, or proof. Then a quick CTA.
- Ad results follow a power law, where the top 5% makes 95% of the income.
- **Kaleidoscope process.** When an ad wins, squeeze it. His example: a Gym Launch ad where customer Kale stood in his full gym and said he had gone from a full-time job and a 2-month-old to a gym with a $250,000 offer. Ways to remix it:
  1. Change the background or backdrop color.
  2. Add props or visuals.
  3. Re-enact it with the same script.
  4. Reorder the sections.
  5. Add visual filters (black and white, sepia, contrast).
  6. Add VFX.
  7. Change fonts and captions.
  8. Change the pacing or speed (1.2x or 1.5x).
  9. Add music.
  10. Keep the winning hook and re-record a different back half.
- His takeaway: "squeeze the living hell out of the winners."

chunks.heading: LTV to CAC and back-to-front business optimization
chunks.text:
- LTV:CAC is the one metric Alex would pick if he could know only one about a business.
- Definitions:
  - LTV is lifetime **gross profit**, not revenue. He uses LTGP.
  - CAC is the all-in cost to acquire a customer: sales, marketing, software, everything.
- Benchmarks are irrelevant. Everything comes back to gross profit.
  - Example: a bow with $500 gross profit, a $20 lead and 1 in 5 leads buying gives a $100 CAC and 5:1. At a $10 lead it would be 10:1.
  - Meal example: $10 meals that cost $9 to deliver leave $1 gross profit. Five weeks of 10 meals is $50 LTGP, so CAC must be about $15 or less.
- Rules of thumb:
  - Aim for at least 3:1 LTV:CAC.
  - Spend at most a third of LTV to acquire a customer.
  - Alex wants to recover CAC in the first 30 days. Sometimes that takes a one-time upfront charge.
- Estimating LTGP: take last year's customers and total gross profit, then divide gross profit by customer count. This underestimates recurring businesses, and he prefers that to overestimating.
- Starbucks makes about $14,000 in LTV per customer. Even a $500 CAC would be 28:1.
- His biggest wins came from ratios of 30:1 up to 100:1 or 200:1. Those windows are short, so dump money into the machine. Wealth is made in short bursts and sustained by 5:1 to 10:1 periods.
  - Ratios fall as you scale. For example, a 100:1 at $1,000 a day may become 5:1 at $100,000 a day. A big starting ratio shows how much room there is.
  - He cares about absolute return, not relative return.
- Back to front: advertise front to back, but optimize the business back to front. LTV sets what you can spend on the front. Either lower CAC or raise LTV. Doing both creates "huge arbitrage."
- Alex estimates it would cost about $50M to become an A-list celebrity, based on a no-name actor in a big Marvel hit. His point is that a $1B-gross-profit sale could fund reaching that many people.

chunks.heading: The core four, the 4-hour rule and the scaling ladder
chunks.text:
- There are only four ways to let people know about your stuff:
  1. Warm outreach (one-to-one, people who know you).
  2. Cold outreach (one-to-one, strangers).
  3. Content (one-to-many, people who know you).
  4. Paid ads (one-to-many, strangers).
- "If you're not spending your day doing one of those core four things, you are not advertising."
- At Gym Con, Alex asked owners doing about $500K-$3M a year who spends the first 4 hours of the day promoting. Nobody raised a hand. "This is why you're small."
- If you're under about $1M-$3M a year, spend the first 4 hours promoting, then run the business. Most businesses would make more money with more leads.
- "Nail it, then scale it": get flow in, fix the back end, then spend more.
- Scaling ladder:
  - $0 to six figures: one product, one avatar, one channel.
  - Six to seven figures: the same, but consistently.
  - Seven to eight figures: one avatar, one channel, two products (an upsell).
  - Multiple eight figures: two channels, one avatar, two products.
  - AG1 is an exception: one product, one avatar, many channels.
- **Awareness and runway.** Alex uses Eugene Schwartz's five levels: unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, most aware.
  - Beginners profit from most-aware audiences (their list and customers). If ads stall at a ceiling ($2K, $10K, $100K a day), the ads usually aren't good enough to reach the next awareness level.
  - His ~$100M/yr portfolio company spends millions a month and targets the most unaware, taking them through all the stages in one ad.
  - "The size of the plane is directly correlated with the length of the runway." More expensive and colder means more selling. Scaling trouble often comes from a mismatch, such as a warm message to a cold audience.
  - Cold audiences are like watermelon seeds: fewer buyers per thousand eyeballs. LTV:CAC may fall from 20:1 to 5:1 to 3:1, but at 100x the spend the absolute return is higher.

chunks.heading: Proof, truth and "say what only you can say"
chunks.text:
- **State the facts, tell the truth.** The top creator told Alex that his titles are clickbait but true, so the truth backs them up.
- Most businesses don't track results. "If you don't track, you don't care." Measurement itself improves outcomes.
- Gym Launch stats: the average gym after 12 months makes $100K+ in added profit. The bottom 20% averages $40,000 in additional revenue, roughly break-even. The top 20% is at $500K+.
- School.com: 30.44% of people who finish their first month make their first dollar online. After a new rollout, ~35% more people are succeeding, which he puts at a little over 40%.
- Steps: collect data at day 1, 30, 60 and 90 and at program end. Improve the product until the data is compelling. Then present four variables: the percentage of people, who achieve X outcome, in Y time or attempts, under Z conditions. Fewer conditions is better, even at a lower result.
- **Say what only you can say, show what only you can show.** Do epic stuff, then talk about it. This is "how I" instead of "how to."
  - Value per second matters more than seconds of value. Curated summaries work. He suggests selling to rich people the "same result in half the time for twice the price."
- Demonstrate rather than tell:
  - Agency: play a one-minute live lead call and ask "could you take 50 of these a month?"
  - Software: run a live demo on the prospect's own video.
  - Door-to-door sale: a salesman scrubbed gum out of Alex's gym turf and sold him $100 of cleaning product in about 13 minutes.
- Prospects discount testimonials by how likely the result is for them, so showing raises that likelihood.
- His portfolio case studies (adding 40 salespeople, cutting refunds by two-thirds) come from doing things, then reporting them.

chunks.heading: Narrow the avatar, expand deliberately, and provide value
chunks.text:
- **Better beats bigger.** A coach-of-coaches making $2M a year asked about going broader. Alex told him to get better, since the best takes the market.
  - Gym Launch served only micro gyms doing weight-loss before-and-afters. It excluded personal trainers, big-box, yoga, spin and Pilates for the first 4-5 years. It still makes $30M+ a year.
- Five ways to expand: up market (bigger, fewer customers), down market (more volume, lower price), adjacent (for example chiropractors or medspas), narrower, or broader. Most businesses need to narrow first.
- Vista Private Equity's lesson: study the customers in the data room, find the top 20% generating 80% of revenue, stop the rest, and expand that 20%. That can give the same size business with 5x the revenue.
- To find the top 20%, compare their psychographics, geographics, demographics and actions. Narrow to 2-3 variables, put those in marketing, and have sales sell only to them.
- Examples: a generalist agency found IT firms were 8% of customers but the most profitable. A second agency found divorce attorneys. Alex says a single avatar can support $100M-$200M a year.
- More than half of the portfolio companies they bought were made narrower. "Better creates bigger. Bigger creates bloat." "Growth is not a goal. Growth is an outcome of inputs."
- "You get far more leverage by doing the same thing a hundred times than doing a hundred things one time."
- **Value equation:** dream outcome, perceived likelihood of achievement, time delay (speed), and effort and sacrifice (ease). The ideal is something people want, with no risk, fast and easy. Find problems from content comments (the "endless content wheel") and from friction points in your own implementation.
- **Give away the secrets, sell the implementation.** Make free stuff better than competitors' paid stuff.
  - A dietitian-billing creator makes just under $1M a year in profit from 5,800 Instagram followers. She sells 5-10 cheat sheets a day at $99 plus 2-3 high-ticket sales a week.
  - Alex's 6-month broad-content test produced views but fewer business owners. Returning to hardcore business content raised opt-ins, book sales, workshop and portfolio applications even as views per video fell.
  - A multi-nine-figure marketing firm owner posts deep SEO content that attracts Fortune 500 executives who want to hire him.
- Steps: give away your best stuff (including low-ticket products). Add CTAs and team follow-up. Frame the CTA as personalization ("help apply this to your business"), not "more."
- 99% of free-content consumers never buy, so free content builds reputation.
- He has moved away from down-sells: 10% of buyers at 1/10th the price changes revenue by only 1%. Give that product away and focus on the best customers.
- **All advertising works. It's a matter of efficiency.** Reframe "Facebook doesn't work for us" as "I don't know how to make Facebook work for us."
- **Reminders over teaching.** "The news never changes, just the names." Repeat concepts in new formats, stories and avatars. Henry Ford's marketing director said "We haven't even started running it yet" after Ford had seen the ad for 3 months. Alex gets a viewer for one of his 50+ daily pieces if lucky.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Compilation of Hormozi's best sales talks: closing as logical decision help, the three-bucket objection map (circumstances, others, self), the CLOSER framework, tone and conviction, and how to scale and compensate a sales team. Includes real case numbers on show rate, close rate and in-house vs outsourced sales.

chunks.heading: Selling with logic: the philosophy behind closing
chunks.text:
- Alex says buyers are a mix of emotion and logic. Emotion lowers the action threshold, but logic makes the decision stick. He cites Charlie Munger: "we have a high moral responsibility to be rational."
- Emotional buyers often get a call two days later asking "I don't know why I bought." Giving the buyer a rational foundation keeps the relationship going after the emotion fades.
- Prospects want to believe you and want to buy. Your job is to help their logical brain justify a decision they already want to make.
- Selling happens before you ask for the sale. Closing begins once you ask.
- Expect "no" and plan for it. If they could decide alone they would already have sent the money.
- "If you didn't get a gasp from a price tag you didn't go high enough." A high anchor lets you walk down. He says $1,000 feels like a rounding error after $100,000, but sounds huge after $10.
- Selling is a transference of belief over a bridge of trust. Hot and cold streaks come from conviction, not skill.
- Trust needs real intent, because people sniff out whether you only care about closing. "The person who cares the most about the prospect wins the sale."
- Closers ask hard questions because they care. Stay curious: "ha, that's so weird, tell me more."
- Win the argument and you lose the sale. Closing is "a dance not a fight."
- Record every sale. Study the hot streaks to see where you paused, what you joked about, and how you asked.
- Red zone analogy: the top five NFL red-zone offenses made the playoffs 90% of the time. A strong closing skill covers many other weaknesses.
- Of 100 prospects, about 10% will never buy and about 10% always buy. Closing skill is for the middle 80%.
- Success metric: did I help them decide? If you are happy when they choose to own their power and not buy, the pressure disappears.

chunks.heading: Obstacles vs. objections, and the three distortions
chunks.text:
- **Obstacles** are disagreements raised before you ask for the sale (for example "I just want more information"). They are easy to break then.
- **Objections** come after the ask. Alex calls handling obstacles early "killing zombies" or "defusing the bomb." Confront things like spouse or time before you state the price.
- For the sale to work, the prospect must want the goal and believe three things: the product gets them the goal (the way they want to get there), others will support them, and it will work for them specifically.
  - Gym Launch lesson: people declined a $100 service but bought $400 of supplements, because they wanted to lose weight their own way.
  - For "it won't work for me," use proof: "How many people would you need to see for it to be more unreasonable not to believe than to believe?"
- Alex uses Albert Ellis's (CBT) three core distortions: circumstances, other people, and self.
- People peel the onion in order: circumstances, then others, then self. Time, money and fit sit on the outside. Authority comes next, then avoidance ("I need to think about it"). "I need to think about it" means you are finally talking to the decision maker.
- Say you understand, then ask a question and walk them one layer deeper. Do not argue.

chunks.heading: Overcoming circumstances: time, money, fit
chunks.text:
**Time**
- Seasonal ("I'm busy"): Do you want this to last? Will you be busy again? Then start now, while busy, so it sticks.
- Micro ("no time in my day"): "My wife pulled out my phone and said 'I guess I just found your time.'" A good program cuts the 90% of what you're doing that isn't working.
- The "when-then" fallacy: "when I have X, I'll do Y" flips the sequence. Examples: "I'll save when I'm rich" or "I'll buy the program that helps me make money once I have money."

**Money (four frames)**
1. A lot is good: "Is this a lot of money to you?" If yes, that's why you'll go all in, and the best stories come from people in your exact situation.
2. A lot in absolute terms but little relative to the result. If it adds $10k/month or gets you in a bikini, is it worth it? If yes, the issue is belief in the product, not price. Compare it to a degree costing $100-200k and four years.
3. "What is money good for anyway?" You will pay either way, in money or in time: "do you want it to take 12 weeks or 12 years?"
4. Resourcefulness over resources. He uses the Shoe Dog story, where Phil Knight borrowed and stalled vendors to survive. Everyone finds money for an unexpected tax bill or a Ferrari at $5,000.

**Fit**
- New identity, new priorities: the Sephora story, where girls were told to budget for makeup as they became women. Show the prospect's spending (nails, outfits) against their goal.
- Change the change: "The way you spend your first four hours of the day makes your bank account look the way it does." Is staying the same more painful than changing?
- Hypothetical: "If this were perfect, would you do it?" or "1 to 10, what makes it a 10?" If no, the issue is trust. If they name a gap ("no broccoli"), fix it ("green beans?") and close.

chunks.heading: Authority and avoidance (spouse, stalls)
chunks.text:
**Spouse or decision maker**
- First sidestep it: "What do you think they wouldn't like?" Then overcome that point directly.
- Use past agreements: "Do they approve of your current struggle? Then why would they oppose fixing it?" Flip the roles: "If your spouse needed this, would you support them?"
- "You're asking for permission instead of support." If you hand off the decision, you will resent them in two years.
- Delayed close: take the card now with a 3-day no-sweat guarantee. Alex jokes about the husband wanting you to sit with Cheetos.

**Avoidance ("I need to think about it") by time frame**
- **Past:** "It's a fast decision" gets sunk cost and "How long have you wanted this?" "Don't let it burn you twice": a bad past program should not block a good one. A 2018 prospect texted him years later with regret.
- **Present:** The rocking chair story. Time is not what they lack, information is, and you are the only source. Three yeses decide it: it can get you the goal, you trust me, it will work for you. Then ask whether they have access to the money.
- **Informed decision:** use a guarantee, "you can only make an informed decision from the inside."
- "Decide" comes from the Latin word meaning to cut off: which future are you killing?
- **Future:** magnify the pain ("five more years of this"), then lay out the options: win, don't try, or try with a guarantee.
  - Only walking out guarantees no result.
  - Other nudges: "Are you tired of another year of almost?" and "Does this move you closer or further from the goal?"

**Bonus close:** the reason you give for not doing it is the reason you need to do it. Fortunes come from risking a little money; invest in skills, because "the time tax of ignorance" costs more than any tax.

chunks.heading: What top salespeople do: opportunities and prep
chunks.text:
- Alex's three jobs for a rep: maximize opportunities, convert the highest percentage, and do both consistently for years.
- **Hours and availability**
  - The top seller works the most hours.
  - His software company Acquisition.com scheduled over 4,000 appointments a day. Availability was the strongest predictor of sales.
  - Nail salon example: the shops that said "no same-day" lost the customer.
- **Pull appointments forward**
  - Drag Thursday's call into an open slot today for a better show rate.
  - If a lead hasn't confirmed, push that slot and fill it with a responsive lead.
  - The solar rep who called every new booking immediately sold about four times more units than the second-best rep. He either closed right away or filled a later slot.
- **Two SOPs:** one for on-call (the script) and one for off-call (follow-ups, dragging appointments, cancelling). Most companies have none for the second.
- **Book a meeting from a meeting (BAMFAM, from Shiron Bamfam):** never end a call without the next meeting set. Address time obstacles on the spot.
- **Don't take rejection personally.** Work leads in volume. Keep a visible "kill list" of whales.
- **Referrals:** ask "who do you know?" so they must name someone. "Who do you know who is as awesome as you?" One new rep was 50% above the next rep just by asking everyone this.
  - Referrals close at roughly 80-90%.
  - If one in four refers, 1 sale in 4 becomes 2 in 5.
- **Prework:** personalized texts before the call ("which shirt size/gift card?") raise show rates.
- **Research and notes**
  - Spend about 10% of call length on prep. Five minutes of research makes the rapport and trust instant.
  - Alex built profiles of gym owners from their socials, noticing the gym layout before calling.
  - Read previous notes at the start of every call so the prospect doesn't repeat their story.

chunks.heading: Running the call: listening, scripts, and looping
chunks.text:
- The best reps listen about twice as much as they talk. The one answering questions is the one being interrogated.
- "They believe nothing you say, they believe everything they say." Answer questions with questions. Example: "What have you done before? What did you like and not like?" Then highlight what they liked.
- Do not ask for the sale until you know the answer, like a lawyer on the stand. If you sense hesitation, ask more questions. Name it: "I'm feeling some hesitation around price, talk to me about that."
- Use commands as well as questions to break patterns, such as "tell me about your day." Use childlike curiosity, with a tilted head and rising tone.
- Tone and emphasis change meaning. The same words delivered badly (say, "what are your main concerns?") land very differently.
- "Breathe the script." Know it cold so you can be fully present.
  - Cut words. Reps add coughs and extra questions that got rewarded by luck, and scripts bloat.
  - Shorter calls let you take more calls.
- Role-play every morning and work on one narrow part at a time (intro, close, "I need to think about it"). Run three good reps in a row. A coach who lists nine fixes gets none.
- Use ghetto tone and humor to confront hard topics in a light way, a trick he learned from Sam Bakhtiar.
- Confront hard things before the close: "What are you most afraid of happening? Let's play it out." Worst case vs. best case. He has probably closed more on this than anything else. One buyer with a Dave Ramsey envelope was handled this way.
- Ask again. "If you do not ask for the sale you will not get it." Handle the concern, then ask again, "looping." He once kept asking because the 3 pm slot was the last of the day.
  - Resolve the concern each time. Do not just repeat the ask.
- Meta skills
  - Three types of salespeople (from Mike Ary): dogs (need feeding), horses (need whipping) and tigers (kill for sport).
  - Treat low-quality leads as free practice. Jacob (his protégé) took the worst leads and improved fastest.
  - No blaming leads or circumstances. Give feedback one-on-one, not on group calls.
- **Metrics:** close rate alone is just an outcome. Track lead-to-booking, show rate, offer rate, close rate, cash collected percentage, and calls per close.
  - Raising the schedule rate 20% equals raising the close rate 20%.
  - Give the best leads to the best closers and the worst leads to new reps. He cites a timeshare rep who 5x'd his income this way and the company rolled it out nationwide.
  - Score leads to do this.

chunks.heading: The CLOSER framework and selling the vacation
chunks.text:
Alex built this from hundreds of scripts. It works for B2C and B2B, at $500 or $100,000. Each step is a milestone.

- **C - Clarify why they are there.**
  - "What made you come in today? What's your goal? Why is that important?"
  - "I just want information" is an obstacle to confront: nobody collects information all day, so what is the problem?
- **L - Label them with a problem.** "What I'm hearing is X, sound right?" They must admit it: "can't cure cancer until you admit you have it."
- **O - Overview past pain.**
  - What have you tried, how long, how did it work? Repeat the "pain cycle" until they run out.
  - Their sense of being understood is what makes them buy. Say it isn't their fault: they were missing one piece.
- **S - Sell the vacation.**
  - The pitch is under 3 minutes, three pillars (fitness, nutrition, accountability; or exclusive, timely, qualified leads), each told as a short anecdote.
  - Examples: brushing teeth for accountability; "do you need motivation to watch Game of Thrones?" for nutrition.
  - "Sell the vacation, not the plane flight." Skip modules, macros and URLs. Everyone gets to Maui (swim, boat, flight, private jet), and the price varies by service level.
- **E - Explain away concerns.**
  - Price: "If we gave away Ferraris at $5,000, they'd find the money."
  - Decision maker: "What if they said no?" Then past agreements, then forgiveness over permission.
  - Stall: teach a decision with three questions (does it meet your needs, do you want to work with us, do you have access to funds).
- **R - Reinforce the decision.**
  - Send a personalized CEO video and a handwritten card.
  - Customers decide in the first 48 hours after a sale whether they believe in you.
  - Memorize two things: your short stories and your obstacle overcomes.
- Train reps on the prospect, not the product. Don't let reps talk about the company's $100 million.
- Conviction fixes tone: re-read testimonials aloud daily, fix everything you can about the product, and never blame the customer. In the mortgage-leads story, the rep John had weak conviction until Alex showed him how he'd talk if he believed.
- Daily training: 60 minutes, five days a week. About 25 minutes reading the script aloud (restart on errors), 5 minutes of obstacles, then listening to a recorded call.

chunks.heading: Scaling a team and the diagnostic sale (case studies)
chunks.text:
**The six C's for scaling:** CLOSER sequence, consistent daily training with conviction, call recordings (Gong), communication cycles with feedback, cut the fat fast, and competition plus career path. Detail on four of them:
- Cut: if a rep can't close in the first one to two weeks, they likely won't. Fire a dud within 14 days.
- Competition: six-week cycles with mini-teams of mixed ability.
- Career path: milestone pay bumps (50, 100, 150 deals).
- No prima donnas or special snowflakes, because one top seller who ignores the process can lower the whole team's output.

**Case 1: replace outsourced "mercenaries" ($21.6M/yr profit gain)**
- The outsourced team took 20% commission, and less than 30% ascended.
- Five steps: hire a director (one who hires many), rebuild the comp, rebuild the process, scale to 40 reps in 12 weeks, and drop the outsourced team.
- Director criteria: been there and done that, metric driven, and humble, servant demeanor.
- Hiring outreach: recruiters, content and outbound. 100 to 1,000 messages is normal.
- Comp: pay Setters and closers, with ratchets (for example 10% to 15% to 25%) so winners win. Overall cost fell from 20% to 9%.
- Show rate rose from 74% to 91% (less aggressive copy, same or next-day bookings, personalized 3-way intros).
- Set-to-close scheduling rose from 53% to 94% (Setters paid on the outcome, not deqing early).
- Close-call show rate went from 63% to 87% (daily role-play, game tape reviews, one-on-ones, end-of-day reports).
- A video sales letter was added between calls, which handled common objections early.
- Close rate fell from 80% to 42%, but throughput rose: the ascension rate went from 20% to 32%.
- Cash collected went from $7M ($1.4M commission) in Q1 to $12M ($1.08M commission) the next quarter, a $5.4M change in one quarter, or $21.6M a year.

**Case 2: lifting a sales team in about 60 days (show rate, offer, close, cash)**
- Starting numbers: show rate 49%, offer rate 83%, close 27%, cash collected 47%, 56 units a month.
- Show rate fixes: ad targeting and the buyer's optimization were wrong (lead cost instead of cost per sale), no double-dialing, slow speed to contact, and no morning-of reminder.
- Org fixes: the CEO was a bad sales manager, so they hired an experienced director first. They then cut the weakest closers, raised Setter targets from two to four a day, made one Setter a lead-nurture specialist, and fixed the discovery script and looping.
- Results: show rate 70%, close 41%, cash collected 82%, units 56 to 93 a month.

**The diagnostic sale (10x recurring revenue)**
- At a 14-location chain (grown to 32), Alex rewrote the sales process in four hours. Average revenue per customer went from $200 to $800, and monthly revenue on that service line went from about $20,000 to over $250,000.
- The seven steps:
  1. Pre-sale questionnaire (agitates the problem).
  2. Collect info and a credit card as "profile setup."
  3. Current state.
  4. Desired state.
  5. The obstacle between them.
  6. Present the price tied to the goal and your vehicle (weight loss: 60 lb ÷ 1.5 lb a week = 45 weeks at $99/week = $4,500, with a guarantee).
  7. Incentivize prepayment.
- Principle: sell the goal, not the membership. Let the customer set the goal (the yogurt-scale analogy).
- Pricing steps (present the highest price first, then step down):
  - Anchor at the full price of $4,500.
  - Prepay discount of 20% ($3,600).
  - Half down for 10% off ($4,050).
  - Third-party financing.
  - Payment plan.
  - Final fallback: "let's book your next session."
  - Presenting full price first, then discounts, beats starting low and adding interest.
- Say "prepayment discount" and not "paid in full," because "paid in full" benefits the seller.
- Upsells should cost about 5x the base price. If 20% buy a $5,000 upsell on a $1,000 product, average ticket doubles.
- Recurring tricks: a friend replaced $300/month with a $10,000 program on a 36-month plan, and customers stayed 8 months instead of 3. Another friend ended a payment plan with an automatic recurring charge at the same price.
- Secret shop your own business. Alex found the chain skipped the pre-sale questionnaire and credit card, and never asked where customers wanted to be.
- Results: recurring revenue share from 9% to 60% of that service line, memberships 0 to 30%, visits from 1 to 4-6.

chunks.heading: Alex's background and operating context
chunks.text:
- He started a gym in Baltimore, then added a phone to the funnel after a Facebook ad slap: front-end ROI went from a 2-to-1 loss to 10-to-1, and he could afford $100 leads instead of $10.
- He did about 4,000 one-on-one sales, with roughly 20 consults a day for four years across his gyms.
- He joined Sam Bakhtiar's $10,000 Mastermind at 22 after waffling. Later a business partner emptied his bank account, leaving him with $1,200 and bankruptcy, which he calls an experience he is grateful for.
- Later he scaled Gym Launch (over 1,000 clients hit $100k a year) and bought sales programs from Grant Cardone and Jordan Belfort. He says "simplicity is what scales."
- His lifetime return on ad spend was 36 to 1 at under $3 million in spend. Alex Becker told him this was the highest on the platform.
- He taught 116 salespeople his closing framework, and they increased how much they closed.
- He says buy education and experiences rather than assets. Skills can't be taken by a government, and the "time tax of ignorance" costs more than any other tax.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: placeholder

chunks.heading: Core Four growth: spend the first 4 hours a day on being known
chunks.text:
- Alex says that under $1 million in revenue, "basically everyone on Earth doesn't know you exist."
- He says the first 4 hours of every day should go to moving from obscurity to awareness.
- The method is the core four: outreach (cold or warm), content, or ads. Pick one, go all in, and spend those 4 hours on it daily.
- He calls advertising a "boom", his internal term for a business order of magnitude change. Optimizations are capped at 100%. For example, raising close rate or opt-in conversion by 10% has a ceiling. Advertising can 100x the number of people who find you.
- He warns against the "optimization mouse trap": nudging a ratio from 10.1 to 10.2 when the answer is "just get 100 times the leads."
- On results: Used Allen reached $1.2M/month by the end of year one, Prestige Labs $1.5M/month, and Gym Launch over $2M/month.

chunks.heading: Shrink competitors by growing, not by attacking
chunks.text:
- Most owners see the market as one pie that each new competitor shrinks. Alex says the real market is far bigger, and you are usually advertising on one slice of one medium.
- Gym example: a gym needs about 200 members to be very profitable. With 1 million people in the city, it needs a tiny fraction of the audience, even if 100 other gyms advertise on the same platform.
- To "shrink your competition," you can grow so big that no one hears them, or you can respond with kindness. His Eminem analogy: "Who?" for the first, and claiming your own flaws for the second.
- On the building analogy: you can knock others down or build the tallest building so they look small. He says to build the biggest building.
- His hate-response rule: start with "you are right." He then adds a compliment, such as congratulating the critic on their audience. This avoids back-and-forth.
- He also states his flaws first, for example "I'm here to make money," so critics have nothing to expose.
- Repetition is not bad. At his 100 Million Dollar Leads launch, with roughly 7 million followers across platforms, 19 out of 20 people he stopped on walks in Las Vegas did not know about the launch. His line: "people need to be more reminded than they need to be taught."

chunks.heading: Clear, not clever
chunks.text:
- Alex analyzed his highest-converting ads and checked the grade level of the language. He ties this to research that the president who spoke at the lowest grade level tended to win.
- His rule is "clear, not clever." For landing pages, ad copy and content, ask: does a third grader understand this?
- He says simple language helps experts understand faster and helps beginners get it at all. He does not see it as talking down.
- Email test: run emails through a reading-grade app and keep editing until they are below fifth grade (third grade is better). He did this on email follow-ups and got a 50% increase in conversion without changing the message.
- Match analogies to the audience. Mechanics get car analogies, realtors get house analogies, baseball people get baseball. A broad audience gets universal ones like food, sleep or driving.
- His reasoning: complexity hurts the value elements of speed and ease. He quotes Feynman: if you can explain it to a third grader, you understand it.

chunks.heading: Proof over promise, and the hook
chunks.text:
- Alex says proof beats promise. Example: a business with a long promise and one review versus one with 11,382 reviews at 4.7 stars. Buyers choose the second.
- Before entering a new space, he gets beta users first. He works for free in exchange for testimonials, reviews, feedback and referrals. He rejects "never work for free", saying it comes from people who don't make much money.
- Show, don't sell. He also says to "do epic stuff first, then talk about what you did." His channel worked mainly because he had sold a company for just under $50 million.
- Keeping early negative feedback quiet is another reason to start free.
- "The hook is greater than everything," because no one sees the proof unless the hook works. Four ways to advertise: warm outreach, cold outreach, paid ads, content.
- A better hook can raise click-through or open rates from 1% to 5% or 2% to 10%, which can move a whole business 2x to 5x.
- His hook formula, from reviewing his top YouTube videos, is proof, promise, plan. He uses both a visual hook and a verbal hook.
- He cites Ogilvy: once you've written the headline, you've spent 80 cents of your advertising dollar.
- Speaker intros: changing the 1-2 minute intro for a 60-minute talk changed the speaker's net promoter score a lot, even though the talk itself was identical.
- Case: his team cut the first 3 seconds of a video before the real hook. It went from about 40,000 views to 780,000, a 19x improvement.

chunks.heading: More, steal from yourself, and low volume looks like volatility
chunks.text:
- Of more, better and new, he calls "more" the highest risk-adjusted return, and says shiny object syndrome is "a cancer." The goal is one to N, not zero to one.
- When you change something that works, you "incur the cost of change" but are not guaranteed the benefit.
- Sales example: a rep closing 30% might reach 40% with effort, a 25% lift overall. Hiring three more reps is a 4x or 300% improvement, and changing the script risks dropping from 30 to 20.
- How to do more: go from 100 to 200 outreaches a day, $100 to $200 a day in ads, or one post to two posts a day. He notes some businesses spend $2 million a day on ads.
- Story: his first gym's flyers. He put out 300 flyers and got one call, from a man who said the flyer damaged his Mercedes. His mentor tested with 5,000 and then ran 5,000 a day for 30 days, about 150,000 flyers. His lesson: "what presents as volatility is typically a symptom of low volume."
- Volume math: if you close 12 customers a year, getting 12 a day takes 365 times the activity.
- Steal from yourself, with the 70/20/10 split. Put 70% of effort on carbon copies of what works, 20% on adjacent variations, and 10% on brand new ideas. He says most owners have this flipped.
- Example of adjacent: rewording "starting school communities is the fastest way to start an online business" into "one of the fastest ways to start an online business is to start a school community." Another is the same hook with a different shirt or setting.
- Portfolio story: a new advertising director's new ideas all failed. Reusing the hook that had worked for 3 years worked again. His Nike "Just do it" point: you get bored of a message long before customers do.
- Building analogy: there is one arrangement of bricks that makes a building and unlimited ways to destroy it, so deviating from what works usually breaks it.

chunks.heading: Negative word of mouth
chunks.text:
- Alex says negative word of mouth is much stronger than positive. He cites a Disney study that 37 tragic moments are needed to make up for one magic moment, and the idea that happy customers tell 5 people.
- Diagnosis: if CPM (cost per thousand impressions) is flat but cost per lead is up 2x to 4x, fewer people are responding. That means word of mouth is working against you.
- The audience that is neutral or has not heard of you shrinks over time.
- His tactic: keep early negative feedback concentrated by working for free and asking customers how to make it right. Introduce strangers only after consistent positive feedback.

chunks.heading: Brand: high-information buyers and the 70/30 give-to-ask ratio
chunks.text:
- Alex rejects the "emotional vs logical buyer" split. He sees a continuum of how much information a buyer needs and how much they have received.
- Low-information buyers are a small pool that everyone fights over. High-information buyers are orders of magnitude more numerous. Direct response alone caps growth because it only reaches the small pool.
- He uses Eugene Schwartz's five awareness levels: unaware (broad curiosity hooks), problem aware, solution aware, product aware, and most aware (where you just make offers).
- New Balance example, via CMO Chris Davis: the budget was 30% broad emotional awareness and 70% "buy these shoes." He flipped it to 70% pairings, endorsements and athletes, and 30% direct asks. Returns took 18 months.
- Alex applies the same ratio to his own impressions: 70% or more should be giving, not asking. He cites the roughly 3.5 to 1 give-to-ask ratio seen in TV (1 minute of ads per 3.5 minutes of content) and in Facebook feeds (1 ad per 3 posts). He also credits TikTok's early ad-free growth.
- When founders leave, executives often flip the ratio and "suck all the water out of the well" without digging the next one.
- B2B version: aspirational outcomes you achieved, outcomes for people like your avatar, and outcomes for the prospect. The prospect's own results come from free content and free products, like his free books and courses. This works because of degrees of separation (two, one, zero), and zero is strongest but slowest.

chunks.heading: Marketing laws: state the facts, say what only you can say, and target the right list
chunks.text:
- Law one is "state the facts and tell the truth." Make the truth more compelling by changing reality (do epic things), and show only what you can show.
