- Martial arts example: the owner was one of six "double secret black belts" in the nation, with none in his area. Alex told him to say exactly that.
- The Mad Men "It's toasted" example: other brands may also toast their tobacco, but only one says so. Narrow down to something unique. Be the best in a puddle: "It's more important that you are the best than what you are the best of."
- Rockefeller overpaid for the biggest Cincinnati refinery to claim the top spot. In the next 30 days he did over 20 M&A deals, which paid for the overpayment.
- The list: wrong audience is why many marketers think marketing doesn't work. A winter coat shown in South Florida fails regardless of offer.
- Targeting by channel: reach people likely to have the problem (outreach), use platform targeting (ads), and note that content is shaped by the algorithm.
- Make the person in the ad look like the avatar. On Gym Launch's thank-you page, swapping his photo for Leila's boosted response and show rates.
- Test of a good list: if the right 1,000 people are in the room, even a mediocre offer gets some response and starts the feedback loop.
- Masters have more ways to win. A recruiting expert asked about time to fill, two-sided fit and cost to acquire talent, metrics Alex had never tracked.
- When he started outbound, his team did an "intervention" after 4 months and one sale. Progress was hidden in milestones: finding a good list provider, enriching data, local numbers, fixing the hook and script, fixing the offer, and fixing no-shows. "A heart surgery looks like murder to somebody from the outside."
- Track leading indicators, not only lagging ones like revenue, churn or sales.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A full sales course drawn from 4,000+ closes. Most revenue gains come from what happens around the sale: selling seven days, sub-minute lead response, 15-minute slots, lead allocation and show-up rates. Inside the call he teaches proof-promise-plan, the pain cycle, AAA overcomes, and never answering a question you can't predict.

chunks.heading: Sales multipliers: sell seven days a week and book weekends
chunks.text:
- Alex has personally closed 4,000 sales over 13 years. He says the biggest gains come from what happens around the sale, not on the call itself. "These are all the things that happen outside of the sale that affect your sales more than anything that happens inside the sale."
- Selling 7 days a week adds 2 days x 52 weeks = 104 selling days a year, a 29% increase over a 5-day week.
- Many prospects are only free outside 9 to 5. In fitness, Alex closed all his sales between 4:00 and 8:00 p.m.
- Skipping weekends stacks Monday with appointments that no-show or reschedule. People click the ad and book on Saturday and Sunday, so give them same-day or next-day slots then.
- In his portfolio companies, many people schedule on Saturdays and Sundays for Monday. Weekend bookings for the weekend also show up at higher rates.
- He cites two data sources: a Harvard Business Review case study across large industries, and Acquisition.com's software company Allen (4,000+ appointments per day), where click-to-close data was visible.
- At Allen, opening up calendar availability was the strongest correlate of overall throughput, more than a 10 to 20% lift in closing percentage. Closing rate can't realistically rise 400%, but these multipliers can.
- Policy: same day or next day only, because show rates are higher. If that leaves appointments unbooked, "you need to hire more sales people".

chunks.heading: Speed to lead and "call now"
chunks.text:
- Contacting a lead within 60 seconds raises the likelihood of closing by 391%. Alex says that alone could 4X a business.
- Beyond 5 minutes, close likelihood drops by 80%, for example from 4 in 5 to 20%. He argues "lead quality is going down" is usually really about how well leads are worked.
- 50% of prospects go with the business that responds first, not the best one. His example: Lila called salons asking "are you available right now?" and booked the one that said yes.
- People have "huge motivation for a tiny period of time". Speed of response also signals how buttoned up the business is. A call within 5 seconds of opting in makes a strong first impression.
- Add a "call now" option on the scheduler. If qualification matters, show it only after the lead is qualified.
- If you lack the sales capacity, hire one more rep when the revenue lift (double or triple) is far bigger than the rep's cost.

chunks.heading: Scheduling design, off-the-call SOP and show rates
chunks.text:
- Alex's team replaced 1-hour slots with 15-minute start increments. A call blocks the next three blocks, then another rep's booking can start. Allen saw higher schedule and show rates because people pick the time that is precisely convenient for them.
- Don't fake busyness by hiding slots. "It doesn't do anything... it just makes it less convenient."
- Awkward gaps between calls are handled by hiring more reps and by an off-the-call SOP (most teams only have an on-the-call one).
- Off-the-call SOP: call booked leads, qualify them, then say "I had an opening later today, do you want the slot?" This turns a three-day-out appointment into a same-day one with a much higher show rate. If they can't move it, you have still contacted them within minutes. It also raises rep utilization and frees a future slot.
- Show rate vs close rate: a 20% lift in show rate equals a 20% lift in close rate, and it is easier if reps already close at 35%. Alex shouts out the closers with the highest show rate every week, optionally with a flat $500 weekly bonus. He says this can lift sales more than sales training.
- Reminder sequence (from Allen): 24 hours before, the morning of, and 1 hour before.
  - Automate the early reminders but don't pretend automation is a person.
  - Add manual ones layered on top. At 24 hours, show prep, for example "I looked over your site, we found three things we can help with", or "I set aside a t-shirt, what size?" for a weight loss customer. Five minutes of prep can lift show rate by 30%.
  - Prefer blue iMessages over green texts, and use voice memos and video.

chunks.heading: Feed the killers: lead allocation
chunks.text:
- Alex's rule: the best leads go to the best closers, and the worst leads go to the worst closers. This minimizes net waste.
- Story: a time-share rep in his building was the top rep out of 3,000, winning five of six years, and earned about $3 million a year. His prize for winning was an hour with the CEO. He used it to argue against round-robin lead distribution. The CEO tested it at his location and his income went from $250,000 to $3 million a year. Rolled out nationwide, it 5x'd the company.
- Fringe benefit: reps will take below-market pay for the shot at being top dog.
- New reps learn on the hardest leads and earn better leads by surviving.
- Lead scoring (greens, yellows, reds) supports this. New reps should "be a trashman" and take as many hard leads as the company allows, treating "yellow equals gold" as free training. Closing the hardest prospects makes easy ones easier. He adds: if someone truly can't benefit, don't sell it.

chunks.heading: Sales training: drills, game tape and culture
chunks.text:
- Most orgs run churn factories. If you can train, you can pay below market, because you turn unskilled hires into good closers. That is the business owner's arbitrage.
- Daily huddles are role plays. Set the frame first: "no one's perfect, that's why we practice". Leaders must drop their ego.
- Give feedback one piece at a time, immediately, and in real time. Say "great, keep going" during the role play, and warn reps you will stop them 30 to 40 times.
- Once they get a line right, have them repeat it 2 to 6 times in quick succession to drill it in. Focus on a single skill for a week or two.
- 1-on-1s: the manager listens to calls, finds all 28 mistakes, then picks the one that most lifts close rate. This is why training is a full-time job. Examples: asking for the card, setting the agenda, losing the frame, zooming out.
- The best closer is usually not the best sales manager (hunter vs patient leader). Coaches like Phil Jackson need not out-play Michael Jordan. Tell the team "I hope you're better than me at sales".
- Competition: make it "us versus them", with a big enemy or rival, rather than rep vs rep. Internal one-upmanship costs closers who thrive in teams.
- Record every call across the customer lifecycle. Run a weekly game tape review with sales and customer success together. They review sales calls and onboarding calls so sales sees what happens after close.
  - This reduced CS resentment at over-promising. CS sometimes offered extra features sales hadn't known about.
  - It cut cold-feet drop-offs of 5% to 10% and improved sales conviction.
  - Alex copied this from software companies when he started Allen.
- When a closer is "hot", record and study those calls: tone, opener, transition to the close, how objections are handled early. "Good closers try and get hot, great closers never get cold."
- In a slump, read testimonials to the team and credit the closer who closed that customer. Conviction fixes tone better than drills. At his gyms, close rates were absurdly high on weigh-out day because prospects had just watched 5 to 20 people show results.
- Sales is "passing conviction from one person to another... over a bridge of trust". If the prospect knew what you know and wouldn't buy, but you got them to, you deceived them.

chunks.heading: Before the sale: pre-framing, qualification and scripts
chunks.text:
- The sale starts at the click. The ad, the setting script and the questions asked all influence the buy, so build a seamless click-to-close experience.
- Setter script (local business): "Hey John, question..." then pause. "It's Alex, you opted in on Facebook for our promotion... I wanted to make sure you weren't a crazy person on the internet." Give three mental cues about what they opted into, since people forget. Offer two time options ("2:00 and 4:00 today, which works better?").
- Edify the closer. A setter says "Sean has helped 400 people just like you... he has an opening this afternoon, let me confirm". It beats "someone will reach out". Edify the business too, for example with a "best of" list that, per Alex, usually costs about five grand to be on.
- Alex admits that early on he pretended his gym had multiple employees. He calls that a white lie and says it was deceiving, so don't do it.
- Qualify with BANT (from an IBM study): Budget, Authority, Need, Timing. Confirm it on the application, the call and again before asking for money.
- Outbound hook: "Hey, I'm calling about [competitor]. Give me a call back." It works by email and voicemail, and curiosity drives response.
- Prep for five minutes before each call. Notes must be in the CRM so the prospect never repeats themselves. Repeating back what they told you helps the sale, and making them repeat it hurts.
- Energy: Alex had a mini trampoline in his sales room. He did 20 to 25 in-person consults a day, up to 48 in a 12-hour day, and jumped between them. "You can't be in a bad mood and jumping on a trampoline."

chunks.heading: The call itself: agenda, script adherence and the CLOSER framework
chunks.text:
- Open with proof, promise, plan, in 15 to 20 seconds, the way he opens content. Example: what you're here to fix, "we've done this with lots of people like you", the process, and "at the end we'll see if it makes sense; if not, no sweat". A banker's "can we skip the foreplay" is the model. His rationale: controlling the frame shows professionalism.
- BF Skinner analogy: control every variable and you could close every prospect, like salting a horse's mouth.
- Follow the script. Script adherence is the first drill. "If everyone follows the script and doesn't close you have a script problem."
  - The script runs up to the ask, and the first two-thirds should be near word for word. After the ask, objection loops branch.
  - Script the tone: emphasis (where you pause), tone (up or down, a question vs a statement), and pacing (slow for key points).
  - Use Google Docs formatting as cues: underline = slow down, caps = emphasize, italics = create space.
  - Keep it to about 12 questions.
- CLOSER framework: Clarify why they're here, Label the problem (the gap between present and desired), Overview past pain, Sell the vacation, Explain away concerns, Reinforce the decision.
- Clarify by reminding them of the action they took (for example "what made you set a call on my calendar?"). People don't want information, they want a problem solved.
- Pain cycle: "the pain is the pitch." Deprivation creates motivation. Quantify time, money and effort spent so far, and the daily cost of inaction. Anything they tried before is an advantage because it failed. Example: "I already have a personal trainer." "Yeah, he's obviously not doing a good job, but... you're here."
- Three-pillar pitch: chunk the offer into three parts, because people think in threes. Weight loss: fitness, nutrition, accountability. Lead gen for mortgage brokers and Realtors: timely, qualified, exclusive. Keep it under 2 minutes and spend about 90% of effort understanding the prospect's pain, not the product.
- Sell the vacation (Maui), not the plane ride (TSA, shoes, security). State the pillar, then give a metaphor. Examples:
  - Three-legged stool.
  - Toothbrush: as a kid you needed a parent's external accountability, and later it became internal habit.
  - The Amazing Race couple who hired a local in the back seat.
  - SEO vs ads as an investment account vs a paycheck.
- Ghosted prospects: send a meme (the Kevin Hart "where you at" meme). He says it has the highest response rate of any message they've sent; sent to 200 cold leads it re-engages roughly 5 to 10.

chunks.heading: Closing and objection handling
chunks.text:
- Train sales back to front. Teach payment collection first, then asking, then the top of the script. "Closing begins once someone says no." No is to be expected.
- When they say yes, shut up and take payment ("don't sell yourself out of a sale").
- If an objection surprises you, you're underprepared. Use AAA: Acknowledge (repeat their last phrase, which buys time and builds rapport), Associate (a positive, or someone like them who got results, or an authority such as a senior engineer), then Ask the next question.
  - Associations act as foils so you can say harsh truths without attacking the prospect: "Someone earlier had the same issue; can I share what I told them?"
  - Get permission first if you hold authority ("can I be a coach instead of a friend?").
- Core laws: "He who asks the most times gets the most sales." The person asking questions is in control. Stay curious ("huh, that's interesting"), don't disagree with prospects, and be "like smoke". You can agree with the reason behind a statement. "Be right, not rich."
- Rapid-fire stall questions, in order:
  - "What's your main concern?"
  - Later in the sale, "What are you afraid of having happen?"
  - "What variables are you using to decide?"
  - "What makes this a yes?"
  - "What makes this a no?"
- All-purpose closes:
  - "Do you think [their objection] is the reason you haven't succeeded so far?"
  - The 1-to-10 close: "What would make it a 10?" If they say 6, ask "why not a 1?", then "are we feeling tennish?"
  - Best case / worst case (strong with a guarantee): both options are risk-free.
  - When lost in the details, say "big picture" and zoom out.
- Details are death traps. Never give a blind answer.
  - Ask a question about their question: "Which certifications are you looking for?"
  - Chunk up to the reason behind the detail, then offer your answer.
  - Use the mechanic/secretary close ("I can't ethically answer before looking under the hood").
  - A detail objection is a preference obstacle: they want your results their way. "You change the variables, you change the outcome."
- "Kill zombies early." Handle BANT items (decision makers, timing, budget) before asking for money, while you are still a guide on the same side of the table. When in doubt, repeat it back.
- Stack closes from different angles on the same obstacle. For "no time": cut 90% of what isn't working, it's a prioritization question, and "will you ever not be busy again?" Don't memorize closes; understand the theory behind each type:
  - Time: it's priorities.
  - Decision maker: support, not permission.
  - Details: preferences.
  - Money: value and resourcefulness, since a Ferrari for five grand would get funded.
  - Stalls: decision avoidance (fear, or not knowing how to decide).
  - Keep only 2 to 3 closes per obstacle.

chunks.heading: Specific overcomes and handling price
chunks.text:
- Cheap competitor: "If ours was the same price as theirs, which would you choose?" Let them list why you're better.
- ID close (in person): ask for ID first. The wallet comes out, the "forgot my card" excuse dies, and you can verify the ZIP code. On Zoom, ask them to hold ID up to the camera.
- Decision maker, in four steps:
  - Ask "what would happen if they said no?" About 1 in 3 say "I'd do it anyway".
  - Ask what the partner's main concern would be, and isolate it.
  - Use past agreements. If they already know about your pain, why wouldn't they approve fixing it?
  - Last resort: support, not permission. Involve spouses or partners earlier for expensive purchases.
- "Give me some time" is decision avoidance. For a "let me circle back in a couple of quarters", ask "what will you do instead?", then "will it make you more than this?", then put math on it. Example: a 30% conversion lift with 90% gross margin and 30% net margin could double profit. If something else really is better for them, he says to let them go.
- No guarantee: the anti-guarantee. "If you're the type who needs a guarantee, this isn't for you", since you can't control what they do.
- "Let me use your free stuff first": agree and say "do that; either you succeed and hit a new problem I can solve, or you fail and I can help."
- Enterprise and government sales, with 6 to 12 month cycles and committees, don't fit this transactional approach. There, the number of contacts between both teams raises the chance to close.
- "Wow, that's expensive" is an observation, not a no. Don't waste bullets on zombies that aren't there.
- Never change price to close. Test prices ahead of time, premeditated. Change terms (payment plan) or components (a feature downsell) instead.
- Reply to "can you do it for less?" with "we could do it for more." Alex says it has never failed him. It counter-anchors, creates fear of missing out, and signals buying intent.
- Reinforce the decision. After payment, do a handshake handoff to customer success, not a hand-off. Introduce the CS person with edification, then restate the proof, promise and plan personalized to the customer's pains.
- BAMFAM (book a meeting from a meeting): every customer knows when and with whom the next meeting is, and that person knows the whole history. This cuts back-outs, cold feet and 30-day refunds.

chunks.heading: Sales team, hiring, comp and mindset
chunks.text:
- Hiring:
  - Resumes don't matter for transactional sales. Twice his teams couldn't scale because they screened resumes heavily. Alex prefers group interviews with 1 to 2 minute turns: stars speak up, communicate clearly and encourage nervous peers.
  - Hire for the lowest skill deficiency, not "attitude over aptitude". Soft traits bundle many skills (kindness may be about 20), and training the script takes only 2 to 3 weeks. This flips for rare technical expertise, and matters less for lower-level roles.
- Compensation recruits but doesn't retain or change behavior. The one exception is paying on cash collected, which gets more cash collected. Fast, low-intensity feedback loops change behavior more. Tip: a Zap from the CRM to Slack for submitted, processed sales, so Slack kudos reflect real closes.
- Sales and marketing are one continuum. He puts them under one revenue leader (a CRO) and says conflict disappeared. Sales is personalized marketing: if marketing covers pieces 1, 2, 3, sales covers 4, 5, 6.
- Trust and belief are continuums, not binary. A bigger purchase needs a longer runway, like a bigger plane. If you need 3 to 5 calls to close, pre-market and educate more so the first call starts near the 5-yard line.
- Mindset as behaviors:
  - The person who cares most about the prospect wins the sale. Turn away people who aren't a fit. Be "kind, not nice", and ask the hard questions. Avoid "commission breath".
  - Volume negates luck. Do double the best closer's effort (the Kobe Bryant model). Skill rises slowly while income spikes at mastery, so don't quit in the early dip. Alex did not close his first sale.
  - Aim for prospects to talk about two-thirds of the call. Let silence sit.
  - "Don't be cute": run the fundamentals every time (from a Long Island serial private-equity CEO's backyard-football analogy: "two fat guys in the middle run to the right"). Great closers always prep, hand off warmly, check notes, and set the agenda.
  - "No for now" is not "no forever". Pulse-check every 3 to 6 months, with memes or short emails.
  - People want to buy. Give them the excuse to justify it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi live-consults a supply-constrained coaching business burning cash on a 5-day challenge funnel. He fixes capacity by changing the delivery ratio, collapses two offers into one simple high-ticket offer, pulls cash forward with layaway, and turns daily organic content and in-person events into the ad and renewal engine.

chunks.heading: Diagnosing the coupleneur business: a supply-constrained offer and a weak front end
chunks.text:
Kyle and Ariel run Couple-preneurs, a coaching business for entrepreneur couples (clients do $150K+ a year). It does $480K revenue and $206K profit (about 43% margin). Alex's read is that the business is "supply constrained", and the founders solved that by building a second product instead of fixing the first.

- **Offer 1, Rise Together:** $5,000 paid in full, or 12 x $500. It has weekly group calls, a replay portal, a Facebook group and quarterly date night challenges.
- **Offer 2, Couple-preneur Accelerator:** $25K paid in full, or 12 x $2,500. It has quarterly 2-on-2 strategy calls, weekly small-group Q&A calls, and Slack access with a 24-48 hour response promise.
- **Current load:** 42 couples, and only 4 left in 12 months (all over payment issues).
- **Slack cost:** The founders say removing Slack would give back about 40% of their time.
- **Alex's diagnosis:** The low-touch product had the same customer acquisition cost as the high-touch one, so the economics broke. He says the better question is to ask what problem they are solving, then "can we just solve this problem in another way" without a new product, new acquisition strategy and new business.
- **Fix:** Sell the same high-value thing with less demand on their time, so they can sell about 3x as many.

chunks.heading: Trimming and stacking the offer: cut Slack, keep few high-value items
chunks.text:
Alex used the "trim and stack" step from his Grand Slam Offer book. First list every asset, then cut and combine to the leanest, most valuable package.

- **Principle:** Offer the few things people really want and remove everything else. "Each thing we add on its own should be worth the price of the whole thing." He quotes Jack Dorsey: "Make all the details perfect. Limit the number of details."
- **Keep:** The deep-dive onboarding, quarterly 2-on-2 sessions, and two in-person events a year. The group is for community and curation, not support.
- **Cut:** Slack, which is "a time suck". He says Slack is something people like after they buy, but it is not why they buy or renew. The weekly group calls were also the clients' least favorite item.
- **Time cost after cuts:** About 10 hours per couple for $25,000 (deep dive plus quarterly calls plus events).
- **Why Slack backfires:** Responding fast trains clients to message more, so the group stays quiet. Questions asked once in a group serve everyone.
- **Planet Fitness example:** Gyms added racquetball, pool and basketball, but 80% of members used mostly cardio and some weights. Extras widen the gap between consumption and non-consumption. People then think "I'm only using 20% of my $59" and cancel. Planet Fitness catered to the 80% and cut price. Unused bonuses hurt renewals, so include only things clients will use.
- **Reason to buy vs. reason to stay:** Free pizza night at Planet Fitness is a purchase reason, not a retention reason.

chunks.heading: Fixing the supply constraint: change the delivery ratio
chunks.text:
Alex lists five ways to solve a supply constraint. He then explains why he picked the ratio option for this business.

1. Raise the price (fewer buyers, more per buyer).
2. Change the delivery ratio (1:1 to 1:4 to 1:6 to one-to-many).
3. Productize.
4. Hire people.
5. Mix of these.

- **Price:** Ruled out. They already struggled to sell the high ticket, and a pricing move would need 3-4x.
- **Productize:** Ruled out. They already tried it and could not sell it at the high price.
- **Hiring:** A hiring path makes the business "a recruiting, training, and culture business". Alex says most coaching businesses fail at scale: if an X factor is easy to teach, it is not valuable. He has not seen anyone get above about $30M a year in that space. Those who do use a more distributed model.
- **Capacity math:** At 1:1, 5 calls a week for 12 weeks maxes out at 60 clients. Alex wants 150. At $25-30K (many on payment plans), that is about $4.5M, roughly 10-11x current revenue. A group of 4 for 90 minutes allows 4 sessions on Monday (6 hours, 24 clients), and he says two days a week of this gets to about 120 clients and roughly $3M, better than the 5 days a week they work now.
- **Shot-glass analogy:** Coaches spread the X factor thin, like pouring bottles into shot glasses and refilling with water. Group delivery gives each client a smaller but undiluted dose of the founders. Because the founders keep improving, the dose gets more concentrated. Tony Robbins is the extreme: one person, 10,000 people, $5,000 each.
- **Key-man risk:** Alex says to ignore it for now and "deal with that problem" at $4M a year.
- **Group size limit:** Beyond about seven, there is not enough individual time. Going from 1:1 to a group is harder than changing cadence.

chunks.heading: Framing group delivery and escalation to clients
chunks.text:
- **Don't apologize:** Don't say "we're doing 1:4 now, it's hard." Sell it as better. Clients hear other people's questions and may find their problem is already solved by someone else.
- **Shame belief:** The founders worried couples would not discuss private issues in a group. Alex says couples' problems are common. Pitch: being a couple-preneur is lonely, and the group shows struggles are shared. "Shame lives in darkness."
- **Definitions:** Shame is breaking other people's rules that you respect. Guilt is breaking your own.
- **Limiting beliefs:** Alex quotes his own line: "We question all of our beliefs except for the ones that we really believe in." He says to disprove beliefs with evidence from other businesses.
- **Fewer interactions:** Don't be available "whenever", because that outsources the client's decisions. Position the service as help with big decisions: a handful decide your life. "The fewest things that make the most impact."
- **Escape valve:** Give clients two or four "911 calls" like the Who Wants to Be a Millionaire lifelines, for emergencies only.
- **Cadence:** It is easier to change cadence (monthly 1:4 sessions) than to change the ratio.
- **Existing clients:** Keep commitments to current clients. The new terms apply only to new agreements.

chunks.heading: Pricing, cash flow and the new offer structure
chunks.text:
- **Offer:** One offer replaces the $5,000 and $25K split: $25K-$30K a year (the higher figure on a payment plan). Alex says the $5,000 offer "will never be sold again" and existing buyers are sunset.
- **Deliverables:** A 1:1 deep dive, quarterly 1:4 sessions in 90 minutes, and 2 in-person events a year.
- **Events:** Reposition them as "getaways", not conferences, and as "marriage insurance". Alex would test selling three a year, and the founders should stay two extra days to vacation. "It's just the little spikes that are the moments that you remember."
- **Cash flow:** Pull cash forward with layaway. Ask for the first quarter upfront: $9K down, because the deep dive is the most intensive part. Then start $2,500-$3,000 monthly payments immediately, not after a gap, to avoid churn.
- **Downsell:** Three payments before onboarding starts. Only prepaid clients get the deep dive and event access (fast-action bonus).
- **Expected effect:** Conversion depends on the first payment. The $9K frames as $2,500-$3,000 a month. He expects about a 5x price lift with similar conversion.

chunks.heading: Fixing the acquisition funnel: date night event and ad creative
chunks.text:
**Current funnel**
- Facebook lead-form ads to a free 5-day virtual challenge, 1 hour a day. About 6 challenges a year, roughly $19,440 ad spend each.
- Per challenge: 511 registrants, 26 attendees, 12 calls booked, 10 held, 6 closed.
- Show-up rate averages 5.25%, with day 1 at about 9%, dropping to 4-5% on day 2. Cost per average attendee is $815. 49% of attendees book a call. About 90-95% of sales come from the top of the funnel (ads/challenges).
- Cash recovery takes months.

**Alex's changes**
- **Lowest-risk bet:** Rerun the existing challenge but sell the new offer.
- **Spicy bet:** Replace the 5-day challenge with a single 2-4 hour "date night" and pitch at the end. The total information needed to decide can be given in 5 hours over 5 days or one session, and he prefers one session. Attendees stay in state and flow, you reach about twice as many people at the pitch, and 3 hours of real content is enough. Frame: "date night is not business or fun. It's both." A possible hook is "the world's biggest date night". He believes the day of the week doesn't matter, and says Friday is fine.
- **Reasoning:** Date night is the clients' favorite feature. It is a unique angle in a crowded 5-day-challenge market. Long single-session events work for high-ticket sales because attendees get a feel for your expertise.

**Creative**
- Post organic content daily (they post about 2 a week), then run the best performers as ads with a 5-second CTA at the end. Organic is a free testing ground for broke businesses. Also slice the podcast where hosts hired them.
- Video is volatile: your best and worst ads will be video. Images win only when videos are bad. Run about 100 images (they ran 12-16), including camera roll photos.
- Once copy works, keep it and change only the creative. For Alex's school business, he spent tens of millions on ads and never changed the copy.
- Lead-form ads beat landing pages for them on CPA and quality in a year-long split test, so he told them to leave that alone. The only metric that matters is CAC. A $1,500 CAC on a $2,500 sale is fine.
- **Ad machine:** Offer a $2,500 rebate when a client posts a video of their first date night (permission to use it, talk about the experience, not money). The business then produces its own marketing, like a "fusion reactor".

chunks.heading: In-person events as the renewal engine
chunks.text:
The founders sold only one high-tier program at their last event and no renewals, because they "went too soft" and barely pitched. Alex's rule: if you pitch, pitch.

- **Run of show:** Intro, two sessions (M1, M2), lunch with a soft re-pitch, M3 and M4, wrap. A dinner for buyers gives a reason to buy there.
- **Re-pitch:** 15-30 minutes, covering objections from the prior day framed as teaching.
- **Pitch:** Give value, stories and frameworks, then "if today was valuable, do you mind if I tell you a little bit more?" Then 15 minutes of stack and close.
- **Hosting:** Greet attendees by name and bring up two facts about each business or marriage. Split attendees into rosters by lanyard color, each handled by a team member.
- **Content diversity:** Cover different avatars and objections: business strong but marriage weak, the reverse, kids.
- **Renewal incentives:** First-class tickets to the next event (about $6K net cost) or a $5K fast-action discount.
- **Sunsetting the low tier:** Existing $5K clients ascend only.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi argues every business is one of four shapes (e-commerce, service, education/info, software), each with a built-in growth curve and a core "hairy problem." What founders mistake for a broken business is usually a feature of the model, and solving that problem is where the enterprise value and competitive edge come from.

chunks.heading: The four business shapes and why the "shape" matters
chunks.text:
- Alex says there are "only four main types of businesses": e-commerce, service, education/consulting/info media, and software (SaaS).
- He says understanding his businesses' shapes helped him build a portfolio at acquisition.com that generates over $250 million a year at acquisition.
- Each shape has its own growth curve, pros and cons, and one "big hairy problem" to solve.
- His main point: most owners think something is wrong with their business when the issue is a feature of the model, not a bug. Examples he gives:
  - Supply chain and cash flow problems (e-commerce).
  - Hard-to-find talent (service).
  - Constant marketing and low retention (education).
  - Cash burn and revenue retention (software).
- He says to put "disproportionate effort" on the core problem of your shape. Competitors in your space often don't know this, and he calls it "the sauce."
- He has seen the same misdiagnosis at $30M, $50M and $100M businesses.
- If you haven't started a business, pick the shape that fits your personality.
  - Software suits someone detail-oriented, creative and willing to suffer for a long time.
  - E-commerce and education suit promotional people who dislike details.
  - Service suits people who love people, develop talent and build culture.
- He has owned all four and done well in each. He notes that the first business someone starts is almost never the last one they own.

chunks.heading: Valuing the hairy problem
chunks.text:
- Ask how much enterprise value you unlock by solving the shape's core problem.
- Example: if a service business can get two people up to speed per month, that might add $10M or $50M of enterprise value. Spending $100,000 or $500,000 to solve a $50M problem is worth it.
- Once you see the value, put the right resources on it. Don't question the business.
- Solve it thoroughly: "not halfass, not duct tape."
- He says the market will pay "gobs of money" to whoever figures out their shape's core problem. "This is what we get paid for."

chunks.heading: E-commerce: fast growth, capital and supply constraints, brand as the moat
chunks.text:
- **Shape:** growth is fast but hits breaking points that flatten it. The unlocks are usually a supply chain unlock or a distribution unlock.
  - Constraints: cash to buy inventory, ad performance, maxed distribution (e.g. 7-Eleven, then CVS), or a manufacturer that can't keep up.
  - Distribution can be physical retail, ads, affiliates or influencers ("synthetic distribution").
- **Alex's experience:** Prestige Labs (retail distribution plus an online store with ads) and his record-breaking book launch. For the launch he needed multiple 3PLs across states that could ship millions of books in 72 hours.
- **Pros:**
  - Fastest to grow revenue, because people spend more on tangible goods.
  - Less key-man risk from the founder, so it is very sellable.
- **Cons:**
  - Capital-intensive. Growth is dictated by free cash flow because profit has to buy the next round of inventory.
  - Example: 10 units, $10 profit each, and 300 units of demand means you can only buy 10 more next month.
  - Founders can reach hundreds of millions in revenue and live mostly on salary.
  - Heavy reliance on partners (raw materials, manufacturing, logistics, lenders). Build redundancy in each.
- **Big problems, in order:** cash flow forecasting (e.g. predicting sales over a 12-week lead time), distribution, supply chain, then brand. Logistics is "relatively well" solved.
- **Brand is the moat.** He calls pure media-arbitrage a "smash and grab" business (buy eyeballs at $10, make $11 gross profit). Anyone can copy a widget. Brand gives:
  - Higher click-through rates.
  - Higher repurchase rates.
  - Premium pricing.
  - Together that means lower CAC, higher LTV and higher gross profit.
- Decide deliberately from day one which affiliates, influencers and discounts fit the brand.
- **The "perfect" e-commerce company:**
  - Owns its manufacturing, with trade secrets or unique ingredient partners. At larger scale it builds decentralized manufacturing per market.
  - Has strong logistics.
  - Runs a lean performance marketing team alongside a brand-first team.
  - Spends about 70/30: 70% on top-of-funnel brand awareness and 30% on direct-to-purchase. Most starting companies spend about 100% on direct purchase.
  - Uses retail partnerships. Modern brands (e.g. Gymshark) start online and open flagship stores later. At saturation, stores cut shipping costs and raise order values, and CAC becomes rent divided by monthly sales.
  - Has "savage" email marketing, including flows, campaigns and attribution.
- The product has to be exceptional. CAC rises as you scale, so the compounding asset is word of mouth: repeat purchase and customers bringing customers.
- He says 60-70% of a new cohort buying again after the first purchase likely means a strong product.

chunks.heading: Service businesses: talent is the bottleneck
chunks.text:
- **Credibility:** six brick-and-mortar gyms, 30-something gym turnarounds over almost two years, a gym consulting firm (B2C and B2B) that reached the mid-$30M range per year, and the acquisition.com advisory practice, which he describes as a nine-figure-plus business.
- Alex says 78% of US businesses are service businesses.
- **Shape:** slow and steady, near a straight line. The front end (attraction) can scale. Conversion and delivery involve people, and good people are harder to find than product.
- **Margins:** run higher gross margins than is typical. The padding absorbs volatility, e.g. a new salesperson converts worse for about 30 days, or a new account rep isn't as good as a 5-year veteran.
- **Hiring is the constraint, not sales.**
  - Done-for-you services usually have no trouble getting customers if they're any good.
  - Fitness coaching is the exception: it is hard to sell and retain because people don't like working out.
  - Talent is hard at every skill level, from maids to trades to white-collar roles with multi-year learning paths.
  - Founders are often the best technician, so every complex problem lands on them.
- **Pros:**
  - Least risky model. You can cut headcount and stay profitable if priced right.
  - High cash flow with little reinvestment (e.g. sell $100K of work at $50K cost, repeat monthly).
  - Sticky customers who don't want to learn the work.
  - The founder can live well along the way, unlike models where money comes mostly at exit.
- **Con:** slowest to scale of the four.
- **Big problem:** recruiting, onboarding and training must become a core competency.
  - A business is the delta between input value and output value. Take under-skilled people, add skills, and sell those skills at a premium.
  - "If you're in a service business, you're actually in a teaching business."
  - Don't expect to train someone in a weekend to do what took you 10 years. Training is front-loaded, but it makes people ramp faster, stay longer and support higher prices.
  - Reduce dependence on the founder's technical expertise by productizing the knowledge.
- **How to win:**
  - Around $1-3M, choose the real customer and avoid "any kind of person with a pulse."
  - Limit deliverables to one to three consistent ones so delivery can be systematized and productized instead of bespoke. That raises operational efficiency and gross margin.
  - Build training for each step, then onboarding, hiring and selection on top.
  - Replace yourself in operations.
  - Define clear career paths so talent stays. The acquisition.com advisory practice runs analyst, junior associate, senior associate and director tracks.
  - Aim for demand to be the constraint rather than supply, which is rare but doable.
- **Reinvest cash in:** talent quality (the "raw materials") and brand. Brand supports premium pricing and attracts premium talent.
- **North-star metric:** what you charge.
  - If you're good, you're supply-constrained, so you raise prices and gross margin. Reputation then brings more demand, and you go after better ICPs who write bigger checks.
- **Low-cost model:** viable only if decided on day one (offshore talent, heavy automation, cheapest as the USP). He prefers premium.
  - "I'd rather be making a million dollars per person" because it justifies the headcount headache.

chunks.heading: Education / consulting / info media: fast cash, no stickiness
chunks.text:
- **Credibility:** he co-owns School, a software platform for info businesses with millions of data points. His 20 million users figure is quoted for School.
- **Shape:** almost a straight line up, then a hard stop.
  - Graduates leave, so you must refill constantly.
  - Taught students can become competitors.
  - Cheap, easy startup brings many competitors.
- **Value logic:** a skill that moves someone from $40K to $100K a year is worth a lot, and the skill duplicates at near-zero cost. He cites education as an industry of about $10 trillion globally.
- **Pros:** fast, easy and cheap to start; the fastest way out of poverty.
- **Cons:**
  - Hard to scale past $1-3M a year (rule of thumb, anecdotal). The cause is usually weak promotional skill.
  - Little retention, constant marketing.
  - Reputation risk if the founder is weak at ops, which is a different skill.
  - Many founders become "offer hoppers," launching a new thing each year.
- **Scaling delivery:** he says to stay one-to-many (which he recommends for many people) or to dilute access without diluting quality.
  - Milk analogy: 10 customers, one glass of milk. Giving each a pure shot beats giving each a glass of watered-down milk.
  - Training coaches in a weekend to deliver a high-priced skill means the product isn't that valuable or you're misrepresenting their ability.
  - The best in the world can give a tiny shot and still beat a mediocre person giving 100%.
  - Technology democratizes access and consolidates production.
- **Big problem:** create stickiness in a fundamentally unsticky model. Tactics:
  - **Consumable component.** Examples: ad creative for an ads course; a weekly list of trending 3D-printing items; community.
  - **Split pricing, "big head, long tail."** Charge a high price for the one-time education and a lower price for recurring elements.
  - **Don't hide the split in a payment plan.** Example: $25,000 education paid as $2,000 a month. After the skill is learned, a math course is worth "approximately zero," so the user feels they're paying $2,000 a month for community alone.
  - **Discount buying.** Group buying power gives members discounts on materials (e.g. paint brushes) that exceed the subscription price, which makes the ROI clear.
  - **Continued education.** News, new techniques and tools. His comparison: about $250,000 to become a doctor versus about $3,000 a year to stay one.
- **How to win:**
  - Price one-time and recurring elements correctly.
  - Add consumables to the recurring layer.
  - Use the cash engine from one-time purchases to fund acquisition.
  - Build brand, the biggest factor.
- **Brand logic:**
  - Harvard versus CCBC calculus, $200,000 versus $2,000.
  - Le Cordon Bleu graduates get hired more, so the school can charge more.
- **Overkill bias:** people want the best (e.g. Tony Hawk teaching an ollie). Real-world proof is the best branding strategy.
  - His content got more attention after his exit.
  - Warren Buffett's teachings would sell less without Berkshire Hathaway's results.
- **Winning path:** become one of the best at the thing first. It is slower, but it pays down the biggest risks. The competition won't do it, since "be patient and do the work" is the differentiator.

chunks.heading: Software and SaaS: slowest start, biggest upside, retention is everything
chunks.text:
- **Shape:** the slowest start, then the steepest curve.
  - Engineering is expensive and has to be fronted for a year or two before income, which is why the venture industry exists.
  - Few businesses sit here, because barriers to entry are higher.
  - Once you have product-market fit, scale is the most of all four models. He cites Y Combinator: before PMF it's pushing a boulder uphill, after it you're chased by the boulder.
- **Vibe coding:** he has yet to see a truly vibe-coded business at $100M a year. He says it is getting better, but it still struggles with robustness and scale. He recounts a conversation with Replit's CEO, Amjad, who cited many $1-2M businesses built on vibe-coded software.
- **Pros:**
  - Infinite scale and very high gross margins.
  - Sticky revenue if done well, because it integrates into workflows.
  - Huge enterprise value. Valuation drivers are gross margin, growth rate and revenue retention.
  - Low risk at point of sale, since another owner gives customers the same experience.
- **Cons:**
  - Slow start, high burn, and founders often quit early.
  - Low willingness to pay, because there's no incremental cost. Enterprise software at a few hundred thousand a year is small versus enterprise spend. Consumer pricing like $9 a month is hard to earn.
  - Needs huge volume, or dependence on VCs and dilution (he mentions ending up owning 4%).
- **Information business versus software:** a software business looks identical to an information business until you have revenue retention.
- **Big problem:** survive the early years before PMF and make sure users keep using it.
  - Marketers struggle here, because you must make something people want and keep wanting.
  - He cites the Dropbox founder paying people from Craigslist to try the product: the first time, five of five users did not upload a file. Keep iterating user flows until they do, then fix the return loop.
  - He cites Facebook's head of growth: growth is users who activate and then never churn, so the base keeps stacking.
- **Retention benchmarks:**
  - Consumer: over 60% logo retention by year end, ideally over 100% revenue retention.
  - Revenue retention example: 10 customers at $10 a month is $100 a month. If a year later those same customers pay $100 or more, that's 100%+ revenue retention, achieved by building ways for them to spend more.
  - Enterprise is easier to retain because switching costs are higher.
- **How to win:**
  - **Product quality and customer feedback.** Be "absolutely militant." Don't give customers everything they ask for, because feature creep builds a "Frankenstein." Complexity is the "antithesis of elegance," so it's like "sanding off the edges."
  - **Friction removal.** Find an outcome everyone wants and remove all the friction between where someone is and that outcome. The iPhone is his example: Steve Jobs asked how to make a phone easy enough for a child to use.
  - **Viral loop.** Aim for each customer to bring 1.1 more. At low price points, paid ads alone get hard. Facebook is his example, and ChatGPT reached a million users in a week through word of mouth.
  - **Talent.** There are 10x and 100x engineers, and they cost 10x or 100x as much. Pay for quality. If you aren't technical, educate yourself or get a strong technical co-founder as a filter. Build with scalable code and good documentation from day one.
  - **Loops.** Build return, referral and upgrade loops into the experience.

chunks.heading: How acquisition.com maps to the shapes
chunks.text:
- **Advisory practice:** pure white-collar service. Analysts, associates and directors learn through an apprenticeship model like accounting, consulting or legal. Many team members are Ivy League graduates or ex-entrepreneurs.
- **Books and media:** a blend of education and media, with a scalable deliverable. The book launch is also literal e-commerce.
- **ACQ AI:** software.
- **Apparel drop:** e-commerce, but it contributes minimal profit.
- **Combined launch:** the books and ACQ AI bundle did a significant amount of revenue in a weekend. He says "zero to 100 million in 60 hours" if you promote well, have a good offer and product, and have audience history. He doesn't cite exact revenue figures here.
- **Why he keeps the products strong:** "I don't care about the first sale, I want to care about the 10th sale." Each product has to be exceptional so the next launch's audience shows up.
- **Investment firm:** he calls it a "vehicle that contains businesses" rather than a business. Capital leverage lets few people make a few big decisions.
- **Portfolio examples:**
  - An insurance company (service-like, high headcount).
  - A teeth-whitening chain (brick-and-mortar service).
  - A B2B operational consulting business, a blend that skews toward service because of strong revenue retention.
- **Brand versus culture:** brand is how you shape customer behavior, and culture is the "internal brand" that does it for employees.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi coaches a two-month-old roofing contractor by finding the highest-return motion (high-volume repairs), then layering a menu close, VSSLs, a maintenance membership and speed upcharges on a door-knocking engine. The business went from under $32K to about $250K in 90 days.

chunks.heading: Pick the highest-return motion when you are small: go all in on what already makes money
chunks.text:
- Alex's frame for a tiny business (here a roofing company 2 months old, about $41K revenue, 59% profit margin): there is one owner and little time and money, so "focus all efforts on the highest return stuff."
- He values reliability of cash. The owner could knock 20 doors and get a deal, which Alex calls the "cats have nine lives" advantage: entrepreneurs need as many lives as they can get, and knowing how to go get money is one of them.
- His advice on scaling: "go all in door to door." "I don't think we need to be cute about this... get really violent with it."
- Reliability early gives the business a heartbeat. Early on everything is "feast or famine"; cash flow lets "water start flowing through the pipes."
- Result after 90 days: revenue went from a little under $32K to about $247K, with 62 five-star reviews (from under 20) and 85 services sold, built and collected on (from 32). The owner reported a "monomaniacal focus" and said he got ROI on every move.
- Alex's point on why advice helps: it is like replaying a video game level. Someone ahead of you saves the months you would stay stuck. After that "the only hold back is just pure execution."

chunks.heading: Find the cast-aside, high-volume offer: repairs instead of replacements
chunks.text:
- Alex likes work other people have cast aside, because competitors "think they're too good for it." He then builds the business so it earns good gross profit on that work.
- The numbers he ran:
  - Replacements: about $7K gross profit each, average ticket $18-25K.
  - Repairs: 64% margin on a $1,500 ticket, about $1,100 gross profit.
  - His test: could the owner sell 3x as many repairs as replacements? The owner said yes.
- His target was to raise the repair ticket to $2.5-5K (a $2K-$4K range was floated as the goal) through bundling and upselling. At that ticket repairs become "an incredibly interesting business" because of volume and reliability.
- Why he likes high-volume businesses:
  - More stability.
  - Reps get many more reps, since sales cycles are shorter.
  - Less admin headache, with no insurance claims or delayed payments.
  - Almost no cash flow constraints.
  - "You just add more of these and that literally becomes the machine."
- Execution result: services per month rose from 15-20 to 60-80, more than 4x. A repair tech did 3-5 jobs a day, and a second tech was expected to take that to 6-8.
- Getting the first sale is the hard part; "getting the approximate sale is significantly easier." Repairs get a foot in the door, and the follow-on work comes from there.

chunks.heading: The menu upsell script for transactional sales
chunks.text:
Alex calls the menu upsell his favorite chapter of his book *Money Models* (in the upsell section; the book is free online). He says it works for any sale that can close in one conversation. His four steps:

1. **Unsell what they don't need.** "Looks like this is fine, you probably have a couple years on this." This builds trust because the customer expects an upsell and does not get one.
2. **Prescribe what they do need.** "You don't need this, this, this. What I am saying is you're probably going to need this and this."
3. **Offer a fake choice (A or B).** Examples: male or female installer, Monday or Tuesday start, neon nails or white nails, coffee or water. "It's a fake choice, but it just makes the close a lot easier."
4. **Card on file.** Put it on the payment method already stored. "Awesome."

- Example flow: compliment the home, rule out what is not needed, then say "would you rather this or this? You want to take care of that on the card on file? We already have the hood popped up."
- Practical tactics:
  - Have the crew arrive with dumpsters out and tarps open so the customer thinks "you might as well have us fix everything while we're here."
  - The sales rep or a separate closer (Amanda, in this case) runs the onboarding call after the first repair is booked.
- The owner's result: prescribing and taking options off the table built trust, and "people are just taking every recommendation." He called it one of his most effective strategies.

chunks.heading: Use two VSLs to pre-frame sales conversations
chunks.text:
- Alex's setup: one video the customer watches before the on-site visit (about the company), and a second before the call with the closer (about the other work they probably need). Each frames the conversation so the rep arrives to a pre-sold prospect.
- The VSL structure he outlined (about 7 minutes):
  1. Intro and promise: what the video will explain and the outcome they want, such as an amazing roof and avoiding past pain.
  2. Proof early: named customers with houses as big as or bigger than theirs, "so you can feel like I work with people of your caliber."
  3. Old way vs. new way: how the industry does it, then the company's named process (the owner's "special K process").
  4. Objections 1 through N: for each, state the belief, why it is wrong, what is true, and proof (a similar customer story). "That's just a belief breaking mechanism over and over again."
- How it helps the rep: it "completely edifies" the company and adds social proof and stats before the rep arrives.
- A VSL is more specific and targeted than a general YouTube channel, and gets more targeted as the sales team grows.
- Resale framing for the second video: homes with a roofing plan resell at higher value, and the worst move is fixing everything the day you sell, so you "fix your house for the next guy."
- The owner said he planned to shoot the VSL the week after the 90-day check-in.

chunks.heading: Add margin with speed incentives (pay to move to the front of the line)
chunks.text:
- Alex's rule: if you are supply constrained, meaning more people want your work than you can deliver, "add speed incentives for people to just move to the front of the line. You do the same amount of work and you just make more money."
- Logic: jobs A, B, C take the same resources. If C will pay $1,000 more and A is still inside an acceptable window, do C first. "Speed's all margin."
- Offer wording for repairs: "We always try to be really fast, but for a lot of our clients time is money. We have a 20% priority boost." The guarantee is that it is done by the end of the week or the boost is free.
- Pitch it at the end of the repair offer, tacked on to the initial sale.
- Result: the owner offered a commercial client next-day work for an extra $300 of "straight margin." The client took it, was satisfied and bought the next job right after.
- With the menu upsell and speed, a crew can do 2-4 repairs a day, "like doing a full roof replacement a day."

chunks.heading: Turn one-time customers into recurring revenue with a maintenance membership
chunks.text:
- Alex's offer, pitched at job completion when you also ask for a review: a VIP or "diamond roofing" annual plan.
  - Price: $15-20 a month, paid annually, so $180-240, depending on market. It can go higher.
  - Credit: $2 of future repair credit for every $1 paid.
  - Annual roof check: it brings the company back to look at the roof once a year.
- A review incentive: price it at $500 a year, but leaving a review drops it to $200. "It's a little carrot."
- The real purpose is not the fee: "We don't even care about the money. We care about the fact that we're going to have an appointment" to see the customer and "sell more stuff."
- Why: it moves the business from one-time to recurring revenue, which is "significantly more valuable" and "dramatically increases LTV."
- Alex's caveat from the follow-up: the owner had not cracked residential adoption yet. Alex suspected timing and the exact script wording, saying "sometimes just tweaking a couple things" makes it click.
- Also covered: stay in contact with past clients every 6-12 months with detailed notes to keep LTV high.

chunks.heading: Commissions, door-to-door scale, and building the team
chunks.text:
- Make commission math simple for door knockers. On a repair averaging about $4K revenue with 10% commission, a rep earns $400. Divided by about 50 doors, it is roughly $10 a door: "Want to make another 10 bucks? Knock that door." The rule: "How much money do you want to make? Just knock that many doors."
- Alex's plan was to build a "door-to-door army" as "the clear straight shot." He called door knocking the main growth engine.
- Treat salespeople as a new customer avatar. Marketing should now recruit them, because with 4-5 reps the owner can manage the team alone.
- At 1 to 4 and 5 to 9 employees, the work is specializing the product, creating free content for marketing, and tracking sales more closely as the team grows.
- Volume brings reliability, and reliability lets you forecast, which lets you cut costs. For example, knowing a volume might let you cut your cost basis by half or two-thirds.
- The owner also added an ERP system, a custom CRM built for his job flow, to run jobs.
- On advice at different sizes: at zero, the steps are identical (for example, form an LLC to accept money). At very large sizes, the advice is unique to the business. "The bigger the business, the more tailored the advice has to be."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Alex explains why asking cold traffic to "book a call" wastes most visitors, and how a free or low-cost mini offer that solves a narrow problem converts far more leads without extra ad spend. He covers three lead magnet types, four delivery formats, naming and testing, and a CTA formula.

chunks.heading: Why Alex says to offer a lead magnet instead of "book a call" or "submit for a quote"
chunks.text:
- Most sites send traffic straight to "buy now" or "submit for a quote." Most visitors aren't ready, so they leave and never return.
- A "book a call" or quote CTA only works with a warm, informed audience that already knows and trusts you. Its only job is lead capture, so Alex asks what else would capture more leads while still signaling buying interest.
- His fix is a mini offer: a complete solution to a narrow problem, free or low cost. Solving it reveals the next problem, which the core offer solves.
- People who take a free or cheap offer are more likely to buy a related higher-priced offer later. "When someone pays with time now, they're more likely to pay with money later."
- Illustration: of 100 people, "buy my thing" might get 1 buyer. "Let me help you first, then ask" might get 3 to 5 times as many.
- This needs no extra traffic or ad spend. It raises conversion on existing traffic, so it "just drops to your bottom line."
- He says he has used it in every business he has invested in, and that it has generated many millions of dollars across the portfolio. He covers it on page 31 of the $100M Leads book.

chunks.heading: Alex's 2016 breakthrough: swapping a failed webinar for a free case study
chunks.text:
- In April 2016 he paid $25,000 to be in a group where everyone told him to run a webinar. His webinar didn't work, because he lacked the skill to run one.
- He then saw an ad for a "free case study" on turning $1 into $120,000 in a weekend. The opt-in was a screen recording of how the guy did it.
- He replaced his webinar with a video headlined "Free case study, how we added 213 members to a gym and $112,000 in San Diego."
- The next morning Leila told him her calendar was full.
- Lesson: the more advanced the audience, the more likely they see a webinar as a sales pitch. "Consume it on your own time, let me show you what I did" got more opt-ins from business owners.
- Webinars work, but he lacked that skill. A screen-record walkthrough of a campaign and its results was easy to make.
- Once someone opts in, he called them to ask how they liked it, then offered to do it at their location with a risk-free offer: no pay if he doesn't perform. That was far easier than making a webinar close.
- If a lead magnet fails, that magnet failed, not lead magnets in general. This is like a bad ad headline not meaning ads don't work.
- Bad lead magnets don't work, and beginners don't realize theirs is bad.

chunks.heading: Why lead magnets work and how to handle objections
chunks.text:
- Costco samples work mainly because people taste something good and want more, not just from reciprocity.
- Three types of lead magnet, which can be combined:
  - A sample or trial.
  - One step in a multi-step process.
  - An assessment that reveals a problem.
- "Freebie seekers and tire kickers": don't give it to everyone. Add a qualifying dropdown, send qualified people to the good thing and the rest to something else.
- "I don't want to give away too much value": don't solve the problem your core product solves. Solve a problem that leads to it.
- Sell at the point of greatest deprivation.
  - Restaurant analogy: someone who just ate an entree won't want another, but may want dessert.
  - Water analogy: right after you give water, they aren't thirsty, so that moment says nothing about whether the water was good.
  - The free "entree" should be free or at cost, and the "dessert" should cost significantly more.
- Packaging matters more than contents. Changing the lead magnet's headline can change demand 2x, 3x or 10x, provided the contents clearly solve a problem.

chunks.heading: The three lead magnet types in detail
chunks.text:
**1. Reveal a problem**
- Alex loves this type. It creates deprivation by showing a problem and how bad it is.
- Bonus: also show what solved looks like and the delta.
- B2B example: a free website speed test. His example claim is that each second of load time costs 3% of conversion. Going from a 9-second to a 3-second load time is an 18% increase. Against the price of a website, that gain is small, so he'd ask "How soon do you want me to start?"
- It works best for problems that worsen while waiting: posture analysis, termite inspections, financial audits (back taxes, cash flow). Worsening problems build urgency.
- Ad example: one of his highest-converting ads for Acquisition.com's software company was "four reasons why you'll never have a million-dollar agency," aimed at small lead-gen agencies. Many readers thought "all four of these reasons I'm also suffering from."
- Be very specific on the negatives and vaguer on the positives. If you nail someone's problems, they assume you can fix them. This also makes marketing more compliant and expectations more realistic.

**2. Free trial**
- This is the Costco sampler or the fitting room. It has the lowest barrier.
- Give a full loop of value, then remove it so the person feels deprived and converts.
- Limit the number of uses, the quantity, the time, or a combination (for example "x-day trial" or "this many hits").
- Gym Launch example: customers bought the monetization system, and Alex gave them agency services (leads) free for four months. Afterward they wanted leads to continue, and could now pay for them. It was a built-in back-end upsell.

**3. One step of many**
- Best for complex products and services.
- Examples: the first coat of several on a garage, a first laser hair removal session (six to eight are needed), or the first two videos of a course.
- Ashley (a personal stylist) could give a color analysis first. It leads to questions about tops, bottoms and formal vs informal wear.

chunks.heading: Four ways to deliver a lead magnet
chunks.text:
**1. Software or tools**
- Spreadsheets that calculate, assessment tools, templates or software.
- Example: Neil Patel's tool where you enter a URL and it assesses the site while collecting your information.
- A tool can reveal a problem, offer a trial, or be one step of many.

**2. Information**
- Mini courses, guides, expert interviews, static templates.
- Costs nothing, scales infinitely, provides value and creates deprivation, with no operational drag.
- Example: his $100 million scaling roadmap, a tool plus information built from 200+ hours of studying businesses. It tells you what scaling stage you're at and how to solve your problems. Opt-ins can book a one-on-one call and may be invited to the headquarters.

**3. Services**
- "People sleep on this so hard." Do free work to create goodwill, but only for qualified prospects: budget, authority, a clear need, and ready to act now.
- Math example: an hour of labor costs $25 hard cost, but the work is worth $250 or more. If 1 in 4 recipients buys, customer acquisition cost is $100. That is worth it if a customer is worth much more.
- Examples: free audits with some implementation, same-day service delivery, any done-for-you component.
- First business: he trained people free for a year in the "free training project" to collect testimonials. After a year he said he had too much demand and asked whether they wanted to pay. Almost all said yes.

**4. Physical products**
- His books are lead magnets, and they lead to calls and to investing in or partnering with businesses. This is a very long game.
- Example: give a CEO hat or shirt only to people who prove they're CEOs. The item costs $3 to $4. At 1 in 20 converting, that is about $100 per customer for a qualified CEO.
- Ask what your ideal customer would want, and give that.

chunks.heading: How to name a lead magnet and test the name
chunks.text:
- Naming is hugely underrated. The name drives engagement more than anything else.
- Advertise the result, not the vehicle.
  - His first gym ran a "Big Booty Boot Camp." The content was a six-week deadlift, squat and hip thrust program.
  - A "six-week deadlift and squat seminar" didn't convert his mostly female audience.
  - Different names attract different people, for example "tight and toned glutes" or "Bubble Butt Boot Camp."
- How he tests names:
  - Define the avatar clearly.
  - Run small ad tests comparing headlines.
  - With no budget, poll your audience via Stories, texts, or "comment A or B" posts. Only qualified people should answer.
- He split-tested six headlines for $100M Leads, plus the cover image and subheadlines, and shows the results in the book. If it takes two years to write a book, he can spend two days testing the headline.
- Short term, the title drives sales. Long term, the contents and word of mouth do.
- Naming formulas:
  - Number + outcome + time frame: "three emails that can turn cold leads into clients in 24 hours."
  - How to [good thing] without [bad thing], even if [greatest insecurity]: "how to build a funnel without hiring a copywriter even if you've never done it before."
  - Adjective + good thing: "the lazy funnel template that converts like crazy."
  - X mistakes that prevent [good thing]: "four mistakes keeping your business under a million dollars a year," or "five ad copy mistakes that are killing your conversion rate."

chunks.heading: Turning the lead magnet into sales with CTAs
chunks.text:
- Most people make a great lead magnet and forget the call to action, or don't ask often enough. Salespeople who ask the most times get the most deals.
- To ask often without turning people off, keep providing value between asks. Maximize your ability to ask times the number of times you ask.
- CTA formula:
  1. Clear, not clever. State exactly what you want.
  2. The exact next action.
  3. A reason to act now.
- Use scarcity, urgency or both when you have them. Any reason beats none, as in the line-cutting study where "because I have a dog" still worked. His examples: a one-year anniversary promotion, or National Dog Day.
- Service businesses have capacity limits. Say so, for example "four more customers will get us to capacity." Customers don't know how small you are, so use that for scarcity. He notes 78% of businesses are service businesses.
- Larger businesses can run rolling cohorts, for example "we start only this many people per week" or "join this Friday."
- Example: each chapter of his books ends with a CTA to a free gift on acquisition.com, which leads on to a monthly workshop and the chance to become a portfolio company.
- Operational summary:
  1. Give value first by revealing a problem, offering a trial, or giving one step of many.
  2. Deliver through software, information, services, physical products, or a mix.
  3. Name it compellingly, or ask your audience.
  4. Put CTAs inside the lead magnet, and before and after it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi explains why he regrets waiting years to email and breaks down the format, segmentation, deliverability, cadence and CTA tactics behind his Money Minute newsletter. The core idea: treat email as content where every step rewards the reader, keep it plain and valuable, and make unsubscribing easy to protect deliverability.

chunks.heading: Why Alex says every business should be emailing
chunks.text:
- Alex says the average ROI for email is roughly 35 to 45x, depending on the source: about $45 back per $1 spent on software or writing time.
- He gives two reasons it pays so well.
  - The contact is already acquired, so email is just a reminder that you exist. The main costs are the software and whoever writes the emails.
  - One writer can reach 10 million people, which is a lot of leverage.
- He cites these usage figures:
  - 61% of people check email several times a day.
  - 20% check it several times an hour.
  - Usage is similar across age groups.
- Email has the same purpose as content: raise the odds that someone buys now or later.
  - Unlike a social post, where the algorithm decides who sees it, an email goes straight to your list.
  - Your past performance decides whether it lands in the inbox.
- Alex calls waiting so long to email "one of the biggest mistakes" of his career.
  - He did not email in most of his businesses. Gym Launch started emailing 2 to 3 years in.
  - He says that was "just saying no to money."
- Scale from his portfolio: Acquisition.com sent just under 10 million emails over 90 days. Across the portfolio, email generates tens of millions of dollars.
- The first email he sent to his own list used the subject "is this on." It opened with his quote: "It only takes 20 hours of focused effort to get proficient at any skill. The problem is most people waste years before they start the first hour."
  - His point is that you can start whenever you want. The day you start is the day you begin getting the return.

chunks.heading: Unsubscribes, list health and deliverability
chunks.text:
- Alex does not treat unsubscribes as a negative.
  - Thousands of people unsubscribe from his Instagram and YouTube every day. He just gains more than he loses.
  - Many people who show up to workshops had unsubscribed. They know who he is, and the inbox they used may just not be the channel they want.
- Make unsubscribing easy.
  - Keeping people captive means they go dormant instead.
  - Mailing an uninterested segment lowers domain deliverability for the people who do want your emails.
  - He hates brands that make unsubscribing hard.
- The first send after a long gap brings a higher unsubscribe rate.
  - He calls this "shaking the tree," or pulling churn forward.
  - Recurring-revenue businesses see the same thing when they finally contact customers.
  - His highest churn was on his first email, just over 1%. Now it is about 0.42% per email, which is fine as long as the list grows faster than that.
- Fear of unsubscribes taken to its logical extreme means never emailing. He compares that to not posting content because people might unfollow.
- Deliverability:
  - For B2B, 16.99% of marketing emails never reach the inbox, let alone the primary tab, because of domain reputation.
  - There is no silver bullet. It comes from many small "golden BBs": consistently sending emails people open, click and read.
  - He says "don't try and figure out hacks." Align with what the email provider wants, which is the best inbox experience for its users.
  - A bad send can hurt more than silence. If he has no good email, he would rather not send one.
- Tactics for staying out of the promo tab:
  - Make the email look like a normal email: mostly plain text, a few sentences, no images.
  - Use one or at most two links.
  - Limit money language, especially in the text and title. He has seen more money language push emails into promo.
  - Get replies, because replies reinforce your reputation with the server.
  - Use Google-native links, such as YouTube, or Google Drive for a sales letter or VSL. They may deliver better, and "hokey" duct-taped assets sometimes convert better too.
  - If people do not open your emails, you end up in the promo tab, which is "kind of email death."

chunks.heading: Structure of a Mosley Money Minute email
chunks.text:
Alex built his newsletter, the "Mosley Money Minute," around one promise: value in under 60 seconds that a business owner can use immediately. He says these are choices, not rules.

- **Subject line:** He keeps a consistent branded name, like a podcast episode title, instead of split-testing hard. He is willing to give up a little short-term open rate so the audience learns to always open it. He notes that proof-over-promise subjects are also a valid choice.
- **Opening reward:** He starts with a quote or tweet, something that can be absorbed in one glance. This rewards the open immediately.
  - He uses tweets that have already been shared the most.
- **Body:**
  - Roughly 200 words or less, about one minute.
  - One concept only. He keeps cutting until one clear idea is left.
  - The structure is a problem, a solution, then an easy tactic.
  - Example: strangers do not believe you because you are biased. The solution is overwhelming social proof. The tactic is to print every five-star review, frame the prints with dollar-store frames and cover the lobby from floor to ceiling.
  - Other emails run longer. Lila's emails go to the highest-revenue businesses and teach through story, and they perform well too.
- **CTA:** A sign-off, then a call to action matched to the reader. Scaling businesses go to the scaling workshops, and beginners go to School.
- **PS statement:** He includes one in every email because it is, after the headline, the most-read part. "Not having a PS statement is PS stupid."
  - He uses it for a related CTA or a meme, and says there is no science to it.
- **Consistent template:** He uses the same format each time, like McDonald's: "I want Big Mac, fries and Coke." Today's Big Mac differs from yesterday's, but it should be just as good.
- **Reward every step:** Behavior is driven by past rewards, not by the trigger before it.
  - Reward the open with the quote, the read with the tactic, and the click with something worth the click.
  - If you send a blog, put an interesting nugget in the email and link to the blog. This trains readers to click.
  - One terrible email among four good ones can make people disengage.

chunks.heading: Segmentation, cadence and send timing
chunks.text:
- **Segmentation:**
  - HubSpot research found segmented lists had a 791% increase in ROI from email.
  - Alex says results depend less on email quality and more on who receives it. A beginner email sent to advanced readers does not apply to them, and the reverse is also true.
  - Acquisition.com uses qualifiers in the opt-in, such as whether they have a business and their revenue. It then sends to segments like 0 to 100K, 500K+ or 5M+.
  - Be honest in the opt-in. Claiming a higher bracket just gets you content that does not apply.
- **Cadence:**
  - The best email marketers he asked recommended about 3 emails a week. Most found that more email converts more.
  - He does not treat that as a rule. His own approach is a quality threshold: if he has two good emails, two go out. If he has none, none go out.
  - If you have not started, begin with once a month.
  - To break his own barrier, he committed to twice a month and wrote 24 emails in about half a day. After that, everything extra is bonus.
  - He now sends significantly more than that. The newsletter goes out twice a week.
  - He avoids separate "promotional" emails. Every email delivers value, with a link available for those who want the next step, like a link in a bio. That way he does not have to balance a give-to-ask ratio.
- **Days:**
  - B2C: Mondays and Tuesdays, with an average open-rate lift of about 18%.
  - B2B: Wednesday is the bigger lift day, comparable to the B2C lift.
  - He got this from Neil Patel and says he may be adding a narrative to explain it.
- **Time of day:** Two sweet spots, about 10 to noon and 1 to 3. First thing in the morning is competitive because people are clearing real business email.
  - This matters mainly for local businesses. Across time zones, he would not lose sleep over it.

chunks.heading: Other tactical email settings
chunks.text:
- **Mobile design:** About 58 to 60% of global internet traffic is mobile. Check emails on both desktop and mobile.
  - Broken layouts, especially with images, look unprofessional and hurt clickthrough. This is especially common in e-commerce.
- **Preview text:**
  - He learned this recently.
  - Without it, the first 150 characters of the email show, which may just be "hey John."
  - Reported data shows a 24% increase in opens, meaning about one in four people check the preview. He thinks the real number may be higher.
  - It takes 10 seconds. Pull your most valuable or curiosity-inducing nugget forward.
- **CTAs:**
  - Give a reason to act now and say exactly what they get.
  - One or two CTAs is fine if there is a clear reason to click one versus the other. Use one per audience or objective. Five gets aggressive.
  - A continued-interest CTA plus a buy CTA is an acceptable pair.
  - Make CTAs contextual to the content, not copy-pasted. He criticizes YouTubers who splice in the same mini-ad. The CTA is the short-term conversion point, so spending 30 extra minutes on it is worth it.
