  - Example: this video's CTA was about email. A beginner topic points to School. Enterprise value points to scaling workshops or the portfolio.
- **A/B test subject lines:** Test on a small percentage, then send the winner to the rest. He compares it to how YouTube tests thumbnails and titles.
- **Metrics:**
  - Many email marketers now track click-through rate (CTR) over open rate, partly because Apple's privacy changes made opens hard to track.
  - Alex's last 3 months: average open rate 35.7%, which he is unsure is accurate, and CTR 8.5%.
  - CTR can be read two ways.
    - Percent of everyone sent to.
    - Percent of openers who clicked. For example, 100,000 sent, 30,000 opens and 10,000 clicks is a 33% click rate among openers but 10% of the list.
  - His CTR of 8.5% means 8,500 clicks per 100,000 sent.
  - He optimizes CTR over time, not per email. Some emails need less of a click ask, so he "deposits before withdrawing."

chunks.heading: The opt-in email: sell them on staying subscribed
chunks.text:
- Alex peels off valuable book chapters that do not fit the book's theme and finishes them to book quality. He gives these to people who opt in, with other chapters saved as launch bonuses.
  - He wants platform-specific bonuses that give people a reason to be subscribed.
- The welcome email after opt-in does four things:
  - Builds anticipation. A big announcement is coming, and subscribers hear first.
  - Delivers on the promise, which reinforces the opt-in.
  - Asks for a reply, "reply yes," before sending the chapter. Replies help the sender's reputation and keep the email out of the promo tab.
  - Re-sells the reader on regular communication.
- He puts the "by the way, here are the other things you get" part near the end, after the immediate promised reward. The reader has huge motivation in that moment and the goal is to capitalize on it.
- The pitch for the secret chapter lists specifics, such as "how to make your advertising 9.5 times as profitable," a list of 5 ways to add hoops that increase lead quality, and 4 ways to display discounts. The chapter is positioned as one he starts almost every new market with.
- He names two failure modes.
  - A good lead magnet with no selling on staying subscribed, so people take it and leave.
  - A lead magnet that makes the opt-in work feel not worth it. That second one "keeps me up at night," because he wants every interaction to return more value than the time spent.
- If someone opts in only for the lead magnet, they do not want regular communication. Sell the ongoing relationship.

chunks.heading: Profit and conversion tactics from the sample emails
chunks.text:
- **Annual renewal fee** (for membership or recurring businesses):
  - A one-time fee charged after the customer has stayed a year, usually the price of 1 to 3 months.
  - It adds 8 to 24% to revenue at no added cost. It does not hurt front-end sales because it happens a year later and is not part of the advertised monthly price.
  - Someone who stays a year is unlikely to leave over it.
  - Example: a $39/month plan with a $99 renewal fee raises annual revenue per customer from $468 to $567, a 21% increase. That makes the effective monthly rate about $47. If $47 were advertised instead, he would likely convert significantly fewer customers.
  - On a 20% margin business, adding 20% revenue with no added cost doubles the profit.
- **Speed to contact:**
  - Call leads within 60 seconds of opt-in.
  - Alex cites a Harvard Business Review study showing an average increase in sales of 391%, or roughly four times.
  - He says that if nothing else on your docket could quadruple sales, this should be the first priority. You can afford the sales staff with the lift it creates.
  - He says he almost started funding the buying of businesses just to implement this tactic.
- **Email follow-up on School:** Before, they did none because of technical issues with the platform. After starting, conversion lifted 40%, which he calls free.
- **Testimonials into ads:**
  - Turning testimonials into ads is profitable but hard, because most testimonials are weak.
  - He reviewed 2,500 Gym Launch testimonials. The top four all shared a pain-based hook.
    - "We were two months away from shutting our doors."
    - "We were barely making enough to survive."
    - "I paid payroll and rent and finished the month with $0 of profit."
    - "I pay all my expenses every month, work all day and end up with $0 of profit."
  - Two of the top four said exactly "zero dollars of profit."
  - Tactic: do not ask how life was before. That produces a long story with no clear hook. Ask for their worst moment.
  - Moments make hooks, and details make them powerful. "Barely making enough to survive" beats "stuff was hard."
- **Social proof:** The email's premise is that businesses already have five-star reviews they are not displaying. Brick-and-mortar shops should print and frame them. Online businesses should use the online version.
- Alex also says that tweets that perform well also tend to perform well as emails, and that people screenshotting the email to their stories brings in new subscribers.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi audits a luxury personal styling business with strong retention and LTV:CAC but a leaky funnel and low lead volume. He prescribes a prioritized plan: fix conversion with a lead magnet and BANT qualification, add attribution and raise ad spend, then 10x a proven affiliate channel through manual outreach.

chunks.heading: Reading a business's economics before prescribing fixes (Ashley, AC Styles case)
chunks.text:
Alex's first pass on any business is to check the unit economics. If those are healthy, the fix is more volume, not a redesign.

**Ashley's numbers (personal styling for luxury clients):**
- Revenue about $309K a year, profit $130K, 42% net margin.
- Four years in, over 1,000 clients served, 40 current clients, 1 churned in the last year.
- Funnel: about 12 leads a month, 8 appointments, 100% show rate, 4 sales, 50% close rate.
- Blended CAC $600, LTV $10K, which is a 16:1 LTV to CAC ratio.

**Alex's read:**
- Losing 1 of 40 customers in a year (about 2.5% annual churn) is "phenomenal".
- Quality of a product or service is "dictated by the percentage of customers that want to buy it again and again."
- The aim is to "acquire a customer once and have them pay you for the rest of their lives."
- Recurring means a membership or subscription. Reoccurring is like Coca-Cola, where people rebuy without a subscription.
- When economics are good, "the N is low": she just needs far more volume.
- He asks what percentage of customers come from each source and where time is spent. Often one source gives 90% of customers while half the time goes to a source giving 10%. Then he asks whether the winning source is tapped out. Most times it isn't.
- Ashley could track this because she had data. Alex says data shows where the leaks are.
- Her mix: about a third from affiliates, about a third from paid (Google and Thumbtack), about a third from referrals.

chunks.heading: Pricing, ascension and continuity for a high-end service
chunks.text:
**Her offer structure:**
- $8,500 onboarding over 60 days, which includes a closet teardown, an inventory and new outfits (5 to 10).
- After that, $2K a month or $4,500 a quarter.
- About 10% of revenue comes from vendor commissions.
- An earlier $3,500 one-time tier was dropped, because the luxury tier made more money.

**Alex's views:**
- He likes that she serves high earners (minimum around $1M income, about $25K a year for the service plus clothing spend). Many owners fear going after high earners. She "doesn't compromise her quality to meet lower-end customers."
- He kept the more expensive monthly option as a price anchor. Even if only 10% take it, it lifts the take rate on the quarterly plan.
- Most existing clients were grandfathered at about $1,500 a quarter (about $500 a month), and only about two had moved to the new pricing.
- Pricing method: "I just keep edging up the price until people stop saying yes," then back down slightly. That gives the price the market will bear for that avatar, offer and message.
- Her continuity was working, so he left it alone. She is small, with limited time and capital, so he recommends only the highest-likelihood, lowest-cost moves first. Other opportunities can wait for more volume and cash flow.

chunks.heading: Avatar clarity
chunks.text:
- Alex asks who her dream customer is and works backward from there.
- Her avatars are mom socialites (kids with many social events, wealthy, private) and men who are CEOs. It's about a 50/50 revenue split, and the wife often starts first.
- He checks the split because some owners serve two types, hate one and love the other, and keep the one they dislike because it pays bills. If 30% of revenue came from a customer he hated and 70% from one he loved, he'd cut the 30% and double down.
- Ashley likes both, so he doesn't make her pick. At $3M to $5M he'd revisit which type stays longer, is worth more and refers more.
- Buying triggers are life transitions: a baby, a changed body, divorce, wanting to start dating, or a promotion to the C-suite or VP.

chunks.heading: Fixing the paid funnel: lead magnet, qualification and friction
chunks.text:
**The leak:** Google ads produced about 1,800 clicks for 8 sales, at $3,400 for the year and a cost per click of $189 as stated. The page had no prices, no video and no reason to opt in. Alex says that if she fixes this, "you could probably 5 to 10x the sales of the business." Thumbtack (about $6K spend, 58 leads, $38 a lead, 8 sales, CAC $750) is 90 to 95% unqualified.

**Benchmarks and lead magnet rules:**
- A qualified-traffic opt-in page with a clear lead magnet gets 20% to 50%, sometimes 60%, opt-ins. He used 30% as the target for her high-intent search traffic.
- A lead magnet should be risk-free, easy and fast. "We don't want the Avatar to work to get the value."
- Work more on the front end so the prospect works less. It's like "pre-digesting the food."
- Between a more valuable lead magnet that takes longer and a less valuable one that is immediate, customers prefer the immediate one.
- For her, he suggests a color analysis by skin, hair and eye color, or a style direction. Another option is "how to best use your existing closet", which sets up a gap she can sell into.
- A costly or unscalable lead magnet can go only to qualified people, a "honey trap for the right type of people."

**Qualification:**
- He uses BANT: budget, authority, need, timing. Ask the fewest questions needed to decide.
- Budget was the biggest one for her. Don't show prices on the page, but describe the service. Ask a few questions and it screens out about 80%.
- Unqualified leads get a free resource instead of a calendar slot.
- Good friction removes only bad leads. Bad friction, like slow page loads, removes everyone. A photo upload is too much friction up front, so move it to follow-up.
- Asking skin, hair and eye color up front lets her prepare one of about 10 palette templates before the call.

**Sales call logic:** A free-sounding offer can get 10x the calls. Closing 30% of 10x the calls still gives about three times the deals. Pre-sell with videos (one on the page, a second between booking and the call) so calls are spent on the person's decision, not repeating the pitch.

chunks.heading: Scaling spend when LTV to CAC is strong
chunks.text:
- With a machine that returns roughly $16 for every $1 within 30 days, "why would you have any kind of limit on that budget?"
- Cheap-channel math as Alex framed it: $3,400 a year at 23x would generate about $78,000.
- Plan: fix the funnel first, then raise spend from $300 a month to $600 to $900 a month. Her capacity was 12 calls a month, and she could double or triple that. CAC may rise a little and that's fine.
- Attribution first: "the first step of running ads is know what happens otherwise you're just spending money in the dark." Alex was unsure which of her sales actually came from the ads versus search.
- He didn't push Facebook ads, because she already had a profitable channel.

chunks.heading: Affiliate program: from 6 to 60
chunks.text:
**Definition (from $100M Leads):** Affiliates are independent businesses that tell their audience to buy your stuff, in exchange for money, free stuff or both. They have their own businesses and their own advertising.

**Her results:**
- About 6 affiliates (4 matchmakers, 2 private clubs) send about a third of revenue, roughly $100K a year.
- She found them with a Google search, then did manual outreach by email, about 40 attempts in all.
- Six closed, about 15% on cold outreach. Alex says normal cold outbound gets 0.5% to 1%, so that's 10 to 15 times normal efficiency.
- Alex's math: each email was worth about $2,500, and a 10x gives roughly a tripling of the business.

**Alex's plan:**
- Send 400 emails at 20 a day. Don't change the manual process or buy software.
- Build four segments: matchmakers and dating, executive coaches, high-end personal trainers, and divorce attorneys.
- Sources: Google, social media, then list brokers narrowed to a city. Re-send to non-responders.
- Remote service is fine (about 50% of her work).
- Affiliates compound: the work is done once and each sends one or two clients every month.
- Keep them active by treating them like customers. Hold 1 to 3 events a year, ideally one event with all of them in the same room, pitched as collaboration rather than competition. Alex's plan is one event per quarter.

chunks.heading: Sequencing and goal setting
chunks.text:
- Her goal was $5M. Alex said that's 17x from $300K and proposed $1M first, then more. "Systems break when they triple," so he thinks in triples. He cited the "Chinese rule of three and 10."
- He held off on her corporate-clients idea. Reaching $2M to $3M from these fixes first might change her mind.
- Priority order, easiest and fastest first:
  1. Video sales letter, plus lead magnet, plus BANT qualification, plus skin tone personalization. It's about half a day to a day of work.
  2. Attribution tracking. He labeled it 1.5.
  3. Raise ad spend to $600 to $900 a month. It's "literally clicking a button."
  4. 20 affiliate emails a day, an event each quarter, and the four affiliate types.
  5. Leave continuity alone.
- His estimates: funnel and ads 2 to 3x (lead flow possibly 2 to 5x), affiliates 3x. Combined, about 12x, which takes $300K to $3.6M.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi defines branding in actionable terms: a deliberate pairing of your product with outcomes your ideal customer likes. Good branding drives premium pricing, better ad response and loyalty. He explains how to build it by curating pairings, recovering from bad ones, and measuring influence, direction and reach.

chunks.heading: What branding is: a deliberate pairing of things through an outcome
chunks.text:
- Alex rejects the popular definitions of brand ("gut feeling", "emotional shorthand", "set of expectations and memories") as vague. None of them tell you what behavior to change.
- He defines learning as "same condition, new behavior". A definition of brand is only useful if it changes what you do.
- His definition: "Branding is a deliberate pairing of things through an outcome."
- Coca-Cola example:
  - The outcome is the "yum" of drinking it and liking it.
  - The action is drinking.
  - The product is Coca-Cola.
  - The next time someone wants the yum, they reach for a Coke.
- Branding always happens. The goal is good branding, meaning a deliberate pairing of your business with good outcomes for your ideal customers.
- What you pair with determines two things:
  - Who pays attention to your business.
  - Whether they move toward the business (like the UFC example) or away from it (like the Dylan Mulvaney example).
- Advertising and branding are different. Advertising is letting people know about your stuff. Branding is the pairing that occurs as a result.

chunks.heading: Good vs. bad branding: judged by money from the ideal customer
chunks.text:
- Alex uses the Bud Light x Dylan Mulvaney collaboration as an example of good advertising and bad branding. Lots of people learned about Bud Light, but many of its customers hated the pairing, fewer people bought, and the business took a loss.
- Bud Light then paired with Shane Gillis (a "man's man" comedian) and the UFC, and sales began to recover.
- A pairing is judged by whether it nets more money, so it is not a matter of opinion. He stresses this is specific to Budweiser's customer base. Gillis and the UFC are not "magic", and Mulvaney is not "unmagic" in general.
- Every pairing has positive and negative reactions because people differ. The test is the share of your ideal customer who likes it:
  - 75% like and 25% hate is better than 25% like and 75% hate, because the first makes more money.
- The same pairing could be good branding for a different product or audience.

chunks.heading: Why a strong brand makes money: the pairing-to-sales mechanism
chunks.text:
- The earliest branding was livestock branding. A burned-in symbol changed behavior:
  - An unmarked cow is left alone.
  - A cow with a neighbor's brand you recognize is treated according to how you feel about the neighbor.
  - A branded cow whose brand you don't recognize is still treated differently from a wild one.
- Step-by-step process:
  1. Start with a brand that means nothing. People know it is a brand but not what it means yet.
  2. Pair it with people, experiences or things your ideal customer likes. Nike pairs with LeBron and Tiger, who are champions and "goats".
  3. The brand starts to mean what the customer likes.
  4. The customer wants to associate with that thing but can't buy it directly. They can buy "a tiny sliver of that association", such as a shirt with the logo.
  5. You get the money. As long as the pairing cost less than the sales it produces, you profit.
- Dolce & Gabbana example: they made a line for Kim Kardashian. A customer who wants to be associated with fame, beauty, wealth and luxury buys the brand to get that transfer.
- The point of building a brand is "to change customer behavior in your favor when they see it with a product."

chunks.heading: The payoffs: pricing power, better ad response, loyalty
chunks.text:
- **Pricing power.** Alex quotes Buffett: "the single most important decision in evaluating a business is pricing power". If you have to hold "a prayer session" before raising the price by 10%, you have a terrible business.
  - A strong brand turns a commoditized $5 white T-shirt into a premium product.
  - His example was a 12x price increase without losing many sales.
- **Cheaper customers and better ads.** A generic white T-shirt might get a 0.5% click rate. The identical shirt with a Nike swoosh might get about six times as many people clicking and buying, at a higher price.
- **Loyalty.** Strong brands drive repeat purchases (his example is Apple buyers) and protect you from competitors stealing the customer later.
- **Summary of what you get:**
  - You can charge up to 10 times or more than competitors.
  - You get higher returns on advertising, so you scale faster.
  - Customers keep buying for life.
- Brands also outperform commodities in every industry and give a lasting competitive advantage that is "theirs to lose".
- He cites Buffett again: "It takes 20 years to build a reputation and 5 minutes to ruin it."

chunks.heading: How to start and grow a brand: the bouquet and the garden
chunks.text:
- Brand elements (products, values, experiences, people) are like loose flowers on a table. They are not a brand until they are repeatedly paired into a bouquet. The brand is the association itself, and if you unravel it, the brand disappears.
- **Narrow vs. broad.** Talk only about tacos to be narrow. Expand to quesadillas and burritos, then food, alcohol and restaurants to go broader.
  - Niche down to go deep, branch out to reach more people.
  - Distant, random pairings hurt a brand because they are hard to associate. He uses a bike, a single flower, socks and a burger as the picture of an incoherent brand.
- Most brands happen by accident, based on whatever they appear next to. Good branding happens on purpose.
- Curate it like a garden: add the good and pull out the weeds. You have to do both.
- Start by deciding which values, people and experiences you want to connect to your product, and which you want to avoid, remove or ignore.
- Early on you only have a few flowers. Each additional pairing with something your customer likes strengthens it, such as going from one flower to a bouquet of red roses.

chunks.heading: Recovering from bad pairings, and the product's role
chunks.text:
- One bad pairing, like a rotten flower or a DUI, changes how everyone sees the bouquet.
- You can't delete it. You recover by overwhelming it with far more of what the majority of your audience likes, until the bad pairing shrinks into irrelevance.
- Kanye is his example. After cancel-culture controversy he kept releasing things people love (a Super Bowl ad, shoes, an album), and people re-associated the good and still bought.
- Most pairings happen before purchase, but the customer has many more experiences with the product afterward, so the product does a lot of the branding.
  - A hole in a Nike shirt's armpit transfers backward: "Nike sucks", and then LeBron too.
  - If the product is "good enough", the brand can carry it the extra distance and shape perceived value.
- Alex's tip is that if you charge a premium price, make sure the product is dialed in so it reinforces the brand instead of conflicting with it.
- Buffett quote he agrees with: "Your premium brand had better be delivering something special." Alex adds that otherwise you get the first purchase but not the ones after it.

chunks.heading: Measuring a brand: influence, direction and reach, and the risk of new pairings
chunks.text:
- Three metrics:
  1. **Influence:** how likely the brand is to change someone's behavior. Do they recognize it and do something?
  2. **Direction:** do they move toward the brand or away from it?
  3. **Reach:** how many people it changes behavior for.
- A weak, neutral brand has few people recognizing it and little reaction. A strong, positive brand has many people recognizing it and moving toward it.
- Strong brands aren't necessarily polarizing:
  - Trump is the polar example, with high influence and strong movement in both directions.
  - Taylor Swift, Mother Teresa and Apple are large, strong and mostly positive. Any brand with a large audience will have some haters.
  - Alex argues you can build a strong positive brand without seeking controversy.
- The concept works at small scale too. Parents have high influence and low reach.
- To test whether growth is working, look at whether more people take the action you ask for (click, download, attend, buy), and whether they do it in the direction you want.
- Every new pairing carries risk. A local band that goes big gambles on losing the old fans ("they sold out") for a larger audience.
  - The same applies to new content, genres and songs.
  - The bet is that more of your ideal audience will like the new thing than dislike it.
  - His advice: "don't let the five mean comments stop you from gaining the 500 new people who like the new thing."

chunks.heading: Alex's own brand as the worked example
chunks.text:
- He built the brand around business value: making people money and growing their businesses. The content and books are for small business owners, who then associate growth and profit with him and consume more.
- People who dislike money or business content won't like his stuff, and he's fine with that.
- Word of mouth extends it. Fans tell others to check him out, and those people get the same positive outcome and make the same pairing.
- Results he attributes to the brand:
  - A 7.8 million person audience across platforms in about 40 months.
  - Over a million copies sold of his last two books.
  - Acquisition deals worth hundreds of millions of dollars for his holding company.
- He ends by pairing himself with value again, offering free video versions of $100M Offers and $100M Leads at acquisition.com/training. The books are also on his podcast, The Game, around episode 570. He also promotes school.com, which he recently became a co-owner of.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi defines branding as pairing something unknown (you) with something people already like, then walks through six steps: what branding is, why it matters (LTV:CAC), pick the who, find what they like, advertise the pairing, and keep your promises. A strong brand lowers CAC, raises prices, and drives repeat purchase.

chunks.heading: Why branding matters: the CAC and LTV math
chunks.text:
- Alex says a strong brand can get people to pay 10x more than they pay a competitor. It can also get customers to convert on ads at 10x the normal rate, so acquisition costs a tenth as much. He calls that a "100x differential" and says it is how massive brands "print money over time."
- He treats the cost of acquiring a customer (CAC) against lifetime value (LTV, the gross profit made over the customer's life) as the basic economic unit of every business. Example: spend $1 to get a customer who produces $10 of gross profit, and the LTV to CAC ratio is 10 to 1.
- A brand improves that ratio in four ways:
  - A higher percentage of the audience converts.
  - Customers buy more times.
  - Customers buy from no one else.
  - Customers pay above the commoditized market price.
- Alex says this is arguably the most important outcome in business, and a strong brand with positive associations in the ideal audience is the most powerful way to get it.
- The catch is that building associations takes time. Once the teaching is done, it pays back in lower CAC, higher prices and repeat purchases, and it starves out competitors.
- He says that in 40 months he went from zero to 8 million subscribers across all channels. His portfolio went from starting out to over $250 million a year.

chunks.heading: What a brand is: pairing and pruning associations
chunks.text:
- Alex defines branding as "the association between two things." The entrepreneur's active verb is pairing: you pair the thing people don't know (your business or personal brand) with something they already know and like.
- Repeat the pairing enough and you can remove the other thing. The positive feeling stays attached to you.
- His illustration is a stage test. Standing next to all the Republican candidates, all the Democrats, or a group of porn stars would each change how people see him. If he appeared with porn stars 100 times in a row, people would assume he works in that industry even after the porn stars were removed.
- Most businesses make these pairings haphazardly. He compares a brand to a front garden: weeds grow naturally, so you have to prune and weed. A garden of all red roses has one strong association. A mix of roses, daffodils and sunflowers means "nothing to nobody."
- Even a harmless element can dilute a brand. He ran a 3 to 6 month stretch of wider topics, including his relationship with Leila, and he calls it a small mistake. His audience is "business first," so he lost some business owners who weren't married.
- His rule is to keep one central pillar that the whole audience shares, which for him is business. Personal uniqueness can be sprinkled around that pillar, but never put ahead of it.
- Every new association trades away part of the audience for a bigger share of the people you want. Good branding means the people you gain are your "who" and the people you lose are not.
- He turns down podcasts in controversial niches, such as black pill or red pill shows and porn-world shows, even when they offer big view counts. He has no moral objection. He says the trade isn't worth it because a segment of his audience cares.

chunks.heading: Step 1: choose the "who" with four qualifications
chunks.text:
Alex says branding starts with who you want to attract. The six steps are the same for a personal brand and a business brand, and only the target avatar changes. He points to the "$100M Offers" book for the full treatment. His four filters:

1. **Growing.** Pick a growing market over a shrinking or flat one. Even if you stay the same size, you grow with it.
2. **Can afford it.** If you want to charge a lot, they need money. Given poor, medium and rich options, he'd pick rich.
3. **Easy to target.** If you can't find them, you can't sell to them. Choose the easy-to-find group.
4. **In pain.** They have to actually want what you sell. A market where nobody wants the service is hard to sell to, even if the people are reachable.

He also says to avoid being a generalist and serve a specific market. That lets you charge a premium, and it is operationally easier because you repeat the same work instead of building custom solutions for each customer.

Worked example: an accounting firm (CPA).
- He picks med spas and anti-aging clinics serving Boomers, riding health trends and aging.
- That market is growing, has money, is easy to find, and its customers are in pain from aging.
- The same firm could instead target residential homeowners or W2 employees. The content and associations would be entirely different even though the business is still accounting.
- He notes you can choose to appeal to one political group, since political party is not a protected class. He warns this would also ward off some people who don't want politics in their accounting.

chunks.heading: Steps 2 and 3: find what they like, then associate through advertising
chunks.text:
- After choosing the who, list what they like and what they struggle with. For med spa owners Alex lists:
  - More customers
  - More profit
  - A sellable business
  - Saving money
  - Making life easier
  - Help recruiting talent, so they work less in the business
  - Retaining talent, because nurses and nurse practitioners are expensive and in high demand
- Then "associate," which he says is code for advertise. You pair yourself with the solutions to their problems, because everyone wants less pain.
- For the accounting firm, that means giving away videos, blogs, written content, cheat sheets and PDFs. Examples:
  - How to pack the refrigerator to fit more stock and free up room for services.
  - How to set up the lobby so more patients are seen in less time.
- Each piece of content is a micro promise kept. That raises the odds they believe the macro promise, that the firm can help them make better decisions and drive profit. It also sets up the firm to help with financials when they sell the business.
- Advertising versus branding:
  - Advertising is the process of making something known.
  - Branding is what you make known, meaning the associations created while advertising.
  - You can have excellent advertising and terrible branding at once.
- His example is Budweiser's Dylan Mulvaney campaign. It reached the whole world, but for Bud Light's core audience it was a bad association.
  - It might have been good branding for a company whose who is very progressive.
  - Alex says it strengthened Bud Light with a sub-segment, but more people hated it, so the brand lost overall.
- He names four ways to advertise: make content, reach out to people you don't know, reach out to people you know, or run ads.

chunks.heading: The three levels of belief: tell, others tell, they experience
chunks.text:
- Alex ranks three levels of influence, using a movie as the model.
  1. **What you tell them.** This is the trailer. It is the least influential level, but a brand-new person judges you 100% on this first exchange, so quality matters.
  2. **What others tell them.** This is word of mouth, and it matters far more than what you say. His example is Top Gun: Maverick. He saw the trailer and thought it looked cool, but he went only after about 10 people told him it was the best movie they'd seen in two years. A bad word of mouth on a Godzilla trailer kills the sale.
  3. **What they experience themselves.** This is seeing the movie and deciding for themselves.
- A movie is a single product and is not really a business. Business owners want repeat purchase, so the promise must be delivered at the product level.
- When customers have a great experience, they believe your next claim and tell others. Alex calls this the virtuous cycle of branding:
  1. Make a promise.
  2. Keep the promise.
  3. People tell others you kept it.
  4. New people try you and you keep the promise again.
- Getting other people to talk on your behalf takes time. Anyone can get a customer to buy once, but only an exceptional business gets repeat purchases.

chunks.heading: Step 4: keep your promises, which he calls the most important step
chunks.text:
- Keeping promises comes down to product. The product does what you said, the way you said, by the time you said.
- Alex says this is very easy to say and very hard to do. Don't over-promise, and over-deliver.
- Apple is his example. Its brand rests on exceptional products tied to the association of elegant, simple, easy-to-use design that makes technology accessible. He says it started as a niche and bet on that becoming the majority. He adds that it gives hope to anyone who isn't premium yet.
- Without the product step, the cycle breaks. With it, branding reinforces itself.

chunks.heading: Proof that a strong brand outperforms direct response tactics
chunks.text:
- Alex's first experience of a strong reputation was launching "LNS," the first beta of what became Acquisition.com's software company, Leila's. He ran a webinar for his existing audience, and the product was automated lead nurture build-outs for gyms, delivered in the order orders were received.
- Busy gym owners who missed the webinar called in saying they didn't know what he was selling, but to "just bill me." Some wanted to pay to get in line sooner.
- He says they behaved that way because every earlier promise to them had been delivered on for more than they had paid.
- His conclusion: direct response "hacks and tricks" become irrelevant once you have a strong positive association. That association makes people more likely to buy frequently, exclusively from you, and at higher prices.
- He admits the path is hard because it takes time and has to be deliberate.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi explains his SPCL framework (status, power, credibility, likeness) for building influence, defined as the likelihood of compliance with requests. He argues for live, long-form, high-volume content aimed at the right avatar rather than chasing views, and for setting realistic view expectations based on niche market size.

chunks.heading: SPCL framework: four components of influence
chunks.text:
- Alex defines influence as the "high likelihood of compliance with requests". Requests range from subscribing, to buying a book, to attending a webinar or workshop. Bigger asks need more influence.
- His framework is SPCL: Status, Power, Credibility, Likeness.
- Any one component gives some influence. Stacking all four gives the most, like "min-maxing" a stat in a role-playing game.
- Each component is a continuum, not a binary. A person with $10,000 has more status than one with $1, and a billionaire has far more.
- Influence is domain-specific. Alex says he would have low influence giving fashion tips, because he has no scarce resources, results or third-party proof there.
- He says the goal is to build influence, not to get as many views as possible.
- He credits 35,000 pieces of content this year and 32.7 million YouTube views in the month. He also cites over $100 million in sales in 72 hours from the $100 Million Money Models book launch.

chunks.heading: Status and power: definitions and examples
chunks.text:
- **Status**: Alex defines it operationally as controlling reinforcers (the "good stuff" people want) in a given environment.
  - Example: a bartender in a busy bar controls a scarce resource, so he has status there. Outside the bar he has none.
  - Money alone gives status, even if inherited.
- **Power**: comes from "say-do correspondence".
  - You say something, the person does it, and a good thing happens. They are then more likely to comply with your next request.
  - Example: someone gives 10 crypto picks, you follow them, they all go up. That person has status and power, so more influence than a trust-fund kid who only has money.
- If forced to pick one component, Alex would pick power.
- One event can check several boxes. The book launch's $100M+ in sales gave him money (status) and third-party credibility. Telling people how to launch similar things, and having it work for them, builds power.
- Parents are his example of maxed-out influence. They control shelter, food and money (status). They have many reinforcement cycles from childhood directions (power). They look and think like you (likeness). Credibility is the one they often lack.

chunks.heading: Credibility and likeness
chunks.text:
- **Credibility** is third-party validation you can observe.
  - For the book launch he paid Guinness judges to be on site, so records were verified by a corporation whose business rests on trust.
  - A $10 million building behind him in ads works because it is "hard to fake".
- **Likeness** is relatability. It covers shared values, a vibe or behaviors that match people who were positive in your life, or looking like you.
  - Example: his audience is about 89% male. Leila's, on nearly the same money and business topics, is about 54% female.
- His likeness advice is to just be you. He says "there's zero ROI" in acting differently from who you are, and that most people are "NPCs" playing archetypes.
- Lean into the quirks that make you unique, and be able to defend why you do what you do.

chunks.heading: Putting SPCL into every video
chunks.text:
Alex builds each video so it demonstrates all four elements:

- **Status**: open with results you control. His intro cited 32.7 million views and the book launch's sales in 72 hours.
- **Power**: tell viewers what the video will teach. If they follow it and it works, they are more likely to comply with the next request. That covers watching the next video and any call to action, whether subscribe, like, share, a small purchase or a booked call.
- **Credibility**: use third-party proof, such as Guinness verifying the launch.
- **Likeness**: be himself. This is why he is moving toward live streams.

chunks.heading: Why live and long-form beat shorts
chunks.text:
- Alex's stated media strategy is two words: "live interactive". He describes this as the Acquisition.com 3.0 / Mosey Media 3.0 direction. He says he "honestly hate[s]" scripted camera-staring videos but will do what's required.
- Applause ranking, as Mr. Beast described it to him at a UK vs US soccer game:
  - Traditional A-list celebrities got almost no applause.
  - Short-form creators got a bit more.
  - Long-form creators (podcasters, YouTubers) got a rowdy response.
  - Live streamers made the whole arena erupt.
- Shorts are a way to get people to risk time on a long. Alex still makes plenty of them.
- Exposure math: 2 hours of long-form equals about 480 shorts at 15 seconds each (4 per minute × 120 minutes). So long-form gives far more reinforcement cycles per prospect.
- He thinks the Trump–Rogan three-hour podcast and the Musk–Tucker Carlson interview nudged the election, because undecided people got hours with a candidate. He frames this as persuasion, not politics.
- His meta-theme: "the internet will always move towards truth". Raw, unscripted formats win over polished, curated ones, provided SPCL is still included.
- His formula is "do SPCL and do it as many times as I possibly can".

chunks.heading: Volume
chunks.text:
- Rogan, PBD and Dave Ramsey each put out hours of content every day.
- Alex contrasts one post a day (365 a year), common for $1-2 million businesses, with his 35,000 pieces. He calls that about 100 times the volume, and says it brings about 100 times the prospects.
- He says the relationship is "far more linear than you would expect".
- Rule of thumb: about 1 in 10 shorts is a 2-3x outlier. The same pattern holds for longs.
- His approach is to put as much as possible through the input-output machine while checking the SPCL boxes.

chunks.heading: Interest media: make content for your avatar, not for views
chunks.text:
- Alex says social media is now "interest media".
- Judging content by views is "dumb". A grandma slapping him would get views from people who like humor, but not from customers.
- If you are an educator, make content for your avatar: "the content is the targeting". The algorithm reads your topic, background and clothing, and shows it to people who watch similar valuable content.
- Example: a piano repair channel may get only 1,000 views per video. That can still be a room of 1,000 people who all want to fix pianos, which is a strong opportunity.
- Do not compare your views to Mr. Beast's. You are playing a different game.
- His preferred feedback is IRL responses. He counts texts from business owners he respects ("that was fire").
- When business owners fly to Vegas and he asks their favorite content, he says it is "dollars to donuts" the Cash Cows format. In it, a business owner presents their business and Alex shows how to improve it. He makes more of it even though the audience is smaller.

chunks.heading: Sizing your market and expectations (US data)
chunks.text:
Alex cites Census Bureau data from memory and notes it may be imperfect:

- About 9% of people own a business, roughly 32-33 million business owners.
- About 95% of those make under $1 million in revenue. About 5% (roughly 1.5 million) make over $1 million.
- Roughly 1 in 250 businesses is over $10 million.
- Roughly 1 in 3,000 reaches $100 million a year, depending on the data source.
- Implication: 100,000 views on a video aimed at $1M+ owners is "crushing it". If 1.5 million views were all business owners, that would be "insane".
- He says to set expectations from the size of your actual market.
- He has looked at two businesses doing over $1 million a year with fewer than 5,000 followers. Small audiences can pay well if the content is directly valuable to them.
- He mentions School, which he co-founded, as a low-cost way to start an online business, at "n bucks a month" after a 14-day trial. (The price is garbled in the transcript, so it is not recorded here.)

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi lays out levers for getting customers quickly: give away what others charge for, keep marketing small and high-skill, ask what it would take to be number one, invest in pre-production, minimize need-to-believes, split test, raise LTV to outspend rivals, build over-generous affiliate deals, and let truth carry your ads.

chunks.heading: Give away what others charge for to generate leads
chunks.text:
- Alex's favorite lead-generation strategy: "look at what other people are charging for", work out the hard cost for you to deliver it, then give it away free.
- Five steps:
  1. See what others charge for.
  2. Calculate your hard cost to deliver it.
  3. Give it away for free.
  4. Count the leads.
  5. Count how many convert.
- The aim is to give away something significantly better than what competitors give away, ideally something others charge for. He says to make it even better than theirs if you want to be a "Savage" about it.
- Example: for Black Friday he spent 200+ hours building a free scaling roadmap. It takes a company from $0 to $100 million in 14 hours of content, across 10 stages of growth and 8 functions: marketing, sales, customer success, product, IT, HR/recruiting and finance. Users fill in questions and get a personalized solution. It is better than what others charge for, and it keeps pulling businesses into his world.
- The free asset is built once and generates unlimited leads, in the spirit of "build once, sell a thousand times", like a book.
- Free stuff also moves people from needing more information to needing less before they buy, which is what branding does at scale.
- Claim: the Alex-affiliated portfolio (acquisition.com) companies get a new lead roughly every 6 seconds.

chunks.heading: Fewer, better marketing people, with the founder close to marketing
chunks.text:
- Alex says every founder must know the core business, how to get customers and how to deliver. Most other things can be outsourced, but not getting customers.
- When he drifts away from marketing, the output of his skill gets diluted. He ends up with a department using their best skills, not his, and the business loses its biggest asset (him).
- Examples: Mr Beast is still involved in creating his videos. Steve Jobs reportedly approved every final Apple ad.
- His motto is "fewer better". Back the talent with money.
- Marketing resembles a developer role with a technical career ladder. Top talent produces outsized returns, like the Google Maps coder who rebuilt the product over a weekend.
- The gap between a zero and a ten marketer is far larger than in manual work. A lawn cutter might be 3x faster, but one skilled person with an iPhone can get a video with 100 million views.
- Marketing is usually understaffed (just him plus a couple of people) or overstaffed (he steps away and someone brings in many bodies).
- Gym Launch had 17 people in marketing. After he removed the leader and moved in, he cut the team from 17 to 5 and output tripled.
- Example math: three people at $75k creating 3x output.
- Pay for performance: keep the best marketers in the highest-leverage positions with incentivized performance, to access their discretionary effort.
- "The best advertisers don't need many people."

chunks.heading: Ask "what would it take to be number one?"
chunks.text:
- He asks his team: "what else would have to be true for us to be number one in our market?"
- It skips incremental thinking (10% or 20% better). You assume the goal outcome and reverse-engineer it into the present, even if you are 1/100th the size of the leader.
- Process:
  1. Name the one or two big things that would have to happen.
  2. Ask what they would cost and whether you have the resources.
  3. Often you do. Then ask why you aren't putting every resource toward them now.
- His own chain of reasoning for becoming a top investor:
  - He can't speed up years of experience, so he needs the most deal flow.
  - Broker networks mean competing on shared deals, so he wanted proprietary inbound deal flow.
  - That requires a massive business brand, which requires better content than everyone else plus a business book.
  - So he put his resources into content and books, even though it meant nothing at the time.
- He credits Stephen Schwarzman (the book "What It Takes"): building a big business is about as hard as building a small one, so "you might as well go after something really big". A restaurant may cap at $1-2 million a year, while a top software company can reach billions.
- It's about resourcefulness, not resources.
- Selling in a vacuum means you don't compete on price or terms. There are two ways:
  - Sell where no one else sells (a pond with no other fishermen).
  - Sell something no one else sells (Elon Musk's approach).
- Inbound demand at scale puts prospects in a "work with you or not at all" position, not choosing between you and six others.

chunks.heading: Pre-production beats post-production, and minimize need-to-believes
chunks.text:
- "An ounce of pre is worth a pound of post." Most people skip planning, hit record or post, then try to fix it in post, which has low leverage and high cost.
- A strong video or ad concept has more leverage than anything else. Even poorly executed, it can get an order of magnitude more views.
- For his School ads, he spends time on pre-production:
  - Reviewing past winners and hooks that keep working.
  - Preparing props and visual aids.
  - Keeping the recording short, which leaves little post-production.
- Post-production in education should only improve comprehension. Razzle-dazzle doesn't make a video more educational.
- What changed his mind: an Indian channel (he calls it "calculus Walla", about physics and calculus) with ~20 million subscribers. Its videos get 10-20 million views and it's just a person at a whiteboard.
- He now writes notes, orders points so nothing needs reordering, and prepares examples and clear language, which makes the team's work easier and faster.
- Need-to-believes (a term he first heard from Perry Belcher): minimize what a customer must believe in order to buy. Ideally zero or one.
  - Bad example, Prestige Labs: he had to convince gym owners that selling supplements is good, and that Prestige Labs was the right supplier. Two hurdles made it a hard sale. Fix: run a multi-layered campaign, first the big belief, later a warmer middle-of-funnel campaign.
  - Good examples:
    - Real estate investing: little to believe, since people already see it as an asset class.
    - Amazon: upload your product and you can make money, with no marketing, sales or support needed.
    - Uber: download an app, upload your license, have a car and a clean record, and believe your phone will ping.
- Going "cradle to grave" in one move sells to a smaller share of the market unless you make the sale a "6-inch putt" for everyone.

chunks.heading: Split test in order of leverage
chunks.text:
- Testing is high leverage. A 10-30% lift in three or four funnel stages can double or triple results. Profit then rises disproportionately to revenue, because extra revenue doesn't carry the same fixed costs.
- His ranking of split tests:
  1. Offers.
  2. Packaging: headlines and subheadlines.
  3. Images tied to the headline and packaging.
  4. Third-party integrations.
- His biggest winners came from #1 and #4. #4 ranks fourth only because it is hard to do.
- Third-party integrations: swap the software you use (CRM, forms, scheduling and so on) and test it. Third-party tools rarely report their own conversion rate or UX data. Alex says swapping a tool caused a company "explosion" in sales and profit four times in his career, even with nearly the same look.
- It is messy to split customers across systems, but valuable.
- Winning tests are mostly permanent lifts: a one-time effort for ongoing gains.
- Thumbnails: he tests YouTube thumbnails because one can 3x views.

chunks.heading: Spend more by raising LTV
chunks.text:
- Small businesses often say lack of customers or leads is their top problem. Alex says the real issue is usually that the business can't afford to acquire them, because it doesn't make enough per customer.
- When a company said "leads cost too much", he says that is rarely the issue. The issue is usually too little money per customer.
- Across companies he sees (he mentions wanting to buy a med spa chain with around $5 million EBITDA), customer acquisition cost is usually only about 1x-2x apart. The big differences are in LTV.
- The rich get richer through LTV. Example: Starbucks LTV is $14,000. Starbucks is likely inefficient at acquisition, but has 40-50 years of optimizing what brings customers back (products, seasons, flavors, options).
- Tip: Google "average cost per customer [industry]" to see if your CAC is in range. If it is, your problem is LTV.
- Small owners often undercut ("those guys overcharge"). Alex says the bigger company charges more because it makes more per customer.
- "The ability to spend more is LTV and LTV is the arms race of advertising."
- Advertising costs only rise over time (impressions, eyeballs), so LTV must rise to keep pace as you reach colder markets on pricier channels.
- Raising prices is among the strongest LTV levers, yet owners fear it. They chase cheaper leads, like addicts chasing the first high.
- The first campaign in a new market or with a new offer always performs best. Lead costs will get worse, so build the business to absorb it.

chunks.heading: Affiliate deals so good it hurts
chunks.text:
- Go to someone who has already built the audience and ask to be promoted. Alex built affiliate businesses by recruiting many smaller businesses ("nodes of new revenue"), not super affiliates.
- Standard 20% referral deals fail because nobody wants to hand over a trusted relationship for 20% of a ticket. The deal must be "so good that it hurts" and large enough to change behavior.
- His method: peel off a piece of your product and give the affiliate 100% of that piece's revenue to sell.
- Massage example (a $100 massage, $30 hard cost):
  - Offer a partner business three massages to sell for at least $300 (the floor protects lead quality). The partner can charge $500 and keep it all.
  - Your cost: 3 x $30 = $90 for a pre-paid, qualified customer. There are no ads, landing pages or lead calls, only a calendar handoff.
  - The partner may use it as an upsell or bundle it into a $1,000 package.
  - If one in three converts to your $2,000 offer, cost to acquire a customer is 3 x $90 = $270 for $2,000.
  - Do this with 100 businesses.
- Discount codes: 10% off doesn't change behavior. Discounts need to be 50%+ to really move demand. He gives 100% of a peeled-off piece, not a cut of the main product.

chunks.heading: Use truth and damaging admissions in marketing
chunks.text:
- "Nothing sells like the truth." Authentic advertising means saying what's true, including facts that seem like weaknesses.
- Small businesses can say so:
  - Limited capacity creates scarcity and implies personalization.
  - Many buyers prefer "Buy Local, Buy small business".
- Admit a flaw, then amplify the good. Formula: bad, bad, bad, "but" good. The "but" amplifies the good thing, and the good should be relevant to the admission.
- Examples:
  - Gym with bad parking: "we don't have the biggest parking lot" or "more equipment than the guys down the street", but members will have so much fun they won't care.
  - A gym owner who was not in great shape: "I'm not the most in-shape guy... even though I like donuts a lot still", but the gym is fun and delivers results.
- Telling a less exciting truth first makes your second claim more believable.
- If people will find out anyway, control the narrative. He compares it to Eminem in 8 Mile saying all the negatives first, so no one else can use them.
- "The hardest thing in all of marketing is getting someone to believe you." Trust building is one of the best ad investments, and truth is the "only long-term strategy".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi explains how to go from zero to first income: work for free for qualified people, use the Core Four to promote, the CLOSER framework to sell, and volume (rule of 100) to improve. He also covers money models, mindset around fear, criticism and focus, and why active income beats speculation.

chunks.heading: Starting a business: sequence, skills first, investing last
chunks.text:
- Alex says the common mistake is conflating sequence. Many people believe making money comes from investing, but "investing is the last thing you do, not the first thing you do."
- He argues active income funds the bets. The people with the most money typically have very high incomes, and the excess cash flow lets them take riskier swings.
- Example: his neighbor owns Panda Express, with about $3.7 billion in revenue and about a 27% net margin. Alex says that is about $935 million in personal income, built over 45 years. The neighbor can take big bets because of that regular cash.
- He rejects "active vs passive" as a false binary. He thinks in "money per unit of time," and says nothing is truly passive (a passive deal means looking at about 100 deals first).
- He dislikes speculative investing as the "greater fool theory." If you don't know the variables, "you are 100% gambling." Retail investors usually hear about things at the peak.
- Rule: "the more it feels like luck is usually where you should have your first red flag." He believes that if you control the variables, you can predict the outcome.
- He says to build income skills first. A business is track (promote), convert (sell), deliver. He says you can build something very big in about 5 to 7 years, but most people spend those years "reliving the same 30 days."
- His five stages: uninformed optimism, informed pessimism, valley of despair, informed optimism, achievement. At stage three, people either jump to a new thing (back to stage one) or stay in the pain and learn. "Staying in the pain is what gives you the catalyst to learn how to get out of pain."

chunks.heading: Picking what to sell: the three Ps, services first, four steps to a business
chunks.text:
- He says most businesses come from one of three Ps: Passion (inherent interest), Profession (what you are already paid for), or Pain (a problem you lived through, e.g. a mom making non-allergenic food for her kids).
- Profession is the fastest route. You already have something valuable, so you only add promotion and conversion.
- He prefers that most people start with services. He cites that 78% of US businesses are service-based. They are the easiest to start (you trade time for money) and the lowest risk.
- Four steps to a business:
  1. Form an LLC.
  2. Open a bank account.
  3. Connect a payment processor.
  4. Ask a stranger to do something in exchange for money.
- "First rule of entrepreneurship is use what you got." Starting is the perfect condition. He calls waiting for the perfect pick the "fallacy of the perfect pick": every path has trade-offs, and you must decide what you are willing to give up.
- Myth 3 he names: overbelief in the idea and underbelief in execution. The idea doesn't have to be the next Facebook.
- Keep your job if you have a family or a mortgage. Use the "5 to 9" (5-9am and 5-9pm). Quit when side income surpasses the job income, and he suggests sustaining that for 6 months, since there will be volatility.

chunks.heading: Getting the first customers: warm outreach, 10 by 10, and the price ladder
chunks.text:
- Start with warm outreach. Look through your phone contacts (e.g. 400) and Facebook friends (e.g. 300). Send a personal video or text saying what you're doing and what you solve, and ask "do you know anybody?" He says you are not asking friends to buy. About 90% of the time the responder says "you could do that for me."
- "Consistency is the currency of credibility." Referrers risk their social capital, so show you're still doing it.
- Add risk reversal: "I'm doing the first 10 for free" to get testimonials, reviews and learning.
- "10 by 10": give 10 people 10 hours of free one-on-one work (or 5 people for 5 hours). It works because even minimum-wage labor has value, and you iterate fast with no tech setup. Build the website or write the copy in front of them.
- Call script:
  1. In the first call, ask what they want to solve and ask permission to tell them what you do at the end.
  2. At the last hour, recap the progress and ask if they're happy.
  3. Use the hours to gather other problems you could solve.
  4. Pitch a longer engagement (e.g. "problems 1, 2 and 3, maybe 6 months").
- Reciprocity builds up. If they say no on the first call, don't continue.
- Qualify with BANT, which he says IBM figured out about 70 years ago: Budget, Authority, Need, Timing. He notes timeshares use roughly six-hour blocks because trust takes time.
- On not wanting to work for free: "I actually think it's entitlement." "You're not working for free. You're learning and then you're earning." Set terms: feedback during the work and a review in three formats, plus a video and a text version. He says a glowing review is worth more than $1,000 long term.
- Pricing: once demand exceeds your time, say "if you want, you can pay." Then "bump the price by 20% every five people until eventually people stop saying yes."
- He names supply and demand and leverage as the two forces he's most moved by. Free work creates artificial demand.

chunks.heading: Core Four, CLOSER, and the Rule of 100
chunks.text:
- Core Four, the only four ways one person can promote:
  1. Warm outreach (one-on-one, people you know).
  2. Cold outreach (one-on-one, strangers).
  3. Posting content (one-to-many).
  4. Paid ads (one-to-many).
- Higher-leverage ways come after: customers who bring customers, affiliates/partners, employees, and agencies. But "everyone must start with the core four."
- CLOSER sales framework:
  - **C**larify: why did they respond?
  - **L**abel: name the problem ("so what I'm hearing is...").
  - **O**verview past experiences: what have you tried, what worked, what didn't. This is the pain cycle, which increases short-term motivation.
  - **S**ell the vacation, not the plane flight. Keep it under about 320 words. Use three points, each with a short anecdote.
  - **E**xplain away concerns after asking for the sale.
  - **R**einforce the decision. He added this later: people judge a business by the first 24 hours after purchase. Restate next steps and tie them to their goals.
- The five concerns, each a fallacy in decision-making:
  - Timing is really priorities.
  - Money is really value.
  - Decision-maker means they need support, not permission (use past agreements, e.g. "your husband knows you're overweight, does he want you to stay that way?").
  - Stall: help them decide.
  - Preferences: "if you change the variables, you change the outcome."
- After each explanation, ask again if it solves that concern, then ask if they're ready to move forward.
- Rule of 100: do 100 per day of either 100 minutes of posting content, $100 a day on ads, or 100 outreaches. Do all three if you want.
- Volatility is "a symptom of insufficient volume." If 700 efforts yield one sale a week, then 700 a day yields about a sale a day. Alex says that compression is what separates small businesses from large ones.
- Story: an influencer told him he wasn't doing anything wrong, "you're just doing too little." He had 4 posts a day on Instagram, 10 on LinkedIn, and 70 to 80 a day total, while Alex posted about every other day.
- Improvement loop: do about 100 reps, find the top 10% (best response, views, clicks), work out what differed, and repeat it in the next 100.

chunks.heading: Persuasion, imposter syndrome, and fear of selling
chunks.text:
- Selling is "arranging the variables to increase the likelihood a sale occurs." The difference between helping and manipulation is intention.
- His persuasion rule: "state the facts and tell the truth." Imposter feelings come from misrepresenting. Once you've done about 20 reps, your conviction rises because you can say "I've done 20 of these."
- Use damaging admissions. In the gym space he told owners with bad parking and old equipment to say so in the ad: "we have the best workouts on this side of the Mississippi."
- Every position has an advantage. When he ran Gym Launch and a software company (Alan, sold in 2021), he told smaller agencies to pitch "you get the CEO, not account rep number 77." Compare the person you'll actually work with, not company size.
- Don't claim to be a one-stop shop. If the facts aren't compelling enough, "do the free work so the facts are compelling."
- Some of the best deals are the ones you never do. Setting expectations up front makes cleaner relationships.
- Fear of rejection: the worst they can say is no. Sales is like dating, a numbers game. The Rule of 100 habituates you, like exposure therapy for phobias.
- Fear of judgment: most people are fine with sucking but not with being judged for it. Name whose voice is in your head.
  - Example: when selling his company for $46.2 million, he realized only "Tom" would judge it as not enough. "If you don't know why you believe what you believe, it's not your belief, it's someone else's."
  - Criticism is a fixed cost: you get criticized if you do nothing and if you do something.
  - It takes about 20 hours to become proficient at most things.
  - Listen to the people closest to your goals, not closest to you.
  - "Fear is a mile wide and an inch deep" (he credits Leila Hormozi).
  - Play out the specific worst case to defuse catastrophizing.
  - Hate translates to "he lives his life in a way that I would not prefer."
- Also: if someone earns more than you, they know something you don't. Use comparison for study, not envy. Separate criticism (gap between expected and actual) from insults.

chunks.heading: Money Models book, value equation, and the economic unit
chunks.text:
- *$100M Money Models* is the third book in the $100M series, after Offers (what to sell) and Leads (how to promote). Alex says he began it in 2019 and has not publicly discussed these structures.
- Definition: a money model is "the core economic unit of the business," a deliberate sequence of offers. Its financial goal is to collect enough cash from one customer in the first 30 days to acquire and serve two more customers.
- Four objectives:
  1. Get more people interested (attraction offers, e.g. buy X get Y free, giveaways).
  2. Get them to spend more.
  3. Get them to spend faster (pull cash flow forward).
  4. Get them to buy again and again (recurring, like a membership, or reoccurring, like Coca-Cola).
- You only need one to start, and he'd start with an attraction offer. The book details five structures that he says he has used.
- Why it matters: "when you have a superior money model, it gives you padding to be bad at everything else." Advertising, sales and offer quality can be weaker, and the cash flow lets you pay down your ignorance debt.
- Alex says the businesses that were exceptionally successful, compared with moderately successful ones, had a better money model.
- Value equation (from Offers):
  - Bigger dream outcome raises value.
  - Higher perceived likelihood of achievement raises value.
  - Shorter time delay raises value.
  - Less effort and sacrifice raises value.

chunks.heading: Feedback, volume, and focus: how he improves and works
chunks.text:
- Behaviorist view: people do things because they were rewarded for them in the past. Explanations beat descriptions ("Timmy is dishonest" is circular).
- Example: an exec who threatened to quit over a title change had never left despite many title changes, so the threat was low risk.
- Education means "same condition, new behavior." Intelligence means rate of learning. If your day looks the same every day, you've learned nothing.
- Good feedback is fast and specific. Story: a high-performing director described as "a dick" didn't change after four talks. Alex stripped out the judgment and asked what behaviors caused it (interrupting, telling people how to do their jobs). He gave a script ("I heard this thing, mind if I share it?") and the change was visible in a week.
- Don't dig for the past narrative. Ask what to do instead under these conditions, like fixing a pickleball serve. He defines trauma as a permanent behavior change from an aversive stimulus, which can be good or bad.
- Push vs pivot: pivot if a need-to-be-true assumption proves false. Push if conditions hold and it's a skill gap. Commitment is "the elimination of alternatives." He cites Naval: "it's not 10,000 hours, it's 10,000 iterations."
- Learn fast with full shutdown days: he finished a web page by noon on a weekend he'd put off for weeks. "Fear is a mile wide and an inch deep. So is ignorance."
- Productivity: "do nothing except for the task you set out to achieve." He gets better results through elimination. His setup is a good night's sleep, knowing what he'll start the day before, caffeine, double earplugs, and a windowless room.
- Fear, inverted thinking: list all the ways to kill your business, then flip them (he credits Charlie Munger). Find a concrete fallback (e.g. a friend's couch for 6 months).
- Seasons: "deleting work life balance for a season nets you more work life balance over a lifetime." He cites Paul Graham's idea that you can endure a million dollars of pain over 40 years or crunch it into four.
- Action beats listening: "if someone just listens to the episode, tomorrow will be the same for you." His example action is recording a selfie video and texting it to 100 people.
- Final five:
  - Best advice: "Do so much work it would be unreasonable for you not to be successful."
  - Worst advice: "Follow your passion."
  - Wish he'd known sooner: find people better than you and help them first.
  - Lesson that took too long: "Focus. One thing all in."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi walks through how to go from zero to six figures: pick one channel, one product, one avatar, start a service business from what you already know, and treat early income as education. He covers his gym story, front-loaded offers, why investing in skills beats the S&P 500, and his content vendor-to-in-house playbook.

chunks.heading: How he prices and uses a cheap book for distribution
chunks.text:
- Alex priced the book "100 Million Dollar Offers" at 99 cents on Amazon. The goal was not book income but putting it in as many hands as possible.
- His reasoning: Amazon pushes products that make money, and a 99-cent book is easy to sell and taps Amazon's traffic. At 99 cents Amazon takes two-thirds of revenue; at 2.99 he would get two-thirds.
- He says a paid book beats a free one because there is "a difference between a customer and a voyeur".
- The book still earns about 60,000 a month, which he calls irrelevant next to his income (his top employee makes a million plus a year).
- The long-term play is inbound deal flow to acquisition.com in about five years: people who consumed his content, grew to 3, 5, 10 or 20 million, and now want to work with him.
- He opens content with "I have nothing to sell you" because early commenters accused him of selling a course. He says this was an accident, not planned positioning.

chunks.heading: Zero to six figures: how to start a business
chunks.text:
- Six figures is "literally just sell something to someone": one channel, one product, one avatar.
- Seven figures is the same thing plus "consistently". Run whatever got you customers (outreach, content, paid ads, affiliates, referrals) consistently. A million a year is only about 20K a week.
- One to three million is mostly raising the main channel's output slightly, baseline efficiencies, and building a core team. The owner usually gets out of delivery, with one or two competent people and a handful of frontline staff (roughly 5-15 employees, only about 2 good ones).
- Three to ten million is where his company takes people on. The minimum bar is three boxes: product-market fit, at least one reliable acquisition channel, and a core team in place, even if dysfunctional.
- Employees see top line as income. A 10M business may pay its owner only around 1M. Early on you are still an employee of your own business wearing all the hats.
- Sequence: pick one of the five ways to advertise, do it consistently, decide what to sell (what the offers book covers), sell it, then break delivery into chunks so five people each do 20% of what you do, rather than finding someone to "do what I do".

chunks.heading: Finding what to sell and why service businesses come first
chunks.text:
- Everybody knows something. He uses three buckets: your parents' jobs (knowledge absorbed by osmosis), your past jobs, and your current interests. Pick the bucket where you can solve a problem that makes someone the most money or that they value most.
- He cites Y Combinator weighting past industry experience because of the "ignorance debt" of knowing nothing about an industry.
- Favors people ask you for are a signal of what you can later charge for.
- Most entrepreneurs have "a graveyard of failures"; only Bezos had a first business become the most valuable. Don't start believing it's the one thing for life, which he calls an employee fallacy.
- "Once you start taking steps, the next step becomes illuminated." Planning 100 steps ahead is irrelevant because "chaos is going to break your plan anyways".
- He favors service businesses to start: lowest risk, no capital, just your time (e.g. cleaning houses, lawn care).
- No novel idea needed: look at what everyone else does and do it better. Look at what people hate (slow dry cleaning, messy lawn trimmings).
- You trade time for money "to learn, not to earn". Most of the value of early income is education, paying down ignorance debt.

chunks.heading: His own path: free pilot, online coaching, then the gym
chunks.text:
- Last year of consulting, age 23: he ran the "free training project". Clients donated 500-1,000 to a charity of their choice instead of paying him, and let him use their before/after pictures and testimonials. He ended up with about 12 strong before/afters.
- He then asked those clients to pay the same amount to "the charity of Alex". All he needed was an LLC, a bank account and a PayPal account.
- Months later (2013) he posted publicly with a website and testimonials, signed about 20 guys at 200 a month (about 4,000 a month). Fulfillment was 4 hours every Saturday updating programs, macros and meal plans, delivered by text.
- He hated doing the same delivery daily, so instead of doing more of it he decided to own a gym.
- He chose between three ideas: a test prep company, a frozen yogurt business (250K to start, which he lacked) and fitness. The test prep plan collapsed after a miscommunication with a professor partner who used the materials without him.
- He emailed 40 gym owners offering to apprentice free. One replied, and Alex paid 10K to join his mastermind before owning a gym. He worked there 4 AM to 4 PM for about 12 weeks, learning sales, email lists and the full customer life cycle.
- He argues small businesses teach more than corporate roles because you see the whole life cycle end to end.
- He spent roughly 50K of savings fitting out a facility and took a 5,000-a-month lease. He calls it the riskiest thing he has done.
- His fallback plans: a business school story, or stripping at night and driving Uber (he estimated 250K a year). After learning to sell, his baseline rose to car sales at around 400K a year.

chunks.heading: Launch offer, Facebook ads and structuring the front-end program
chunks.text:
- Two weeks before opening he spent 3,000 on a weekend Facebook ads workshop (2013). It was the only reason the gym worked; his mentor's Groupon strategy failed for him in a competitive Orange County market.
- First ads: about 1,000 spent, 27 sign-ups in two weeks at 300 each (about 8,700), which paid the first month's rent. He had an empty gym with turf and a table.
- The offer was a six-week challenge: lose 20 pounds in six weeks or get your money back. About 80% succeeded.
- The core was food: meal plan, grocery list, prep instructions, eating-out guides, plus gym sessions (five days a week, later three).
- The close for people who hit it: "Do you think working out six weeks and then going back to not working out is a good long-term solution?" He credited the 300 toward a year, often selling the year halfway through the challenge.
- His principle: define a front-end program with a specific outcome and timeline. It works as onboarding, and you can charge roughly three to four times more than on a recurring basis, which pays back acquisition cost faster. He has used this in almost every business.
- He did about 4,000 sales consults before consuming any sales training.
- Growth: 5K a month at start, 35K a month by month nine, gym outsourced so he only managed it. By month 15 he took profit to open gym two (pre-launched at full capacity), then locations three to five.

chunks.heading: Buying education, skill stacking and the earn-vs-invest argument
chunks.text:
- On paid courses: you can learn it on YouTube; you pay for speed, troubleshooting and someone who has already made the mistakes.
- He paid a coach 750 an hour for 8 sessions (about 5,600) to learn retargeting, and used them to learn how the expert thinks while he clicked the buttons himself.
- Skills stack and multiply: ads for gyms alone could make 10-20K a month with no employees; adding sales made it a 100K-a-month skill. Running ads, working the leads and selling them himself, he made 100K a month with no employees working 14-hour days.
- He argues investing in your ability to earn beats the S&P 500 for most people. His example: a minimum-wage worker spends 500 on a two-day phlebotomy certification and goes from 7 to 25 an hour, versus saving 500 to earn a few dollars a year in an index fund.
- "They don't have an investing problem, they have an income problem."
- He notes 4% inflation compounding means 4 million at retirement is worth about 1 million today.
- On college: 2,000 a month on a Mastermind or skill course for 6 months each (ads, selling, courses) returns more than a four-year degree. He gives an example of a friend who used student loans to buy rentals.
- He says 88% of his followers (from his site survey) want to start a business.

chunks.heading: Scaling model: turnkey, licensing and the content engine
chunks.text:
- Stagnating with the gyms, he joined an internet mastermind and was told to teach others how to fill gyms. He moved to a turnkey model: fly out, run marketing and sales, and keep 100% of the cash collected, with no employees (about 100K a month, 30 employees later at four times the gym revenue).
- After losing money twice and selling the gyms, he moved to a licensing model in 2017. The first year did 7 million and the next 26 million, with headcount going from 8 to about 30.
- Gyms are a great learning vehicle (many sales reps, a service business with heavy headcount) but a limited vehicle for money. Someone who runs a multi-seven-figure gym can run a 10 million business elsewhere.
- Content: his YouTube costs about a dollar per subscriber per year versus over a dollar per subscriber in AdSense. YouTube earns about 41-42K a month; his wife Layla's about 6-7K. Content spend is around 100K a month.
- Team: four in-house plus vendors for podcast, LinkedIn, YouTube and shorts/TikTok/Reels. He still does Twitter himself.
- His outsourcing playbook: find the best person already doing it, pay whatever to get them, say upfront the intent is to take it in-house, hire an interface person with the skill, then split volume half vendor and half in-house, and "when the in-house person beats the vendor you fire the vendor".
- His team sends video ideas with talking points drawn from his other videos; he picks three and uses them as a loose outline.
- He wants content that is both wide and deep, e.g. reframing sales as "persuasion" to widen the audience.
- Targets: 10 billion, with the mission to make real business education available to everyone. He plans bigger media investment, majority acquisitions of companies in his portfolio (e.g. an accounting firm held in-house), and says he spends about 5% of what he earns while keeping large cash reserves.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Hormozi explains how he built sales systems after thousands of in-person gym sales: compress the script, drill it until reps breathe it, ask questions instead of making statements, and fix show-up rates through availability and speed. He also covers team incentives, culture, and why fewer, better things make communities stick.

chunks.heading: Closing is a decision, not a sale: Alex's sales philosophy
chunks.text:
- Alex learned sales by doing, not studying. He took roughly 4,000 sales before he found out sales training existed. He ran Facebook ads from 2013, got cheap leads, and for four to five years took about 20 in-person consults a day at his gyms.
