- Diagnostic test: if your cost to acquire a customer rises faster than CPMs in your market, word of mouth is working against you.
- Alex says you have far more detractors than you think. People who see your ad ask others about you and then decide not to buy. Conversion drops and owners blame ads when "the invisible hand of your product sucking" is the cause.

chunks.heading: Brand as a promise-keeping loop
chunks.text:
- Brand loop: you make a promise, you keep it, and the people you kept it for tell others.
- Marketers who launch a new business or offer every six months are "so front-end obsessed". Alex's warning sign: the same person changing offers every six months can't keep promises. They lack product, delivery, and the ability to recruit, hire and manage a team that delivers. Their reputation degrades over time.
- Pure direct-response marketers who arbitrage media across the "ocean of humanity" for one transaction have a cash-flow job, not a business.
- Brand is "the associations that people have with your product". Positive associations let you charge more for the same thing, because perceived likelihood of achievement rises and perceived risk falls. Customers pay a premium even if your time delay is slower.
- Brand-driven advertising is slower but far more profitable than pure direct response. He puts ROAS at "30x, 100x" versus 2x or 3x, and cites Apple as printing money from customers who trust it to deliver.
- Gym Launch example: about a year in, he launched "automated lead nurture" (ALN) with a big webinar. Gym owners who missed the live event sent credit card numbers anyway, saying that if he launched it, it was good. He wanted that to be the norm, which reinforced keeping promises.

chunks.heading: Widen the gap between value, price and cost with "100 BBs"
chunks.text:
- Keep three lines in view: the price you charge, the value they get, and the cost to deliver. Make all of them as far apart as possible: very high value, a premium price, and plenty of margin over cost.
- You create that gap by doing the hundred small details competitors won't do. He says "no silver bullets, 100 BBs".
- Restaurant examples he gives:
  - Learn the customer's name and greet them by it.
  - Waitresses write the name on the receipt.
  - Water within 30 seconds of sitting down.
  - Bread within two minutes.
  - Check-ins at a tested cadence.
  - Ask whether it's a fast dinner or a leisurely one, and match the customer's cadence. Asking may itself improve the experience.
- "Your competition is lazy as fuck." Many customers are "a hair away from being detractors". Example: his pool guy was inconsistent, Alex kept paying out of hassle, and he told a neighbor not to use him.

chunks.heading: The cookie business: spend a year on the product before scaling
chunks.text:
- A friend visited top cookie bakers around the country to learn how they baked. Some said no and some let him hang out.
- Back home he baked a new dozen cookies every day for a year, numbered the 365 batches, and gave them to tasters for feedback.
- The free tasting also collected phone numbers and leads in his area.
- He then opened a premium cookie store in a local market and it was a smashing success, because he "spent 365 days doing the work to figure out the hundred tiny details that make a perfect cookie".
- Alex's lesson: whatever your business (sandwiches, SEO, mechanic work), find what makes the cookie better. "That's the work that no one's willing to do, and that's the good news."
- Once the second batch was good, the goal wasn't more volume. It was refining product and service, onboarding, recruiting, hiring and training so quality holds at scale or improves.
- Alex says a sandwich shop with mediocre sandwiches stays stuck hunting for a new hook. The offer gets people in the door (he wrote a book on offers, important early), but delivery keeps them paying and referring.

chunks.heading: Phase one: learn, not earn
chunks.text:
- "The point in the first phase is to learn, not to earn."
- Run only enough advertising to test and fix the product. He would stay at a revenue level until, for example, "referrals over 30%".
- If he started a cleaning business tomorrow, year one would be about nailing the model so no one leaves. His example: sell ten customers a month, retain all, and you have 10, 20, 30, 40. "If you do not lose customers, your business will not stop growing."
- Product progress pays off with a delay. Sales and lead improvements show an immediate jump, which is addictive, but "the monster money comes from the back end."
- Improving the product is the highest-leverage move because everyone gets it: "cut once, sell a hundred times". Marketing is linear, so each extra customer costs more marketing.
- He calls entrepreneurship "more a battle of wills than a battle of intellect". You must delay gratification and "eat glass" through the failures until the product is right.
- Reason to wait: businesses that grow only by jamming sales and marketing slow down, even at $10M, $30M or $100M and far from their market. Buyers pay 20x or 50x multiples only for businesses they trust to compound. A business that depends on marketing "is only as good as its last month".

chunks.heading: Measure what drives retention: activation points
chunks.text:
- Product metrics to track: the price you can command, number of repeat purchases or orders per lifetime, and churn for subscriptions or memberships.
- Inputs are activation metrics. Method:
  1. Take the cohort of customers who don't cancel.
  2. Run a regression-style analysis of what happened to them that didn't happen to others.
  3. Treat those events as your first guess at activation (retention) points.
  4. Drive onboarding toward them, then re-measure.
- Examples: for an SEO agency, if landing a sale from SEO sharply cuts cancellation, onboarding should get clients a sale quickly. For weight loss, if losing seven pounds in the first two weeks predicts staying, focus onboarding on that.
- Product-led repeat example: many $100M Offers readers bought his second book. The first book still sells thousands of copies every month with no advertising. Alex says the books sell nearly $1M a month without advertising, driven by readers posting and telling friends.
- Don't trust "because" explanations without data. He asks "How do you know that?" and ignores gut feel. Many owners misattribute success: the gym owners who thought their music and layout mattered, when being the only gym within five miles was the real driver. He quotes Stanford's Professor Burgelman: "It's better to know why you have failed than to succeed and not know why."

Here’s how I made $100,000 in 30 days starting with only $1,000 to my name:

1) I reached out to local gym owners, since it was what I knew. But any small local business would work. 

2) I asked them if how many clients they could handle without changing anything about their capacity.

3) I asked them if I could fill up that capacity for them. They wouldn’t have to do anything but let me. Zero work. Zero capital. Zero time. 

4) But here was the deal: I would front the work. I’d work the leads. I’d close the sales. Then they’d have to deliver the package I sold them for free. But after that point, they’d have the entire LTV of a customer they got for free (or on COGS technically). 

5) “I’ll fill your gym for free in 30 days” became the offer. 

6) I had $1000 in my checking account and a credit card. I put the ads in my credit card and started calling leads. 

7) The leads cost me $5. I’d close 1/5 on a $500 package. Getting me 25:1 return on ad spend.

8) I spent $1000 in the first 7 days. Made back $25,000. Then spent another $1000 per week after that.

9) At the end of the first month, I made $100,000 starting with only $1000 in my bank account.

It’s actually what I did to comeback from the dead (twice actually).

It helped me a ton, so I figured I'd share it.

I hope you find it valuable:

Most of my successful friends use text like email.

To expect an immediate response is to assume that you are more important than their goals.

Which, if you do, you won’t stay friends for long.

A lot of young leaders think that the point of their job is to keep everyone on their team happy, when in fact, it’s to keep the best people on their team happy.

And allow the rest to rise to the occasion or weed themselves out.

Yes - that means low performers will whine.
It also doesn’t matter.

Society only considers something charity if it hurts the giver.

Ex: if a business makes a product that helps people, and makes money, it’s not charity.

If they give it for free, to fewer people, it’s charity.

If you’re a billionaire, nothing you do is charity because you don’t make yourself broke in the process. You either give too little or nothing at all. Both make you worthy of criticism.

Tough.

Success is rarely one big idea. It’s usually one thousand tiny details you figure out one at a time over years of trial and error.

One-at-a-fucking-time…for. years.

If you have < $10,000 saved up, don’t buy crypto.

Buy the ability to make more money. 

Then you can restart the game as many times as you want.

I’ve noticed a lot of business lessons I need to relearn at each level. 

How I started:

Focus on one thing
Hire smart people
Think long term

Each of these lessons I’ve had to relearn as companies scaled because:

Focus is even harder when opportunities grow like weeds. They must be trimmed.

What you think smart looks like at $100k per year is very different from what smart looks like at $100M per year.

What feels like long term thinking when you start out is a quarter and eventually becomes multiple years (or decades).

Some lessons are like wine - they age and develop with time.

If you’re an entrepreneur, you need to memorize this response:

“That’s an amazing idea. It’s not a priority right now. But I will add it to our big ideas list. Thank you for sharing it.”

Businesses rarely die from a lack of good ideas. They die from a lack of good execution.

How to *actually* make something happen faster:

1) go from weekly meetings to first thing & last thing daily
2) eliminate team’s unrelated tasks
3) check in every hour or two
4) make progress front and center for all to see
5) put a big pot of gold at the end when it happens

To get leads in any niche:

1) Make something good

2) Advertise it

3) Trade it for contact info

To make money:

1) Follow up with them

2) Offer them:

A) More of that thing you gave for free 

OR 

B) More help using that thing

For more leads, do more step 2 or make 1 better

Excellence comes from sucking. 
Then doing it again.
Trying to suck less. 
Still sucking. 
But doing a little better. 
Then trying again. 
And you keep trying until there’s nothing that sucks about what you do at all.
Then you’ll be “good.”
And people will ask u how it came easy.

The cost of ignorance is easy to quantify but hard to comprehend.

The cost of not knowing how to get what you want is the value of the thing you want.

And that education costs time and money.

You pay with the one you value least.

You win by outlasting your competition, not beating them head to head.

You wait for them to give up, not for them give in.

Otherwise, you’re only scoring a made up goal on a made up timeline with rules that never existed to begin with.

Entrepreneurs often think that to grow they need to hire more people - but there are so many more times I’ve found I need to trade bad people for better people, or raise expectations on the people I have (while supporting by deleting irrelevant work that somehow always expands).
Despite what the internet would have you believe, you should learn how to make money before trying to learn how to make your money, make you money.

The life you want is on the other side of a few hard conversations.

And you’re living a life you hate because you’re too afraid to have them.

The difference between a $1M and a $10M business is something barely working to something kinda working.

And the difference between a $10M business and a $100M is something kinda working to something actually working.

But everytime it takes work to go from one to the next.
You’ll build a bigger brand making content for 6 months off a decade of experience than you will off a decade of content with only 6 months of experience.

Brand is simple to understand but hard to do.

Think of the most aspirational outcome your ideal customer wants.

Associate with closer and closer versions of that outcome.

If you don’t stop, your brand eventually becomes synonymous with the aspiration itself.

Then, stay there.

In business, I find it’s more profitable to focus on what’s practical rather than what’s principled.

If someone wrongs you, it may be right to do something about it. But practically, it costs you more in time & attention than the cost for the wrong doing.

Salespeople are paid so well because they’re willing to deal with rejection.

They’re able to get socially punched in the face a hundred times a day and still come back for more with a smile.
Saving money won’t make you money, but it will give you the security to think farther out and take bigger risks…which will absolutely make you more money.
